The discussion concerning the letters that occur at the opening of this surah is like the discussion concerning Alif-Lam-Mim.

The phrase ﴿from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ is the predicate about it. The word ﴿a Book﴾ is an apposition (*badal*) to ﴿a revelation﴾. The resulting meaning is: the revelation from God is a Book, whose verses are made distinct, characterized as an Arabic Qur'an. From this construction it follows that the Qur'an is sent down from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, made distinct, in Arabic.

You may also treat ﴿from the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ as a qualifier of the subject, and make ﴿a Book﴾ the predicate of the subject. Under both analyses this is a majestic style, and a similar one has already occurred in God's words ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad﴾ [al-A'raf: 1] ﴿A Book sent down to you﴾ [al-A'raf: 2].

The intended meaning is that it is sent down. The verbal noun (*masdar*) here carries the sense of the passive participle, as in God's words ﴿And indeed it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 192] ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 193]. This is an intensification of the statement that God Himself caused it to be sent down, affirming that it is revealed and not copied from the scriptures of earlier peoples.

*Kitab* (book) is the name for a collection of letters indicating meaningful words. The Qur'an is called a Book because God revealed its words and commanded His Messenger ﷺ to write down what was revealed to him. For this reason the Messenger ﷺ appointed scribes who wrote down everything of the Qur'an that was revealed to him.

The choice of the two attributes ﴿the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ over other lofty attributes indicates that this revelation is a mercy from God to His servants, to bring them out of darkness into light. Compare God's words ﴿There has certainly come to you clear proof from your Lord, and guidance and mercy﴾ [al-An'am: 157], and ﴿We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 107], and ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book, which is recited to them? Indeed in this is mercy and a reminder for a people who believe﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 51].

The combination of the two attributes ﴿the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ indicates that mercy is an essential attribute of God, and that its object extends throughout creation, as was explained at the beginning of Surah al-Fatiha and the basmala.

In this there is also an indication of the foolishness of those who turned away from being guided by this Book: they turned away from mercy. Those who were guided by it are the people of mercy, as God says afterwards: ﴿Say: It is, for those who believe, guidance and healing; and as for those who do not believe, there is deafness in their ears, and it is blindness for them﴾ [Fussilat: 44].

The meaning of ﴿its verses are made distinct﴾ is that they are made clear. *Tafsil* (distinction, detailed exposition) means clarification and freedom from ambiguity.

The intended meaning is that the verses of the Qur'an have clear purposes, and are not ambiguous except to someone obstinate, regarding the indication of each verse of its intended meaning, its placement, and the distinguishing of one from another in meaning according to the different branches of rhetorical meaning that they contain. This was mentioned at the opening of Surah Hud.

Among the perfection of its distinctness is that it was in a language rich in meanings, broad in its branches, and eloquent in its words. It was therefore free from ambiguity of indication and from obscurity of words, while combining abundant non-contradictory meanings with concise structures. Thus describing it as Arabic is one of the things that complete the statement about its distinctness. The praise of the Qur'an from this aspect has been repeated, as in God's words ﴿in a clear Arabic tongue﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 195]. For this reason, the censure of those who turned away from it is consequently stated here: ﴿but most of them turned away, and so they do not hear﴾; and there in God's words ﴿Thus We have caused it to enter the hearts of the criminals. They do not believe in it until they see the painful punishment﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 200–201].

*Al-Qur'an* means the speech that is read and recited. Its being called *Qur'an* is one of the attributes of its perfection: it is easy to memorize and easy to recite, as God said: ﴿And We have indeed made the Qur'an easy for remembrance﴾ [al-Qamar: 17]. For this reason it was the practice of the Messenger ﷺ to memorize the Qur'an by heart, and the practice of the Muslims was to follow him in this according to their resolve and capacity. The Prophet ﷺ used to indicate the superiority of the believers by the amount of Qur'an they had.

On the day of Uhud, those among the martyrs who had memorized the most Qur'an were placed first in the grave, as a reminder of the excellence of memorizing the Qur'an in addition to the excellence of that martyrdom.

The word *Qur'anan* is in the accusative as a detached qualifier (*na't maqta'*) for the purpose of specifically praising it. Otherwise it would be in the nominative, as a third predicate or as a qualifier of the second predicate. The mention of *Qur'anan* is intended to point to this distinction, which it alone holds among all the religious books. Had it not been for this, one would have said: "a Book whose verses are made distinct, Arabic," as God said in Surah al-Shu'ara': ﴿in a clear Arabic tongue﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 195].

You may also treat it as accusative of circumstance (*hal*).

God's words ﴿for a people who know﴾ are a qualifier of *Qur'anan*, a stable adverbial phrase (*zarf mustaqirr*), meaning: existing for a people who know, in view of what the phrase ﴿Arabic Qur'an﴾ conveys of clarity of indication and the brightness of proof. Alternatively, ﴿for a people who know﴾ may be connected to ﴿a revelation﴾ or to ﴿its verses are made distinct﴾, meaning the benefits of its revelation and its distinction are for a people who know, and not for others, so it is as though it was revealed only for them. That is, there is no wonder if the obstinate turn away from understanding it, for they are a people who do not know. This is like God's words ﴿And the signs and warnings do not avail a people who do not believe﴾ [Yunus: 101], and His words ﴿And none understand them except those who have knowledge﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 43], and His words ﴿Indeed We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an, so that you may understand﴾ [Yusuf: 2], and His words ﴿Rather, it is clear signs in the breasts of those who have been given knowledge﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 49].

*Al-Bashir* is the name for one who gives good news, that is, one who informs of news that pleases the one informed. *Al-Nadhir* is one who informs of a frightening matter. The Qur'an is compared to a bringer of good news in what it contains of verses giving glad tidings to righteous believers, and to a warner in what it contains of threat to disbelievers and to the people of sins. Thus the statement is an eloquent comparison. ﴿Bashiran﴾ and ﴿nadhiran﴾ are not active participles (*ism fa'il*), for had that been intended, it would have said *mubashiran* and *mundhiran*.

The combination of *bashiran* and *nadhiran* is of the kind of rhetorical embellishment called *tibaq* (antithesis).

The combination of ﴿bashiran﴾ as a second circumstantial accusative (*hal thaniya*) of *Kitab*, or as a qualifier of *Qur'anan*. A qualifier of a circumstance is in meaning a circumstance, and the preferable reading is that it is a second circumstance.

The phrase ﴿nadhiran﴾ is introduced with a conjunctive *wa* (and) to draw attention to the difference in the position of each of the two circumstances: it is a bringer of good news to one group, namely those who followed it, and a warner to others, namely those who turn away from it. It is not that it combines good news and warning for a single group. Thus the *wa* here is like the *wa* in God's words ﴿previously married and virgins﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5], after God's words ﴿submissive, believing, obedient, repentant, worshipping, and travelling﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5].

The result of ﴿but most of them turned away﴾ follows from what has been mentioned of the attributes of the Qur'an. The pronoun in ﴿most of them﴾ refers to what is known from the context, namely the polytheists, as is the habit of the Qur'an in more than one place.

The meaning is: most of these people turned away from what is in the Qur'an of guidance, and so they were not guided; and from its good news, and so they were not concerned with it; and from its warning, and so they did not beware of it. Thus they were in the utmost foolishness, for they were not concerned with good, nor did they beware of evil, and so they did not take precautions for themselves. It does not refer back to ﴿a people who know﴾, because none of those who know turns away.

The *fa'* in God's words ﴿so they do not hear﴾ indicates a consequence of the turning away: that is, they do not lend their ears to the Qur'an, let alone reflect upon it. This is a summary of their turning away.

The placement of the subject ﴿they﴾ before the verbal predicate in ﴿so they do not hear﴾, rather than saying ﴿so they do not hear﴾ without it, serves to strengthen and emphasize the judgment.

The conjunction of "they said" (*wa-qalū*) is either coordinated with "so he turned away" (*fa-aʿraḍa*) in verse 4, or it is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from "most of them" (*aktharuhum*) in verse 4, or it is coordinated with "they do not hear" (*lā yasmaʿūna*), or it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in that phrase. The meaning is that they turned away while openly declaring their indifference and taking up a stance of harshness and hostility.

This is a detailed account of the turning away from the attributes by which the Qur'an was described, which are supposed to bring them closer to receiving it, not to make them distance themselves and turn away. The detail is given through their statements, which deprived them of benefiting from the Qur'an one by one, as you will see.

"The hearts" (*al-qulūb*) here means the intellects. This is expressed in their own idiom, since they use "heart" to mean intellect.

*Akinna* is the plural of *kinān*, like *ghiṭāʾ* and *aghiya* in both form and meaning. Coverings were attributed to their hearts by way of *takhyīl* (imaginative representation, attributing to a thing features that belong to something else in order to evoke it), and the hearts were likened to covered things by way of the implicit metaphor (*istiʿāra makniyya*, where the comparison is left implicit). The point of resemblance is the prevention of the call from reaching their intellects, just as a cover or sheath prevents one from grasping what lies beneath it.

What "he calls them to" (*mā tadʿūnā ilayhi*) includes everything he called them to of the matters signified and their proofs, among them the proof of the Qur'an's inimitability and what it contains of the proof that the Messenger ﷺ was unlettered, such as God's saying: ﴿You did not recite any Book before it, nor did you write one with your right hand﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 48].

[Page 234]

The hearts were described as being "in coverings" to convey the meaning of the preposition *fī* ("in"), which denotes that the container encompasses what is contained. Likewise, deafness (*waqr*) was described as being in the hearts, to convey that it penetrates their perception.

The *min* in "from what you call us to" (*mimmā tadʿūnā ilayhi*) has the sense of *ʿan* ("from" or "about"), as in God's saying: ﴿Woe to those whose hearts are hardened against the remembrance of God﴾ [al-Zumar: 22], and as in the saying "We were indeed heedless of this." The meaning is: their hearts are in coverings, so they are far from what you call them to, and it does not penetrate to them.

*Al-waqr*, with a fatḥa on the waw, is heaviness of hearing, which is deafness. It seems the lexicographers took it from *al-wiqr*, with a kasra on the waw, which means a load, because a load weighs down a beast and prevents it from moving. They applied it to the non-movement of hearing when a sound strikes it. This usage became so common that it rivaled the literal meaning, so they gave the waw a fatḥa to distinguish the literal from the figurative, just as they distinguished the literal bite (*ʿaḍḍ*) from the bite of time (*ʿaẓẓ al-dahr*, i.e., misfortune) by changing its *ḍād* into a *ẓāʾ*.

The coverings and deafness have already been mentioned in God's saying: ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness﴾ [al-Anʿām: 25], in Surat al-Anʿām and in Surat al-Isrāʾ.

*Al-ḥijāb* is that which screens the visible, such as a wall or a cloth. They applied the name *ḥijāb* to what prevents their souls from embracing the religion the Prophet ﷺ brought, out of aversion to his religion and reluctance to adopt it. The shared feature is that a barrier comes between the seer and the seen, so neither sees the other nor reaches them. What they intend is to disavow it.

He depicted the deafness of their hearts to accepting Islam and believing in it by the state of things that are in coverings, and the lack of impact of their hearing from his call by the deafness of ears. And the lack of closeness between what they are upon and what he is upon by the stretched barrier between him and them, so there is no meeting and no seeing.

They combined the three states in this depiction to emphasize that they do not accept what he calls them to.

The particle *min* in "and between us and you there is a barrier" (*wa-min bayninā wa-baynika ḥijāb*) is used to strengthen the meaning of the barrier between the two parties and the firm establishment of its implication, which is the distance separating the two parties, because this *min* is an extra particle (*ziyāda*) used to emphasize the content of the sentence.

[Page 235]

The pronoun in *bayninā* refers back to what the pronoun in "most of them" (*aktharuhum*) in verse 4 refers to.

The conjunction in "and between you" (*wa-baynika*) is for emphasis, since the conjunction *wa* already covers it. Most usage of *bayn* is when it is coordinated with a similar term, as in God's saying: ﴿He said: "Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts!"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 38].

Ibn Mālik considered the *min* that enters on *qabl* ("before") and *baʿd* ("after") to be extra, so that *bayn* is analogous to *qabl* and *baʿd*, since all of them are adverbs of place and time (*ẓurūf*).

This statement, which the Qur'an reports of them with "they said", may be something the Qur'an related in meaning, so that the Qur'an, with its concision and eloquence, gathered what they had lengthened in argument and extended in obstinacy. Or it may be that the Qur'an related it in their own words, in which case it was something one of their eloquent men said in their assemblies that brought them together with the Prophet ﷺ. This is the apparent meaning in the *Sīra* of Ibn Isḥāq, who claimed that they said it mockingly, and that God related it in Surat al-Kahf.

It is also possible that they picked it up from what they heard in the Qur'an about the description of their hearts, their hearing, and their distance, such as God's saying: ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness﴾ [Al-Isrāʾ: 46] in Surat al-Isrāʾ. Surat al-Isrāʾ is counted among the surahs revealed before Surat Fuṣṣilat.

Likewise, God's saying: ﴿When you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a hidden barrier﴾ [Al-Isrāʾ: 45], also in Surat al-Isrāʾ. They gathered these and argued with them against the Messenger. So the eloquence found in this verse may have been borrowed from other verses.

It is said that the one who said it was Abū Jahl in a gathering of Quraysh, and therefore the saying is attributed to all of them, because they supported it.

The report of their statements contains a detailed correspondence to the attributes of the Qur'an mentioned earlier: ﴿A revelation from the Most Merciful, the Ever-Merciful﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 2] and ﴿A Book whose verses are made distinct, an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 3]. Since its being a revelation from the Most Merciful, the Ever-Merciful, requires understanding it and benefiting from what it contains, this was answered with their saying: ﴿Our hearts are in coverings from what you call us to﴾. Since its verses being made distinct requires receiving them and listening to them, this was answered with: ﴿and in our ears is deafness﴾, meaning we do not hear its detail. Since its being an Arabic Qur'an makes it a stronger obligation on them to understand it, this was answered with what cuts off that argument,

[Page 236]

which is: ﴿and between us and you there is a barrier﴾, meaning his speech does not reach them and does not come near their side. These are the details of their turning away from the attributes of the Qur'an.

Their saying: ﴿So act, for indeed we are acting﴾ follows from their despair of the Messenger's call being accepted by them. Their saying this was set in contrast to the description of the Qur'an as a bringer of good news and a warner, since it is evident that its being a warner means it warns them of a great punishment. Because they turned away, what is related is their explicit declaration that they do not care about its warning. If it has any harm, then let him harm them with it. This is like Pharaoh's saying: ﴿Leave me to kill Moses, and let him call upon his Lord﴾ [Ghāfir: 26].

The two objects of *iʿmal* ("act") and *ʿāmilūna* ("acting") are omitted so that the expression covers everything each party could do with the other, that which suits each.

The imperative in ﴿fa-ʿmal﴾ is used in the sense of equalization (*taswiya*, treating the options as equal), like the saying of ʿAntara ibn al-Akhras al-Muʿannī:

"Prolong your bearing of hatred toward me and my enmity, and live as you wish; then see whom it harms."

And like God's saying: ﴿Do what you will; indeed He sees what you do﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 40].

The predicate in ﴿innā ʿāmilūna﴾ ("indeed we are acting") is used in the sense of threat.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 41, verses 6–7:

﴿Say: "I am only a human being like you. It is revealed to me that your God is one God. So take a straight path toward Him and seek His forgiveness."﴾

This is a fresh resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), in which the Messenger ﷺ is instructed to answer their statement ﴿So do; indeed we are doing﴾ [Fussilat: 5], which follows from their words ﴿Our hearts are in coverings against what you call us to﴾ [Fussilat: 5] to the end of the passage. It is a reply to one who disclaims having any power or strength to compel them into faith, because he is only a human being like them in humanity, with no power to turn misguided hearts toward guidance. His only duty is to convey what God has revealed to him. This statement implies, by way of kinaya (implicature, indirect meaning), the entrusting of the matter of their recompense for their deeds to God Most High, as if he were saying: "What can I do with you? I am a messenger from God, so your reckoning is upon God."

The restrictive form in ﴿I am only a human being like you﴾ (innama) conveys a qasr idafi (a restriction relative to a specific context): that is, I am restricted to humanity, without any control over the hearts of people.

It also distinguishes him from them, as a precaution against their seizing upon his words ﴿I am only a human being like you﴾ in the way that one who has obtained his opponent's admission that his argument stands seizes upon it, by affirming the difference between him and them in humanity. This is the content of the clause ﴿It is revealed to me﴾. This is so that they are on record as rejecting their well-known, repeated claim that his being a human prevents his being sent from God Most High, as they said: ﴿What is this messenger who eats food and walks in the markets? Why was not an angel sent down to him so that he would be a warner with him?﴾ [Al-Furqan: 7], and similar statements repeated in the Qur'an. Similar to this precaution is what God relates of the disbelievers' words to their messengers: ﴿You are only human beings like us, who want to turn us away from what our fathers worshipped, so bring us a clear authority﴾ [Ibrahim: 10], and ﴿Their messengers said to them: "We are only human beings like you, but God bestows His favour upon whom He wills of His servants"﴾ [Ibrahim: 11].

Out of eagerness to convey guidance to them, he explained what is revealed to him with the words ﴿that your God is one God﴾, as a repetition of what he had conveyed to them more than once. This is the way of one who guides people: he does not let slip any opportunity to convey the truth to them without seizing it. A parallel to this is found in the dialogue between Musa and Fir'awn: ﴿Pharaoh said: "And what is the Lord of the worlds?"﴾ [Al-Shu'ara: 23] ﴿He said: "The Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, if you are certain"﴾ [Al-Shu'ara: 24] ﴿He said to those around him: "Do you not listen?"﴾ [Al-Shu'ara: 25] ﴿He said: "Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones"﴾ [Al-Shu'ara: 26] ﴿He said: "Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is mad"﴾ [Al-Shu'ara: 27] ﴿He said: "Lord of the east and the west and what is between them, if you were reasoning"﴾ [Al-Shu'ara: 28].

The hamza of "anna" (in ﴿annama﴾) is opened. It is the sister of "innama" with the hamza kasra. The hamza of "innama" is opened when it occurs as an object governed by what precedes it and is not at the beginning of a sentence, just as the hamza of "anna" is opened, while the hamza of "inna" is kasra, because "innama" or "annama" is compounded of "inna" or "anna" together with the restrictive, additive "ma" (kaffa), to indicate the meaning of "ma" and "illa" (only). Some have gone so far as to think that the "ma" accompanying it is the negative "ma", being deceived by the fact that the meaning of restriction is the affirmation of a ruling for what is mentioned and its negation for everything else, as with "ma" and "illa". There should be no hesitation that "annama" with the hamza opened conveys restriction just like its sister with the hamza kasra. al-Zamakhshari affirmed this in his tafsir of Surah al-Anbiya', and what Abu Hayyan refuted against him is merely unfounded assertion. This has already been mentioned at the words of God Most High ﴿Say: It is only revealed to me that your God is one God; so will you submit?﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 108] in Surah al-Anbiya'.

So His words ﴿that your God is one God﴾ are an idmaj (embedding) of the call to the truth within the midst of the reply, out of eagerness for guidance.

Likewise is the consequence expressed in His words ﴿So take a straight path toward Him and seek His forgiveness﴾, for it completes that embedding by deriving its benefit as a consequence. This is because affirming that God is one God is meant only to single Him out for worship and to reject association (shirk). This is the aspect in explaining the connection of ﴿Say: I am only a human being﴾ with their words ﴿Our hearts are in coverings﴾ [Fussilat: 5], etc.

The position of ﴿that your God is one God﴾ is as a deputy subject (na'ib fa'il) of ﴿It is revealed to me﴾, meaning: what is revealed to me is the meaning of the verbal noun formed from ﴿that your God is one God﴾, which is the restriction of God Most High's attribute to being One, that is, without partner.

Its being like them: the likeness is in humanity, so it confirms that he is a human being.

Al-istiqama (straightness) is the thing being upright, that is, without crookedness. It is used metaphorically for the thing being a pure truth, with no admixture of deceit or falsehood. It is also used for a person being truthful in his dealings or his covenant, not mixing with them anything of trickery or betrayal; so one says: "So-and-so is a straight man", meaning truthful in character. If his truthfulness toward others is intended, one says: "istaqama lahu," meaning he was straight for his sake, that is, for the sake of dealing with him. From this is His saying: ﴿So as long as they are straight with you, be straight with them﴾ [Al-Tawba: 7]. Here istiqama is in this sense. It is followed by the preposition "ila" (toward) because the two often interchange with "li" (for), as one says: "dhahabat lahu" and "dhahabat ilayhi" (she went for him / toward him). The better view is that the choice of "ila" here is to imply in "istaqimu" the meaning of "tawajjahu" (turn toward), because tawhid is a turning, that is, directing the face toward God alone without other, as is related of Ibrahim: ﴿Indeed I have turned my face toward He who created the heavens and the earth, as a hanif, and I am not of the polytheists﴾ [Al-An'am: 79]. Or "istaqimu" is implied to mean "anibu" (turn in repentance), that is, repent from polytheism, as is indicated by the conjoining of ﴿and seek His forgiveness﴾.

Al-istighfar is seeking pardon for past sin or disobedience, and it derives from ghafr, which is covering.

The meaning: so devote yourselves sincerely to God in His worship, do not associate anything with Him, and ask Him to overlook what has passed from you of association and obstinacy.

* * *

﴿And woe to the polytheists, those who do not give zakat and who are, in the Hereafter, disbelievers﴾.

This is a threat to the polytheists of an evil state and wretchedness in the Hereafter. It may be part of the speech that the Messenger ﷺ was commanded to say, and so it is conjoined to the clause ﴿I am only a human being﴾.

It may also be a parenthetical statement from God Most High, so that the waw is parenthetical (i'tiradiyya) between the clause ﴿Say: I am only a human being﴾ and the clause ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in He who created the earth﴾ [Fussilat: 9], meaning: answer them with your saying, "I am a human being like you, to whom it is revealed," and "We have prepared for them woe and wretchedness if they do not accept what you call them to." In that case this is information from God Most High.

The mention of the polytheists is an explicit noun in the place of a pronoun. It is understood that the threat is linked to their persistence in disbelief, from the report that woe is established for the polytheists and for those described as "those who do not give zakat" and as "disbelievers in the resurrection." This is because attaching a ruling to a derived noun (mushtaqq) indicates that what the derivation comes from is the cause. Also, the relative construction indicates an allusion to the reason for the predicate being built as it is.

As for polytheism and denial of resurrection being causes of woe, this is obvious. As for not giving zakat being a cause of woe, that is because it brings upon them what accompanies polytheism and denial of resurrection, namely not benefiting from the deeds which Islam brought. So mentioning that here serves to disfigure their disbelief and to make their polytheism and denial of resurrection appear hideous, since these two lead them to withholding zakat, that is, to harshness toward the poor and weak and to stinginess with wealth. This is enough to disfigure them in the judgment of morals and in the judgment of custom among them, for they are shamed by baseness, yet they spend wealth in other than its proper way and deny it to those who deserve it.

[Page 240]

From this it is known that the one among the Muslims who withholds zakat has a share of the woe that the polytheists deserve for withholding zakat within their polytheism. For this reason Abu Bakr saw fit to fight those who withheld zakat from among those who had not apostatized from Islam but withheld zakat along with the apostates, and all the companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ agreed with him.

Zakat in the verse is therefore sadaqa (charity), since it occurs as the object of "yu'tuna" (give). In that day there was no obligatory zakat in Islam other than the sadaqa, without specifying the nisab or the categories of produce subject to zakat. Sadaqa was obligatory in general, and for some sadaqa there was a fixed time, namely the sadaqa before private consultation with the Messenger ﷺ. God Most High said: ﴿O you who have believed, when you consult the Messenger privately, precede your private consultation with a charity﴾ [Al-Mujadila: 12].

The clause ﴿and who are, in the Hereafter, disbelievers﴾ is either a hal (circumstantial clause) from the pronoun in "yu'tuna" or is conjoined to the relative clause.

The pronoun in ﴿they are disbelievers﴾ is a pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl), which here serves only to confirm the ruling. It resembles a verbal emphasis rather than a pronoun of separation. Similar to it is His saying ﴿and they, in the Hereafter, they are disbelievers﴾ in Surah Yusuf, and His saying ﴿Indeed I am God﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14] in Surah Ta-Ha.

The fronting of ﴿in the Hereafter﴾ before its governing element, ﴿disbelievers﴾, serves to express concern (ihtimam).

Zakat in the verse is therefore sadaqa (charity), since it occurs as the object of "yu'tuna" (give). In that day there was no obligatory zakat in Islam other than the sadaqa, without specifying the nisab or the categories of produce subject to zakat. Sadaqa was obligatory in general, and for some sadaqa there was a fixed time, namely the sadaqa before private consultation with the Messenger ﷺ. God Most High said: ﴿O you who have believed, when you consult the Messenger privately, precede your private consultation with a charity﴾ [Al-Mujadila: 12].

The clause ﴿and who are, in the Hereafter, disbelievers﴾ is either a hal (circumstantial clause) from the pronoun in "yu'tuna" or is conjoined to the relative clause.

The pronoun in ﴿they are disbelievers﴾ is a pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl), which here serves only to confirm the ruling. It resembles a verbal emphasis rather than a pronoun of separation. Similar to it is His saying ﴿and they, in the Hereafter, they are disbelievers﴾ in Surah Yusuf, and His saying ﴿Indeed I am God﴾ [Ta-Ha: 14] in Surah Ta-Ha.

The fronting of ﴿in the Hereafter﴾ before its governing element, ﴿disbelievers﴾, serves to express concern (ihtimam).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 41, verse 8:

﴿Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds will have a reward that is never cut off.﴾

This is a resumptive explanatory sentence (isti'naf bayani) arising from the threat that was directed at the polytheists after they were commanded to go straight towards God and to seek His forgiveness for what had passed from them. It is as if a questioner asks: "If they take heed and desist, what will be their recompense?" So it is stated that, at that time, they will be among the company of those who have believed and done righteous deeds, for whom there is a reward that is never cut off. In this there is an honouring of the believers.

The placing of "lahum" (for them) at the front is for the sake of giving them importance.

Al-ajr (the reward) is the beneficial recompense for righteous action, or it is what they are given of the bliss of Paradise.

Al-mamnun is a passive participle from al-mann, which is mentioning a favour to the one on whom it is bestowed. The implied sense is "not reminded of as a favour upon them," and this is a metonymy (kinaya) for the fact that it is given to them as thanks for the righteous deeds they had sent forward, for God is Most Forgiving, Most Appreciative. The meaning is that the bestowal upon them in Paradise is accompanied by honour and praise, so they do not feel the shame of a gift. This is of the same kind as His saying, ﴿Do not nullify your charities with reminders and injury﴾ [al-Baqarah: 264]. Thus their reward is like a thing owned by them that no one has given them, and that is an act of grace from God.

Close to this is the verse of Labid:

Sharp-eyed, hunting (wolves/dogs) whose food is not given as a favour; that is, they take their food by themselves, so no one has a favour upon them for it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 41, verse 9:

﴿Say: "Do you indeed disbelieve in He who created the earth in two days, and you set up rivals to Him? That is the Lord of the worlds."﴾

After Allah commanded His Messenger ﷺ to answer the polytheists that he is only a human being to whom revelation is sent, and that he has no power to compel them to faith, He commanded him, following that, to return to guiding them to the truth by way of questioning them about their disbelief in Allah. Within this he incorporated a reminder of the proofs indicating that Allah is One, in the manner of rebuke for their associating others with Him, at a time when the evidences of His singularity in creation and His being characterized by perfect power and knowledge are clear.

So the sentence ﴿Say: "Do you indeed disbelieve…﴾ to its end is a second, independent resumptive statement (isti'naf ibtida'i), being a second answer to the content of their saying ﴿Indeed, we are doers [of our own deeds]﴾ [Fussilat: 5].

The interrogative hamza with which the speech opens is used for rebuke. His saying ﴿Do you indeed disbelieve﴾ is like His saying in Surat al-Baqarah ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28].

In opening with the interrogative and the two particles of emphasis there is an arousing of interest, to prepare the listener to receive what follows, indicating that a matter of importance is about to be conveyed to them. The emphasis of the statement with inna and the lam of initiation after a rebuking or wondering interrogative is a usage that occurs frequently in eloquent speech, so that the denial concerns a established matter. Here it is based on the fact that they reckon themselves to be guided, and on their ignoring the necessary connection between being the sole creator and deserving to be singled out for worship. So they are informed, with emphasis, that they are disbelievers, and are rebuked for that. The rebuke derived from the interrogative is directed at establishing their disbelief in Allah, and this is of the highest rank in eloquence. The possibility that the emphasis is directed at the rebuke and denial is an inversion of the structure of the speech.

The use of the verb (tak'furun) in the present form indicates that the renewal of their disbelief day after day, despite the clarity of the proofs which demand abandoning it, is more deserving of rebuke.

The meaning of disbelief in Him is disbelief in His being singled out for divinity. When they associated others with Him, they fell into nullifying His divinity, because plurality contradicts the reality of divinity; thus it is as though they denied His existence, since, having denied the attributes of His essence, they conceived of Him in a way other than His true reality.

Incorporated into this argument is an explanation of the creation of these worlds. The locus of the argument is the relative clause (silat al-mawsul), and what is connected to it is an incorporation (idmaj).

Al-ardh (the earth): it is the terrestrial sphere with what is in it of dry land and seas, that is, the creation of its body.

Al-yawmani (the two days): the dual of yawm (day), which is the period between the rising of the sun from the east and its rising again. The intended meaning is: within a span equal to two days of what people know, after the creation of the earth; for the light and darkness by whose appearance the day is measured did not appear on the earth until after the earth was created, and this has been discussed in Surat al-A'raf.

The mention of the creation of the earth was begun with because its effects are more evident to the eye and within the reach of man; therefore the proof against them by the creation of the earth was more immediate in its establishment. And because the blessing contained in the earth is stronger and more general, the ugliness of ingratitude toward its Creator appears more clearly and more repugnant.

The conjunction of ﴿and you set up for Him rivals﴾ with ﴿you disbelieve﴾ is an explanation of their disbelief in Allah. The apparent requirement was that an explanation is not conjoined, but he deviated to conjoining it so that its content would be independent in itself.

Al-andad (rivals): the plural of nidd, with a kasra on the nun, which is an equal. The intended meaning: rivals in divinity.

The expression of the Majesty (al-Jalalah) by a relative pronoun rather than the proper name is because of what the relative clause indicates of the cause of the rebuke, since He who created the earth is the one deserving of worship.

The indication by ﴿That is the Lord of the worlds﴾ refers to ﴿He who created the earth in two days﴾, and in the indication there is a call to their dullness of judgment, since they did not perceive that He who created the earth is the Lord of the worlds, because He is the Creator of the earth and what is in it, nor that His lordship requires the negation of any equal or partner. And since He is the Lord of the worlds, He is the Lord of what is below the worlds, of the kinds that are lower than rational beings, such as the stones and wood from which their idols were made.

The sentence ﴿That is the Lord of the worlds﴾ is a parenthetical clause (mu'taridah) between the conjoined elements that follow the relative clause.

[Page 244 is not printed here; the passage begins mid-commentary.]

It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the verb of the relative clause (ṣilah, the clause that completes the relative pronoun), not with the object of the verb (maʿmūl, the grammatical object). Therefore the clause ﴿And He placed therein firmly fixed mountains﴾ and what follows is, in meaning, a second relative clause. For this reason a verb other than "created" (khalaqa) is used, because this placing is another act of creation that took place after the earth was created. It is the creation of parts joined to the earth, either of its own kind, like the mountains, or of a different kind, like the sustenance. For this reason, after the phrase ﴿in two days﴾ [Fussilat: 9], it is followed by ﴿in four days﴾.

Al-rawāsī means the firmly fixed things. It is an adjective of the mountains, because mountains are stone that does not move, unlike sand and dunes, which are abundant in the lands of the Arabs. The noun being described is omitted because the adjective indicates it, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And among His signs are the ships gliding in the sea﴾ [al-Shura: 32], meaning the gliding ships. Its explanation has already been given at His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And We placed firmly fixed mountains in the earth, lest it shake with them﴾ [al-Anbiya: 31], in Surat al-Anbiya.

The description of the firmly fixed mountains as ﴿from above it﴾ is to evoke the striking image of the sights of the mountains. Among them is what is beautiful to see, covered with greenery or clad in snow, and among them is what is terrifying to behold, like the fire mountains (volcanoes) and the black metallic mountains.

﴿And He blessed it﴾ means He made blessing (barakah) in it. Barakah is beneficial good. The earth contains many goods: in it is the provision of humans and their livestock, and in it are dust, stones and minerals, and all of these are blessings.

﴿And He measured﴾ means He made a measure (qadr), that is, a quantity, as He, exalted is He, said, ﴿Indeed, Allah has set a measure for everything﴾ [al-Talaq: 3]. Al-miqdār is a defined portion limited by kind or quantity. So the meaning of ﴿He measured therein its sustenance﴾ is that He created in the earth the powers from which sustenance arises, and created the original kinds and types of sustenance: from grain, the grains; for the pasture and the truffle, the herbs; for fruits, the seeds (pits); and the heat by which the generation of animals is affected, among land animals and birds, and what generates fish and the creatures of seas and rivers.

Among the measuring is the measuring of each kind with what suits it of times, whether of heat, cold or moderation. This is indicated by His saying, ﴿And Allah caused you to grow from the earth a growth﴾ [Nuh: 17], whose discussion will come, and His saying, ﴿And He made for you garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81], and His saying, ﴿And He made for you from the hides of cattle houses﴾ [al-Nahl: 80], and so on.

The plural of sustenance (aqwāt), when made a construct with the pronoun of the earth, conveys generality, meaning all its sustenance. Its generality is in view of the multiplicity of those who eat. So for the beasts there are sustenance, for the birds there is sustenance, for the wild animals there is sustenance, for the reptiles there is sustenance, and for the insects there is sustenance. And for humans is made all of those sustenance, of what they find good among them, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates, ﴿He is the One who created for you all that is in the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29]. The discussion of it has passed in Surat al-Baqarah.

His saying, ﴿in four days﴾, is a summation (fadhlakah) of the total duration of the creation of the earth's body, what is upon it of firmly fixed mountains, and what is in it of powers. So the two days mentioned in His saying, ﴿in two days﴾ [Fussilat: 12], are included in these four days. It is as if it were said: in two other days; so these are four days. Therefore His saying, ﴿in four days﴾, is a summation. But it was turned away from that to what is in the structure of the verse for the purpose of brevity

[Page 245]

and relying on what comes after it, His saying, ﴿then He completed them as seven heavens in two days﴾ [Fussilat: 12]. If the two days in which He completed the creation of the heavens were additional to the six days that elapsed in the creation of the earth and what is upon it, the total of the days would become eight, and that contradicts the indication to the number of days of the week, since the seventh day is a day of rest from the creation. The wisdom of extending the creation is that it should occur in a complete and proportionate form.

(﴿And equal﴾ [Ya-Sin: 10]) Al-Jumhur read it in the accusative (naṣb) as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of "days", meaning complete, with no deficiency in them and no excess. Abu Ja'far read it in the nominative (marfūʿ) as the subject of a nominal sentence, with the implied predicate: "it is equal". Ya'qub read it in the genitive (majrūr) as an adjective of "days".

﴿for those who ask﴾: the phrase is governed by each of the verbs "placed", "blessed" and "measured". So "those who ask" (al-sā'ilīn) is the plural of sā'il in the sense of one who seeks knowledge. It may also be connected to an omitted verb, meaning: "We have explained that to those who ask." It may also be that "for those who ask" is connected to the verb of ﴿He measured therein its sustenance﴾, in which case the intended meaning of "those who ask" is those who seek sustenance.

[Page 246]

*Thumma* (then) is used for the sequence of rank (*al-tartib al-rutbi*, sequence by rank), and it indicates that the content of the conjoined clause is more important in rank than the content of the clause it is conjoined to. The creation of the heavens is greater than the creation of the earth, and their worlds are more numerous and greater. So the particle of rank-sequence is used after the importance of mentioning the creation of the earth has been satisfied, so that both matters are given their due. This does not require that the Will became attached to the creation of the heaven only after the completion of the creation of the earth, nor does it require that the creation of the heaven occurred after the creation of the earth, as will come.

*Istiwa'* (directing oneself) means intending a thing immediately, without anything else intervening. It is a figurative representation of the attachment of God Most High's will to bringing the heavens into existence. It has already been discussed in His saying: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on earth; then He directed Himself to the heaven﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:29], in Surat al-Baqarah. Perhaps His saying ﴿So He said to it and to the earth: "Come, willingly or unwillingly"﴾ is an indication that His Will was directed at the creation of the heavens and the earth with a single direction, and then the time of the executive (*tanjizi*) Will differed in actualizing that. So His Will became attached, in execution, to the creation of the heaven and then to the creation of the earth. He expressed the attachment of the Will, in execution, to the creation of the heaven by the direction of the Will toward the heaven, and that direction He expressed as *istiwa'*. His saying ﴿So He said to it and to the earth: "Come, willingly or unwillingly." They said: "We come willingly"﴾ indicates this. The verb *i'tiya* (come) is an imperative of creation (*amr li'l-takwin*).

*Al-dukhan* (smoke) is what rises from fuel when a fire ignites in it.

His saying ﴿and it was smoke﴾ is an eloquent simile (*tashbih baligh*), meaning: it was like smoke. A hadith has been transmitted: «Indeed it was ʿamāʾ» (a thin cloud, i.e., a fine moisture).

It has been said that by *dukhan* here is meant something dark, which agrees with what is in the Book of Genesis in the words: "and darkness was upon the face of the deep." But this is far from the saying of the Prophet ﷺ that there was nothing in existence of the events except the ʿamāʾ. The ʿamāʾ is a thin cloud, that is, a fine moisture, and it is an approximation of the original element from which God created the existents. This is what fits the heaven being created before the earth.

The meaning of ﴿and it was smoke﴾ is that the origin of the heaven is that entity likened to smoke. That is, the heaven was formed from that smoke, just as you say: "I resorted to this palm-tree, which is a seed, and chose for it the most fertile soil." Thus the material of the heaven existed before the existence of the earth.

His saying ﴿So He said to it and to the earth﴾ is a consequence (*tafri'*) of the verb ﴿directed Himself to the heaven, and it was smoke﴾. The speech is then directed to the heaven and the earth at that time, that is, before the creation of the heaven without doubt and before the creation of the earth, because He made the speech to it (the earth) accompany the speech to the heaven. It is a speech of creation. That is, the attachment of power to the heaven and the earth, that is, to the material of their formation, which is the smoke, because the heaven was formed from the ʿamāʾ by the congealing of a part of it called a skin (*jild*), and from it the heaven came to be. Along with the heaven, water was formed, and the earth was formed by a dryness that appeared in that water, as the first chapter of the Book of Genesis of the Torah has come.

The *ityan* (coming) in His saying *i'tiya* originally means arrival and approach. Since its literal meaning is not intended, because it cannot be conceived that the heaven and the earth would come, nor that obedience or unwillingness could be conceived from them, since they are not among the people of intellect and perception, nor can it be conceived that God would compel them to that, because that would entail their being outside His power from the very beginning, the meaning must be diverted from the literal sense. This is in one of two ways, each of which has the highest rank of eloquence:

The first way: that *ityan* is used metaphorically for accepting the creation, just as *idbar* (turning back) is used metaphorically for disobedience in His saying: ﴿Then he turned back, striving﴾ [al-Nazi'at 79:22], and in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to Musaylima when he refused faith and obedience in the delegation of his people, Banu Hanifa: «If you turn your back, God will surely cut you down». Likewise flight and escape are used metaphorically for disobedience.

So the meaning of *i'tiya* is: comply with the command of creation. This compliance is used metaphorically for acceptance, and it is of the building of metaphor upon metaphor, and it has a standing in eloquence. The speech on this way is a metaphor for the attachment of power to the thing empowered, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, when He wills a thing, His command is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin 36:82].

His saying ﴿willingly or unwillingly﴾ is a kinaya (allusive expression) for the lack of any alternative to accepting the command. It is a figurative representation of the power's capacity to bring them into existence in accordance with God Most High's will. Thus the phrase ﴿willingly or unwillingly﴾ functions as a proverbial expression.

*Taw'an* and *karhan* (willingly and unwillingly) are two verbal nouns (*masdar*) that stand as circumstantial accusatives (*hal*) from the pronoun in *i'tiya*, meaning: obedient or unwilling.

The second way: that the clause ﴿So He said to it and to the earth: "Come, willingly or unwillingly"﴾ is used as a representation of the form of the attachment of God Most High's power to the creation of the heaven and the earth, in order to magnify their Creator, in the form of a command issued by a commander who is obeyed to a servant who has been permitted to attend a difficult task, saying to him: "Come to this task willingly or unwillingly," because of the expectation that he would refuse to undertake that task. This is without regard to the resemblance of the parts of the composite form to the parts of the form it resembles. So there is no speaking and no spoken word, and it is only a representation. In this case, ﴿willingly or unwillingly﴾ is part of the complete likened form.

The aim, on both considerations, is to depict the greatness of divine power and its effectiveness over things capable of being done, whether small or great.

As for His saying ﴿They said: "We come, obedient"﴾, it may be that the speech of the heaven and the earth is a metaphor to indicate the swiftness of their formation, by likening it to the swiftness of an obedient subordinate's compliance, since he does not hesitate or delay, in the manner of the metaphor by allusion (*makniyya*) and imagination (*takhyil*), from the line of the rajaz verse whose author is unknown:

"The basin filled and said: 'Enough!'" and this is common.

It may also be that it is a representation of the form of the formation of the heaven and the earth when God Most High's power attaches to their creation, in the form of one commanded with a task whom he accepts willingly. These two considerations are close to each other, except that the speech, the coming, and the obedience, on the first consideration, are metaphors, while on the second consideration they are literal. The metaphor lies in the composition, as is known from the distinction between the single metaphor and the compound metaphor in the science of rhetoric (*fann al-bayan*).

The saying "obedient" came in the plural form because the word "heaven" encompasses seven heavens, as God Most High said right after this: ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens﴾ [Fussilat 41:12]. So the compliance proceeds from a plurality. As for its being in the masculine plural form, that is because the heaven and the earth have no true feminine gender.

As for its being in the plural form of rational beings, that is an elaboration (*tarshih*) of the aforementioned allusive metaphor (*makniyya*), like His saying: ﴿Indeed I saw eleven stars, and the sun and the moon; I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf 12:4].

*[p. 249]*

﴿فَقَضاهُنَّ سَبْعَ سَماواتٍ في يَوْمَيْنِ﴾ [So He completed them as seven heavens in two days].

This follows from His words ﴿Then He said to it and to the earth, "Come willingly or by compulsion"﴾ [Fussilat: 11].

*Al-qada'* (completion, decree) means creative bringing-into-being, because it carries the sense of perfecting and determining. It therefore implies innovation and haste, as in the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali:

*"Upon them are two coats of mail that Dawud completed, or that Tubba' the maker of flowing armour produced."*

The pronoun in *faqadahunna* refers to the heavens, taking into account the feminine form of the word *samawat*. This is a stylistic variation (*tafannun*).

*[p. 249 continued]* The accusative *sab'a samawat* is either a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) from the pronoun in *qadahunna*, or an appositive (*'atf bayan*) to it. It is also permitted that it is a second object of *qadahunna*, since *qada* is here used in the sense of *sayyarahunna* (made them). This is like His words in Surat al-Baqarah ﴿and He completed them as seven heavens﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29].

The creation of the heavens in two days took place before the four days in which the earth and what is in it were created. In Surat al-Baqarah we explained that the more evident view is that the creation of the heaven came before the creation of the earth, and this is consistent with the principles of the science of cosmology (*'ilm al-hay'a*). Nothing in this verse requires otherwise.

The duration of the creation of the seven heavens was shorter than that of the earth, even though the worlds of the heavens are greater and more numerous, because God created the heavens in a manner that was faster. Perhaps the creation of the heavens occurred by some of them separating from others, and by the bursting forth of their bodies, with some emerging from others. This is what the ancient Greek philosophers approximated with what they called the emanation of the ten intellects, some from others. The speed of the emergence of some from others was conditioned by states suited to the substances from which they were composed.

As for the creation of the earth, it is most likely that it occurred through a slow process of generation, because it was formed from natural elements, so the generation of some of them from others was also gradual. ﴿And none knows the hosts of your Lord except Him﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31].

These days were the origin of the convention for the order of the days of the week. Commentators have disputed the determination of the starting point of these days. The books of the Jews state that the starting point of these days is Sunday, that the sixth of them is Friday, and that God made Saturday free from creation so that it would accord with the rituals of their religion, which make Saturday a day of rest for people and their animals, in imitation of the completion of the creation of the worlds.

On this basis, the Arabs named the days beginning with *al-Ahad*, which means "first" or "one". In classical Arabic its name is *awwal*. This spread to them from the teachings of the Jews, or from an earlier teaching that was the original source for the convention of both nations.

What the reports from the Sunnah (the Prophetic tradition) testify is that God created Adam on Friday, that it is the best and most excellent day of the week, and that the Jews and Christians differed in determining the most excellent day of the week, and that God guided the Muslims to it. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "This day, that is Friday, is the day about which they differed, and God guided us to it. People are following us in this: the Jews tomorrow and the Christians the day after tomorrow."

There is no disagreement that God created Adam after the completion of the creation of the heaven and the earth, so it is determined that the day of his creation was the seventh day. Muslim related in his Sahih from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that "God began the creation on Saturday." Al-Bukhari and Ibn al-Madini declared this report weak, on the grounds that it is a saying of Ka'b al-Ahbar which he related to Abu Hurayrah, and that it was confused for some of its narrators, who took it to be a report traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

These are details of no real benefit, and I have touched on them here only so that the commentary is not devoid of them, lest one who encounters them elsewhere become bewildered. The purpose of the Qur'an is admonition.

﴿And He revealed in each heaven its command, and We adorned the lowest heaven with lamps and as a guard﴾.

*Wa awha* is coordinated (*'atf*) with *faqadahunna*.

*Al-wahy* is hidden speech. The term *wahy* is also applied to the arising of knowledge in the soul of one for whom it is intended, without speech. From this is His saying, relating about Zakariyya, ﴿so he signalled to them﴾ [Ibrahim: 13], meaning he gestured to them with what indicated the meaning: "Glorify (God) in the morning and the evening." This is also the verse of Abu Dawud:

*"They shoot with long sermons, and at times with the signalling of glances, for fear of the watchers."*

Then the term is extended to refer to God's inspiring the created beings with what they seek that is beneficial to them, as in His saying ﴿And your Lord inspired the bee: "Take for yourselves houses in the mountains"﴾ [al-Nahl: 68], meaning He formed it to perceive and seek that. It is also applied to God's subjecting some of His creatures to receive the effect of His power, as in His saying ﴿When the earth is shaken with its [final] earthquake﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 1], down to His saying ﴿because your Lord has inspired it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 5].

The *wahy* in the heaven encompasses all these meanings, using the term in its literal and figurative senses. So He revealed in the heavens the decrees of the systems of their gravitation and the decrees of the motion of their stars. He revealed within them the creation of the angels in them, and He revealed to the angels what they receive of the command concerning what they do. He, exalted is He, said ﴿and they act by His command﴾ [al-Anbiya': 27], and said ﴿they glorify Him night and day, never tiring﴾ [al-Anbiya': 20].

*Amraha* means "its affair", and this applies to everything that pertains to it: its inhabitants, its stars, the cohesion of its body, and the gravitation between it and what is adjacent to it. This corresponds to His words concerning the creation of the earth ﴿and He placed in it firm mountains from above it, and blessed it, and determined in it its sustenance﴾ [Fussilat: 10].

*Amraha* is in the accusative by removal of the preposition, meaning *bi-amraha* ("with its command"), or else *awha* is taken to include the sense of *qadara* (decreed) or *awda'a* (deposited).

There is a shift (*iltifat*) from the third person to the first person of speech in His words ﴿and We adorned the lowest heaven with lamps﴾. This renews the attentiveness of the listeners, given the long use of the third-person form from His words ﴿The One who created the earth in two days﴾ [Fussilat: 9] onward. It also shows special concern by singling out this creation, which benefits people in both religion and worldly life, namely the creation of the stars, the fine lights and the meteors, by mentioning it specifically within the generality of ﴿and He revealed in each heaven its command﴾. The lowest heaven is only one of the heavens, and the stars and meteors are only part of its command.

*Al-masabih* is the plural of *misbah*, which is what is kindled by fire in oil for illumination. It is derived from *al-sabah* (morning), because they try to make it a substitute for morning. The intended meaning of *al-masabih* is the stars, and lamps are used as a metaphor for them because of the light that appears from them.

*Hifzan* is in the accusative as an object of purpose for an omitted verb indicated by the verb *zayyanna*. The implied meaning is: "and We made them as a guard." The intended meaning is a guard for the heaven against the devils who eavesdrop by stealing hearing. The discussion of its parallel has already been presented in Surat al-Saffat.
