﴿That is the decree of the Almighty, the All-Knowing﴾.

The demonstrative refers to what was mentioned from His words ﴿and He placed in it firm mountains from above it﴾ [Fussilat: 10] down to His words ﴿and We adorned the lowest heaven with lamps and as a guard﴾.

*Al-taqdir* is placing a thing at a specific measure. Its parallel has already been discussed in Surat Ya Sin. The reason for choosing the two attributes ﴿the Almighty, the All-Knowing﴾ for mention has already been explained.

*[p. 252]*

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 41, verse 13:**

﴿And if they turn away, then say: "I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of 'Ad and Thamud."﴾ ﴿When the messengers came to them from before them and from behind them, saying: "Do not worship except Allah."﴾ [Fussilat: 13–14]

After the proof had struck them, a proof that leaves no avenue for doubt to enter souls thereafter, that Allah is singular in divinity, because He is singular in bringing all worlds into existence. The establishment of Oneness was, by its nature, to remove the suspicion that the Qur'an is sent down from Allah, because they only disbelieved in it on account of its proclamation of the negation of partners from Allah, the Exalted. So when this became clear, the proper course was for them to return to affirming the Messenger and believing in the Qur'an, and to desist from their aversion described at the beginning of the surah by His saying ﴿But most of them turn away, so they do not hear﴾ [Fussilat: 4], etc. Therefore their persistence in aversion after those proofs was made into a supposed matter, as an impossibility is supposed, so the particle ''in'' (إنْ) was used in its regard, whose original function is to occur in a position where there is no certainty of the condition being fulfilled, like His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Shall We then turn away the reminder from you, altogether, because you are a transgressing people?﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 5], according to the reading of one who read with a kasra on the hamza of (إنْ).

So the meaning of ﴿And if they turn away﴾ is: if they persist in their aversion after I have guided them with clear proofs and they obstinately resisted them. The verb is therefore used in the sense of persistence, like His saying ﴿O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [An-Nisa': 136].

The warning (al-indhar) is intimidation, and here it is intimidation by the anticipation of a punishment like the punishment of those who resembled them in aversion, out of fear that what befell those people may befall them, based on the known principle that Allah's acts proceed according to one uniform pattern. It is not a threat of a specific sentence, because the Quraysh were not struck by a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of 'Ad and Thamud, although they equalled them in denial, in aversion from the messengers, and in the excuses they offered, such as their saying ﴿If our Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels﴾ [Fussilat: 14]. Allah granted the Quraysh respite until many of them believed, and He uprooted their disbelievers with a special punishment.

Page 253
The literal meaning of the thunderbolt (sa'iqah) is fire that comes out with lightning and burns whatever it strikes. It was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿They put their fingers in their ears because of the thunderbolts﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 19] in Surat al-Baqarah. It is also applied to a catastrophic event that destroys swiftly. Since "thunderbolt" is here attributed to 'Ad and Thamud, and 'Ad were not destroyed by a thunderbolt (rather, they were destroyed by a wind), while Thamud were destroyed by a thunderbolt, the word "thunderbolt" is used here in both its literal and figurative senses, or it is a case of general application (umum al-mujawiz) that permits this on both considerations, for the sake of brevity; and the summary is followed afterwards by detail in His saying ﴿As for 'Ad﴾ [Fussilat: 15] up to His saying ﴿for what they used to earn﴾ [Fussilat: 17].

"Idh" (إذْ) is a temporal adverb referring to the past, and the meaning is: "like their thunderbolt at the time the messengers came to them," to the end of the verses. Ibn Ishaq related in his Sirah that "'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah spoke to the Prophet ﷺ about what he had brought of opposition to his people, so the Prophet ﷺ recited to them ﴿Ha Mim﴾ [Fussilat: 1] ﴿A revelation from the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ [Fussilat: 2], until he reached ﴿So say: I have warned you of a thunderbolt﴾, the verse, whereupon 'Utbah put his hand over the mouth of the Prophet ﷺ and said to him: "I adjure you by Allah and by kinship."

The pronoun in (جاءَتْهم) refers to 'Ad and Thamud, taking into account the number of each tribe among them.

The plural "messengers" here is an instance of using the plural form for two, like His saying ﴿Your two hearts have certainly inclined﴾ [At-Tahrim: 4]. The context is clear, and this usage is not rare. In fact there came to them two messengers, Hud and Salih.

His saying ﴿from before them and from behind them﴾ [Fussilat: 14] is an image of the eagerness of each messenger for their guidance, such that he leaves no means by which the religion could be conveyed to them unused. This is depicted by coming to each of them sometimes from in front of him and sometimes from behind him, leaving him no direction, as one eager to obtain something seeks it repeatedly and covers all the places where it may be found or heard. This image is similar to that in His saying, Exalted is He, quoting Satan: ﴿Then I will certainly come to them from before them and from behind them and from their right and from their left﴾ [Al-A'raf: 17].

The verse limits itself to two directions and does not include all four, as was done in the depiction of Satan's whispering, because the purpose here is only to depict eagerness, and that has been achieved. In the account about Satan, the purpose is to depict eagerness together with yearning, as a warning against it and to stir hatred of it in people's souls.

﴿That do not worship except Allah﴾ [Fussilat: 14] is an explanation of the clause ﴿the messengers came to them﴾ [Fussilat: 14], because the coming includes the meaning of conveying, given that the agent of the coming is described as messengers. Thus "an" (أنْ) is explanatory (tafsiriyyah) relative to (جاءَتْهم) on this interpretation, as in the words of the poet:

If you two carry a need for me, a light burden to carry, you would earn a favour and a hand from me in return,
That you two recite to Asma', woe to you both, my greetings, and that you not inform anyone.

Here he explained the need as reciting greetings to Asma', because by "need" he meant the message. This follows the view of al-Zamakhshari and the verifiers that it is not a condition that a clause carrying the sense of speech precede it without its particles; rather it suffices that what is intended by the sense of speech precede it, even if it is not a full clause, contrary to what the author of Mughni al-Labib extended with discussions that the discerning would not approve; or it is because the title "messengers" includes the notion of conveying a message.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 41, verse 14:

﴿They said: "If our Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels. So we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent."﴾

The report of the reply of 'Ad and Thamud to their messengers. Their reply was one of identical form, because it arose from identical reasoning. The reasoning of minds that lack insight tends to be built on imaginary conceptions, fanciful analogies and sophistical arguments. They conceive of the attributes and actions of God, exalted is He, in ways that do not match His true reality, and they measure them by the conditions of created beings. For this reason the state of people of ignorance is the same in this respect, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Thus did no messenger come to those before them without their saying, "A sorcerer or a madman!"﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 52] ﴿Did they bequeath this saying to one another? Nay, they are a people who transgress﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 53], meaning: rather, they are alike in transgression, that is, in severe disbelief, so their imaginings dictate to them identical propositions.

Because their reply occurred within the context of a dialogue, the report of their words came without a conjunction, in the manner of direct speech (muqawalah), as was previously explained at His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I am going to place upon the earth a successive authority"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30].

Page 255

The saying of the messengers to them, "Worship none but God," has been reported by a verb that indicates the saying, namely the verb "came to them," as was previously mentioned just above.

Thus their saying ﴿If our Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels﴾ implies the nullification of the mission of human beings from God, exalted is He.

The object of "willed" is omitted, and the context indicates it. That is, "If our Lord had willed to send to us, He would have sent down angels from the heaven as messengers to us." This is a specific ellipsis, different from the common ellipsis of the object of the verb of willing, because that common form occurs when the omitted object is indicated by the apodosis of "if" (law), as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then if He had willed, He would have guided you all﴾ [al-An'am: 149]. Its subtle purpose is to create ambiguity and then clarify. The ellipsis in this verse, however, relies on the evidence of the context, and it is brevity (ijaz). It is a rare ellipsis of the object of the verb of willing. A parallel to it is the saying of al-Ma'arri:

If you wish, claim that those above its surface
are your slaves, and call upon your God, He will testify.

Their speech contained an exceptive conditional syllogism (qiyas istithna'i), whose structure is: "If our Lord had willed to send a messenger, He would have sent angels to descend to us from the heaven. But He did not send angels down to us. Therefore He did not will to send a messenger to us." This is an allusion to their denial of the messengers, and for this reason they built upon it the statement ﴿So we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent﴾, meaning: we deny your mission. This is also a kinayah (implicature, indirect expression) for denial.

﴿Then as for ʿĀd, they were arrogant on earth without right, and said, "Who is mightier than us in strength?" Did they not see that God, who created them, is mightier than them in strength? And they used to deny Our signs.﴾ ﴿So We sent upon them a furious wind, on days of misfortune, that We might let them taste the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world. But the punishment of the Hereafter is more disgracing, and they will not be helped.﴾

After mentioning what ʿĀd and Thamūd shared, namely obstinacy and persistence in disbelief, he now details some of the particular forms of disbelief that each of the two nations was distinguished by, and he mentions those that relate to the punishment that befell each nation.

[p. 256]

The *fāʾ* (فَ) is a consequential connective (*tafrīʿ*) following the sentence ﴿They said, "If our Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels"﴾ [Fussilat: 14], which implies that they rejected the call of their two messengers and did not accept their guidance and reasoning.

As for *ammā* (أمّا), it is a conditional and differentiating particle, and its discussion has already been given when God says ﴿As for those who believe, they know that it is the truth from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The meaning is: As for ʿĀd, their arrogance prevented them from accepting guidance.

*Istikbār* (اسْتِكْبار) is an intensification of *kibr* (الكِبْر), that is, considering oneself great and despising people. The *sīn* and *tāʾ* in it are for intensification, like *istajāba* (اسْتَجابَ). The definiteness of "the earth" (الأرْض) is for a known reference, that is, their known land. The reason why arrogance is mentioned among their faults is that their pride was what diverted them from following their messenger and from anticipating God's punishment.

His saying *bi-ghayri al-ḥaqq* (بِغَيْرِ الحَقِّ), "without right," is an added censure of their arrogance, for arrogance is never with right, since there is no justification for pride in any respect. All the things that tempt a person toward pride, such as knowledge, wealth, authority, strength, and other things, do not bring a human being to a state free of deficiency, and a weak deficient person has no right to pride. For this reason, pride is among the attributes peculiar to God the Exalted. They had been deceived by the strength of their bodies and the might of their nation, and they claimed that no one could overcome them. This is the meaning of their saying (﴿Who is mightier than us in strength?﴾). Thus their saying that is the cause of their arrogance, because it produced in them contempt for all others. When Hūd came to them denying what they were upon of idolatry and tyranny, this greatly offended them, because they had become accustomed to self-admiration and to their own condition, so they denied their messenger.

Since their self-deception through their strength was what drove them to disbelief, and their saying (﴿Who is mightier than us in strength?﴾) was an evidence of it, it was singled out for mention.

It was introduced with the conjunction *wa* (و) even though it serves as an explanation of God's words ﴿they were arrogant on earth without right﴾, to indicate that it is independently what makes them deserving of censure, because their saying itself is a reprehensible utterance. So it was mentioned by coordination with the verb *istakbarū* (اسْتَكْبَرُوا), because the nature of coordination requires difference between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined, and it informs us by context that this saying was what prompted them to arrogance.

[p. 257]

The clause ﴿Did they not see that God, who created them, is mightier than them in strength?﴾ is a parenthetical clause (*jumla muʿtaridha*), and the *wāw* in it is parenthetical (*iʿtirāḍiyya*). *Al-ruʾya* (الرُّؤْيَة) here is cognitive ("seeing" in the sense of knowing), and the interrogative is one of denial. The meaning is a denunciation of their lack of knowledge that God is mightier than them in strength, since they turned away from the messenger of their Lord and from his warning to them, turning away like one who pays no attention to the greatness of God the Exalted. For if they had reckoned with it, they would have anticipated His punishment, and they would have turned toward the proofs of their messenger's truthfulness.

The attribute *alladhī khalaqahum* (الَّذِي خَلَقَهم), "who created them," is applied to the name of majesty (Allah) because of what the relative clause carries of an allusion to the reason for the denunciation of them, namely their ignorance that God is stronger than them. For their being created is known to them by necessity, so knowledge of this was sufficient to indicate that He is mightier than them in strength, and that He is worthy of their reckoning His anger, so that they would look into the evidences of the truthfulness of His messenger that were brought to them.

The pronoun in *huwa ashaddu minhum* (هو أشَدُّ مِنهم) is a *ḍamīr al-faṣl* (ضمير الفصل, the separating pronoun), and it serves to strengthen the judgment by making its clarity more evident. When that judgment is established, their lack of knowledge of its requirement becomes more shameful, and their excuse for ignorance of it is removed.

The true meaning of *al-quwwa* (القُوَّة) is a state in the body by which one is able to perform arduous actions. It is also applied to what follows from that of power and the means of accomplishing actions. Its application was explained earlier in God's words ﴿so take it with strength﴾ in Surat al-Aʿrāf. Here what is intended is its literal, metaphorical (*kināʾī*), and figurative (*majāzī*) senses. It is used in its literal meaning explicitly and by metaphor, and its figurative sense refers to the means of subduing difficult matters that they possessed, through the strength of their bodies and the strength of their minds. The Arabs use ʿĀd as a proverbial example for the soundness of their opinions, so they say "the wisdom of ʿĀd" (أحْلامُ عادٍ). Al-Nābigha said:

"The wisdom of ʿĀd, and bodies purified
From the defect, the calamities, and the sin."

And they say, describing things whose like is rarely made, *ʿādiyya* (عادِيَّة): "an ʿādiyya well" (بِئْرٌ عادِيَّةٌ), and "an ʿādī building" (بِناءٌ عادِيٌّ).

Since strength entails breadth of power, he attributed strength to God the Exalted, in the sense that His power is not thwarted by anything whose existence His will is related to. This is what is meant here in His words ﴿that God, who created them, is mightier than them in strength﴾, that is, He is of greater power than their power. So the application of *quwwa* to the power of God the Exalted means perfection of power, that is, the generality of its effect and its relation to all possible things in accordance with will, such that no possible thing is beyond the reach of His power, and the perfection of His self-sufficiency from being affected by others. This was discussed earlier in His words ﴿Indeed God is strong and severe in punishment﴾ in Surat al-Anfāl.

[p. 258]

The clause ﴿Did they not see that God, who created them, is mightier than them in strength﴾ is a parenthetical clause between the conjoined clauses, and the *wāw* in it is parenthetical.

As for His words *wa-kānū bi-āyātinā yajḥadūn* (وكانُوا بِآياتِنا يَجْحَدُونَ), "and they used to deny Our signs," it may be that what is meant by the signs (*āyāt*) is the miracles of their messenger Hūd, but they did not believe in them and persisted in obstinacy. The Qur'an does not mention for Hūd any signs other than that he warned them of a punishment coming to them from the sky. God says ﴿But when they saw it as a cloud approaching their valleys, they said, "This is a cloud bringing us rain." Rather, it is what you sought to hasten: a wind in which is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Aḥqāf: 24]. This is part of their denial of the first signs.

It may also be that what is meant by the signs is the proofs of divine unity contained in the call of their messenger, and reminders of God's blessings upon them, as in His words ﴿And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah and increased you in stature abundantly﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 69], and His words ﴿Fear the One who has provided you with what you know﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 132], ﴿He has provided you with livestock and sons﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 133], ﴿and gardens and springs﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 134].

The verb *kānū* (كانُوا) indicates that denial of the signs was rooted in them. The form of the present tense in *yajḥadūn* (يَجْحَدُونَ) indicates that denial was recurrent in them and renewed.

On this he arranged the description of their punishment: that God sent upon them a wind. The *fāʾ* indicates that their punishment was caused by the state of their disbelief in its manner, for what drove their disbelief was their self-deception through their strength. So God destroyed them with what people do not expect destruction by. For people say of a thing that is not regarded: "It is a wind" (هو رِيحٌ), so that He might show them that God is of great might, and that He places might in a light thing like the wind so that it becomes a punishment and disgrace, that is, a humiliation, as He said ﴿that We might let them taste the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world﴾. And what disgrace is greater than that the wind should hurl them into the air like feathers, and cast them down dead upon the ground, all of them, so that passersby see them in their dwellings as corpses lying prostrate, their skins shriveled and their bodies decayed, as if they were trunks of hollow palm trees?

[p. 259]

*Al-rīḥ* (الرِّيح) is a movement in the air that arises from the alternation of heat and cold, and its waves travel as the waves of the sea travel. The wind that struck ʿĀd is the *dabūr* (الدَّبُور), which blows from the direction of the sunset. It was named *dabūr* with a fatḥa on the *dāl* and a lightened *bāʾ*, because it blows from the direction of the back (*dubur*) of the Kaʿba. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I was helped by the *ṣabā* (east wind), and ʿĀd was destroyed by the *dabūr* (west wind)."

The wind that struck ʿĀd had this power only because of a strong compression in the air that was not customary. For compression makes a weak thing strong, as has been observed in our age: minute bodies made of chemical parts called the atom become, by compression, capable of destroying an entire city. This is called atomic energy, and by it a large part of the land of Japan was destroyed in the World War.

*Al-ṣarṣar* (الصَّرْصَر) is the violent wind that has a *ṣarṣara*, that is, a loud noise in its blowing, because of the intensity of the speed of its movement. The doubling of its middle radical is for intensifying its severity among the members of its kind, like the doubling of *kubkib* for intensifying *kabb*. Its root is *ṣarra*, that is, it cried out. It is a descriptive word whose form is not feminized, because it applies only to wind, and wind is of feminine grammatical gender by implication.

*Al-naḥisāt* (النَّحِسات), with a fatḥa on the *nūn* and sukūn on the *ḥāʾ*, is the plural of *naḥis* without feminine marking, because it is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) of the verb *naḥisa* like *ʿalima*, as in God's words ﴿on a day of continuous misfortune﴾ [al-Qamar: 19].

Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, and Yaʿqūb read it with sukūn on the *ḥāʾ*. It is permissible to read it with kasra on the *ḥāʾ*, and the rest of the readers (al-baqiyya) read it thus, as an adjective (ṣifa mushabbaha) from *naḥs*, when one is struck by *naḥs*, that is, by evil or severe harm.

Its opposite is *bakht* (البَخْت), good fortune, in the imagination of the common people. Neither *naḥs* nor *bakht* has any reality, but they are both accidents that befall a person. *Naḥs* befalls him from the badness of his character and temperament, or from his negligence, or from the corruption of his environment or his people. *Bakht* befalls him as a result of the opposite of these. Some of both kinds are chance matters, and perhaps some of them are a recompense from God for a good or evil deed of His servants, or in their religion, as happened to ʿĀd and the people of the pre-Islamic age (*ahl al-jāhiliyya*). Most nations imagine *naḥs* and *bakht* to be a kind of *ṭiyara* (طِيَرة, superstitious omen-reading) and of *tashāʾum* (تَشاؤُم, belief in ill omen) and *tayammun* (تَيَمُّن, belief in good omen). From it come *zajr* (زَجْر, omen-reading by birds' movements) and *ʿiyāfa* (عِيافَة, omen-reading by birds) among the Arabs in the pre-Islamic age, and from it come the belief that events are foretold by the stars and the days among most ignorant or corrupt-creed nations. Islam refuted all of this, that is, uncovered its falsehood, with what no earlier teaching among the religions that appeared before Islam had preceded.

So the meaning of describing the days as *naḥisāt* is that they were days of great evil that befell them, namely the punishment of the wind. They were eight days, as God said ﴿He subjected it against them for seven nights and eight days in succession﴾ [al-Ḥāqqa: 7]. The meaning is that those specific days were misfortune, and that their misfortune was upon them and not upon other people on earth, because ʿĀd were the ones targeted by the punishment. It does not mean that those days recur every year as days of misfortune for humankind, for that is not sound, since it would require that all nations suffered evil on those days.

Those days were described as *naḥisāt* because nothing happened in them but evil for them: the suffering of crushing blows that inevitably led to death, the sight of their dead relatives, the death of their livestock, and the uprooting of their palm trees.

The storytellers (*ahl al-qiṣaṣ*) invented the naming of eight days, half of which are the last part of the month of Shabāṭ and half the month of Ādhār, in which winds commonly blow frequently, and they called them *ayyām al-ḥusūm* (أيّام الحُسُوم, "days of unbroken continuity"). Then they built on this that these are the days described with *ḥusūm* in God's words in Surat al-Ḥāqqa ﴿He subjected it against them for seven nights and eight days in succession﴾ [al-Ḥāqqa: 7]. They claimed that these are the days corresponding to the days of the wind that struck ʿĀd. Then they built on that that these are days of misfortune every year, and they lied about some of the early authorities, such as Ibn ʿAbbās, with fabrications about this. This is "a handful of thorns upon a bundle of thorns" (ḍighth ʿalā ibāla), and a variation in the illusions of error.

*Naḥisāt* (نَحِساتٍ) was pluralized with *alif* and *tāʾ* because it is an adjective for a plural of non-rational beings, namely *ayyām* (أيّام, days).

The *lām* in *li-nudhīqahum* (لِنُذِيقَهم) is for causation and is related to *arsalnā* (أرْسَلْنا). The "tasting" (*idhāqa*, إذاقَة) is an imaginative representation (*takhyīl*) within a metaphor (*makniyya*): the punishment is likened to a food prepared for them, in the manner of mockery (*tahakkum*), just as ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm called the raid "hospitality" (*qirā*) in his saying:

[p. 260]

"We hosted you, then we hastened your hospitality
Just before dawn, a crushing, grinding (blow)."

[p. 261]

The "tasting" is an imaginative representation (*takhyīl*) drawn from the things that are agreeable in the food that is the object of comparison.

Al-khizy (ignominy) means humiliation. The annexation of "torment" (ʿadhāb) to "ignominy" (al-khizy) is the annexation of a qualified noun to its qualifier, as evidenced by its contrast with the phrase "and the torment of the Hereafter is more ignominious" (wa-la-ʿadhābu al-ākhirati akhzā), meaning it is more intensely humiliating than the humiliation of the torment of this world. This is because ignominy is a description of the torment through the usage of a verbal noun or noun of action, for the sake of emphasis on that torment being humiliating to the one who is tormented by it.

The meaning of the torment being humiliating is that it is a cause of ignominy. Describing the torment as "ignominy" in the sense of "humiliating" is metaphor of the rational kind (al-majāz al-ʿaqlī). Before the annexation, it would be estimated as: "that We may make them taste a torment of ignominy" (li-nudhīqahum ʿadhāban khizyan), i.e., humiliating. When the annexation of the qualified noun to its qualifier was intended, it was said: "the torment of ignominy" (ʿadhāb al-khizy), also for emphasis, because the annexation of the qualified noun to its qualifier is an emphasis on the attribute, to the extent that the qualifier is treated as though it were another person to whom the qualified noun is annexed. This is close to the figure of speech known as muḥassin al-tajrīd. Thus two emphases arise in the phrase "ʿadhāb al-khizy": the emphasis of describing with a verbal noun, and the emphasis of annexing the qualified noun to its qualifier.

The clause "and the torment of the Hereafter is more ignominious" (wa-la-ʿadhābu al-ākhirati akhzā) is a precaution lest the listeners suppose that the share of those people of punishment is the torment of destruction by the wind; so it is followed by the report that the torment of the Hereafter is more ignominious, that is, for them and for everyone who is tormented in this world by God's wrath upon him.

Akhzā is an elative (ism al-tafḍīl) formed contrary to analogy; its analogical form would be "ashaddu ikhzāʾan" (more intense in humiliation), since one does not say khazāhu meaning akhzāhu, i.e., he humiliated him. A similar formation of the elative is frequent in usage.

The clause "and they will not be helped" (wa-hum lā yunṣarūn) is a conclusion (tadhyīl), i.e., no one will help them to repel the torment from them, nor anyone who will intercede for them, nor anyone who will bring them out of it after a respite.

﴿Then as for ʿĀd, they were arrogant on earth without right, and said, "Who is mightier than us in strength?" Did they not see that God, who created them, is mightier than them in strength? And they used to deny Our signs.﴾ ﴿So We sent upon them a furious wind, on days of misfortune, that We might let them taste the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world. But the punishment of the Hereafter is more disgracing, and they will not be helped.﴾

After mentioning what ʿĀd and Thamūd shared, namely obstinacy and persistence in disbelief, he now details some of the particular forms of disbelief that each of the two nations was distinguished by, and he mentions those that relate to the punishment that befell each nation.

[p. 256]

The *fāʾ* (فَ) is a consequential connective (*tafrīʿ*) following the sentence ﴿They said, "If our Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels"﴾ [Fussilat: 14], which implies that they rejected the call of their two messengers and did not accept their guidance and reasoning.

As for *ammā* (أمّا), it is a conditional and differentiating particle, and its discussion has already been given when God says ﴿As for those who believe, they know that it is the truth from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The meaning is: As for ʿĀd, their arrogance prevented them from accepting guidance.

*Istikbār* (اسْتِكْبار) is an intensification of *kibr* (الكِبْر), that is, considering oneself great and despising people. The *sīn* and *tāʾ* in it are for intensification, like *istajāba* (اسْتَجابَ). The definiteness of "the earth" (الأرْض) is for a known reference, that is, their known land. The reason why arrogance is mentioned among their faults is that their pride was what diverted them from following their messenger and from anticipating God's punishment.

His saying *bi-ghayri al-ḥaqq* (بِغَيْرِ الحَقِّ), "without right," is an added censure of their arrogance, for arrogance is never with right, since there is no justification for pride in any respect. All the things that tempt a person toward pride, such as knowledge, wealth, authority, strength, and other things, do not bring a human being to a state free of deficiency, and a weak deficient person has no right to pride. For this reason, pride is among the attributes peculiar to God the Exalted. They had been deceived by the strength of their bodies and the might of their nation, and they claimed that no one could overcome them. This is the meaning of their saying (﴿Who is mightier than us in strength?﴾). Thus their saying that is the cause of their arrogance, because it produced in them contempt for all others. When Hūd came to them denying what they were upon of idolatry and tyranny, this greatly offended them, because they had become accustomed to self-admiration and to their own condition, so they denied their messenger.

Since their self-deception through their strength was what drove them to disbelief, and their saying (﴿Who is mightier than us in strength?﴾) was an evidence of it, it was singled out for mention.

It was introduced with the conjunction *wa* (و) even though it serves as an explanation of God's words ﴿they were arrogant on earth without right﴾, to indicate that it is independently what makes them deserving of censure, because their saying itself is a reprehensible utterance. So it was mentioned by coordination with the verb *istakbarū* (اسْتَكْبَرُوا), because the nature of coordination requires difference between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined, and it informs us by context that this saying was what prompted them to arrogance.

[p. 257]

The clause ﴿Did they not see that God, who created them, is mightier than them in strength?﴾ is a parenthetical clause (*jumla muʿtaridha*), and the *wāw* in it is parenthetical (*iʿtirāḍiyya*). *Al-ruʾya* (الرُّؤْيَة) here is cognitive ("seeing" in the sense of knowing), and the interrogative is one of denial. The meaning is a denunciation of their lack of knowledge that God is mightier than them in strength, since they turned away from the messenger of their Lord and from his warning to them, turning away like one who pays no attention to the greatness of God the Exalted. For if they had reckoned with it, they would have anticipated His punishment, and they would have turned toward the proofs of their messenger's truthfulness.

The attribute *alladhī khalaqahum* (الَّذِي خَلَقَهم), "who created them," is applied to the name of majesty (Allah) because of what the relative clause carries of an allusion to the reason for the denunciation of them, namely their ignorance that God is stronger than them. For their being created is known to them by necessity, so knowledge of this was sufficient to indicate that He is mightier than them in strength, and that He is worthy of their reckoning His anger, so that they would look into the evidences of the truthfulness of His messenger that were brought to them.

The pronoun in *huwa ashaddu minhum* (هو أشَدُّ مِنهم) is a *ḍamīr al-faṣl* (ضمير الفصل, the separating pronoun), and it serves to strengthen the judgment by making its clarity more evident. When that judgment is established, their lack of knowledge of its requirement becomes more shameful, and their excuse for ignorance of it is removed.

The true meaning of *al-quwwa* (القُوَّة) is a state in the body by which one is able to perform arduous actions. It is also applied to what follows from that of power and the means of accomplishing actions. Its application was explained earlier in God's words ﴿so take it with strength﴾ in Surat al-Aʿrāf. Here what is intended is its literal, metaphorical (*kināʾī*), and figurative (*majāzī*) senses. It is used in its literal meaning explicitly and by metaphor, and its figurative sense refers to the means of subduing difficult matters that they possessed, through the strength of their bodies and the strength of their minds. The Arabs use ʿĀd as a proverbial example for the soundness of their opinions, so they say "the wisdom of ʿĀd" (أحْلامُ عادٍ). Al-Nābigha said:

"The wisdom of ʿĀd, and bodies purified
From the defect, the calamities, and the sin."

And they say, describing things whose like is rarely made, *ʿādiyya* (عادِيَّة): "an ʿādiyya well" (بِئْرٌ عادِيَّةٌ), and "an ʿādī building" (بِناءٌ عادِيٌّ).

Since strength entails breadth of power, he attributed strength to God the Exalted, in the sense that His power is not thwarted by anything whose existence His will is related to. This is what is meant here in His words ﴿that God, who created them, is mightier than them in strength﴾, that is, He is of greater power than their power. So the application of *quwwa* to the power of God the Exalted means perfection of power, that is, the generality of its effect and its relation to all possible things in accordance with will, such that no possible thing is beyond the reach of His power, and the perfection of His self-sufficiency from being affected by others. This was discussed earlier in His words ﴿Indeed God is strong and severe in punishment﴾ in Surat al-Anfāl.

[p. 258]

The clause ﴿Did they not see that God, who created them, is mightier than them in strength﴾ is a parenthetical clause between the conjoined clauses, and the *wāw* in it is parenthetical.

As for His words *wa-kānū bi-āyātinā yajḥadūn* (وكانُوا بِآياتِنا يَجْحَدُونَ), "and they used to deny Our signs," it may be that what is meant by the signs (*āyāt*) is the miracles of their messenger Hūd, but they did not believe in them and persisted in obstinacy. The Qur'an does not mention for Hūd any signs other than that he warned them of a punishment coming to them from the sky. God says ﴿But when they saw it as a cloud approaching their valleys, they said, "This is a cloud bringing us rain." Rather, it is what you sought to hasten: a wind in which is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Aḥqāf: 24]. This is part of their denial of the first signs.

It may also be that what is meant by the signs is the proofs of divine unity contained in the call of their messenger, and reminders of God's blessings upon them, as in His words ﴿And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah and increased you in stature abundantly﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 69], and His words ﴿Fear the One who has provided you with what you know﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 132], ﴿He has provided you with livestock and sons﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 133], ﴿and gardens and springs﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 134].

The verb *kānū* (كانُوا) indicates that denial of the signs was rooted in them. The form of the present tense in *yajḥadūn* (يَجْحَدُونَ) indicates that denial was recurrent in them and renewed.

On this he arranged the description of their punishment: that God sent upon them a wind. The *fāʾ* indicates that their punishment was caused by the state of their disbelief in its manner, for what drove their disbelief was their self-deception through their strength. So God destroyed them with what people do not expect destruction by. For people say of a thing that is not regarded: "It is a wind" (هو رِيحٌ), so that He might show them that God is of great might, and that He places might in a light thing like the wind so that it becomes a punishment and disgrace, that is, a humiliation, as He said ﴿that We might let them taste the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world﴾. And what disgrace is greater than that the wind should hurl them into the air like feathers, and cast them down dead upon the ground, all of them, so that passersby see them in their dwellings as corpses lying prostrate, their skins shriveled and their bodies decayed, as if they were trunks of hollow palm trees?

[p. 259]

*Al-rīḥ* (الرِّيح) is a movement in the air that arises from the alternation of heat and cold, and its waves travel as the waves of the sea travel. The wind that struck ʿĀd is the *dabūr* (الدَّبُور), which blows from the direction of the sunset. It was named *dabūr* with a fatḥa on the *dāl* and a lightened *bāʾ*, because it blows from the direction of the back (*dubur*) of the Kaʿba. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I was helped by the *ṣabā* (east wind), and ʿĀd was destroyed by the *dabūr* (west wind)."

The wind that struck ʿĀd had this power only because of a strong compression in the air that was not customary. For compression makes a weak thing strong, as has been observed in our age: minute bodies made of chemical parts called the atom become, by compression, capable of destroying an entire city. This is called atomic energy, and by it a large part of the land of Japan was destroyed in the World War.

*Al-ṣarṣar* (الصَّرْصَر) is the violent wind that has a *ṣarṣara*, that is, a loud noise in its blowing, because of the intensity of the speed of its movement. The doubling of its middle radical is for intensifying its severity among the members of its kind, like the doubling of *kubkib* for intensifying *kabb*. Its root is *ṣarra*, that is, it cried out. It is a descriptive word whose form is not feminized, because it applies only to wind, and wind is of feminine grammatical gender by implication.

*Al-naḥisāt* (النَّحِسات), with a fatḥa on the *nūn* and sukūn on the *ḥāʾ*, is the plural of *naḥis* without feminine marking, because it is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) of the verb *naḥisa* like *ʿalima*, as in God's words ﴿on a day of continuous misfortune﴾ [al-Qamar: 19].

Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, and Yaʿqūb read it with sukūn on the *ḥāʾ*. It is permissible to read it with kasra on the *ḥāʾ*, and the rest of the readers (al-baqiyya) read it thus, as an adjective (ṣifa mushabbaha) from *naḥs*, when one is struck by *naḥs*, that is, by evil or severe harm.

Its opposite is *bakht* (البَخْت), good fortune, in the imagination of the common people. Neither *naḥs* nor *bakht* has any reality, but they are both accidents that befall a person. *Naḥs* befalls him from the badness of his character and temperament, or from his negligence, or from the corruption of his environment or his people. *Bakht* befalls him as a result of the opposite of these. Some of both kinds are chance matters, and perhaps some of them are a recompense from God for a good or evil deed of His servants, or in their religion, as happened to ʿĀd and the people of the pre-Islamic age (*ahl al-jāhiliyya*). Most nations imagine *naḥs* and *bakht* to be a kind of *ṭiyara* (طِيَرة, superstitious omen-reading) and of *tashāʾum* (تَشاؤُم, belief in ill omen) and *tayammun* (تَيَمُّن, belief in good omen). From it come *zajr* (زَجْر, omen-reading by birds' movements) and *ʿiyāfa* (عِيافَة, omen-reading by birds) among the Arabs in the pre-Islamic age, and from it come the belief that events are foretold by the stars and the days among most ignorant or corrupt-creed nations. Islam refuted all of this, that is, uncovered its falsehood, with what no earlier teaching among the religions that appeared before Islam had preceded.

So the meaning of describing the days as *naḥisāt* is that they were days of great evil that befell them, namely the punishment of the wind. They were eight days, as God said ﴿He subjected it against them for seven nights and eight days in succession﴾ [al-Ḥāqqa: 7]. The meaning is that those specific days were misfortune, and that their misfortune was upon them and not upon other people on earth, because ʿĀd were the ones targeted by the punishment. It does not mean that those days recur every year as days of misfortune for humankind, for that is not sound, since it would require that all nations suffered evil on those days.

Those days were described as *naḥisāt* because nothing happened in them but evil for them: the suffering of crushing blows that inevitably led to death, the sight of their dead relatives, the death of their livestock, and the uprooting of their palm trees.

The storytellers (*ahl al-qiṣaṣ*) invented the naming of eight days, half of which are the last part of the month of Shabāṭ and half the month of Ādhār, in which winds commonly blow frequently, and they called them *ayyām al-ḥusūm* (أيّام الحُسُوم, "days of unbroken continuity"). Then they built on this that these are the days described with *ḥusūm* in God's words in Surat al-Ḥāqqa ﴿He subjected it against them for seven nights and eight days in succession﴾ [al-Ḥāqqa: 7]. They claimed that these are the days corresponding to the days of the wind that struck ʿĀd. Then they built on that that these are days of misfortune every year, and they lied about some of the early authorities, such as Ibn ʿAbbās, with fabrications about this. This is "a handful of thorns upon a bundle of thorns" (ḍighth ʿalā ibāla), and a variation in the illusions of error.

*Naḥisāt* (نَحِساتٍ) was pluralized with *alif* and *tāʾ* because it is an adjective for a plural of non-rational beings, namely *ayyām* (أيّام, days).

The *lām* in *li-nudhīqahum* (لِنُذِيقَهم) is for causation and is related to *arsalnā* (أرْسَلْنا). The "tasting" (*idhāqa*, إذاقَة) is an imaginative representation (*takhyīl*) within a metaphor (*makniyya*): the punishment is likened to a food prepared for them, in the manner of mockery (*tahakkum*), just as ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm called the raid "hospitality" (*qirā*) in his saying:

[p. 260]

"We hosted you, then we hastened your hospitality
Just before dawn, a crushing, grinding (blow)."

[p. 261]

The "tasting" is an imaginative representation (*takhyīl*) drawn from the things that are agreeable in the food that is the object of comparison.

Al-khizy (ignominy) means humiliation. The annexation of "torment" (ʿadhāb) to "ignominy" (al-khizy) is the annexation of a qualified noun to its qualifier, as evidenced by its contrast with the phrase "and the torment of the Hereafter is more ignominious" (wa-la-ʿadhābu al-ākhirati akhzā), meaning it is more intensely humiliating than the humiliation of the torment of this world. This is because ignominy is a description of the torment through the usage of a verbal noun or noun of action, for the sake of emphasis on that torment being humiliating to the one who is tormented by it.

The meaning of the torment being humiliating is that it is a cause of ignominy. Describing the torment as "ignominy" in the sense of "humiliating" is metaphor of the rational kind (al-majāz al-ʿaqlī). Before the annexation, it would be estimated as: "that We may make them taste a torment of ignominy" (li-nudhīqahum ʿadhāban khizyan), i.e., humiliating. When the annexation of the qualified noun to its qualifier was intended, it was said: "the torment of ignominy" (ʿadhāb al-khizy), also for emphasis, because the annexation of the qualified noun to its qualifier is an emphasis on the attribute, to the extent that the qualifier is treated as though it were another person to whom the qualified noun is annexed. This is close to the figure of speech known as muḥassin al-tajrīd. Thus two emphases arise in the phrase "ʿadhāb al-khizy": the emphasis of describing with a verbal noun, and the emphasis of annexing the qualified noun to its qualifier.

The clause "and the torment of the Hereafter is more ignominious" (wa-la-ʿadhābu al-ākhirati akhzā) is a precaution lest the listeners suppose that the share of those people of punishment is the torment of destruction by the wind; so it is followed by the report that the torment of the Hereafter is more ignominious, that is, for them and for everyone who is tormented in this world by God's wrath upon him.

Akhzā is an elative (ism al-tafḍīl) formed contrary to analogy; its analogical form would be "ashaddu ikhzāʾan" (more intense in humiliation), since one does not say khazāhu meaning akhzāhu, i.e., he humiliated him. A similar formation of the elative is frequent in usage.

The clause "and they will not be helped" (wa-hum lā yunṣarūn) is a conclusion (tadhyīl), i.e., no one will help them to repel the torment from them, nor anyone who will intercede for them, nor anyone who will bring them out of it after a respite.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 41, verse 17:

Page 262
﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance, so the thunderbolt of the humiliating punishment seized them for what they had earned.﴾

The remainder of the detail found in His saying: "As for 'Ad, they were arrogant."

Since the condition of the two nations was one in their refusal of guidance from Allah, Exalted is He, as His saying Exalted is He indicates, "They said: Had our Lord willed, He would have sent down angels" (41:14), the report about Thamud, that Allah guided them, implies that He guided 'Ad in the same way He guided Thamud, and that 'Ad preferred blindness over guidance just as Thamud did.

The meaning: "As for Thamud, We guided them" with the guidance of instruction (irshad), by sending to them Our Messenger and supporting him with the sign of the she-camel which We brought forth for them from the earth.

So the guidance intended here is the guidance of instruction and obligation (al-irshad al-taklifi), and it is other than the guidance in His saying: "Whomever Allah guides, none can mislead him" (39:37), for that is the guidance of creation (al-hidayah al-takwiniyyah), since it is contrasted with His saying: "And whomever Allah misleads, none can guide him."

"Istahabbu al-'ama" (they preferred blindness) means: they loved it. The sin and the ta' here are for emphasis, like them in His saying "They were arrogant upon the earth without right" (41:15), meaning blindness was beloved to them.

"Al-'ama" here is a metaphor for misguidance in opinion, i.e., they chose error by their own earning. "Istahabbu" has been made to imply the meaning of "fa-dallu" (they went astray), and what made this implicit meaning possible is its being joined with the sin and ta' for emphasis, because intensity in love entails preference over the rest of the beloved things. For this reason "istahabbu" was followed by the particle "ʿala" (over), i.e., they preferred by their choice. And the linking of "ʿala al-huda" (over guidance) with the verb "istahabbu" is because it implies the meaning of "faddalu" (they favored) and "athharu" (they chose).

And it is followed by: "So the thunderbolt of the humiliating punishment seized them." The punishment was appropriate to the offence, because they preferred misguidance, which is like blindness; whoever prefers it, his state is to love blindness. So their recompense was the thunderbolt, because it blinds their eyes at the same time as it destroys them. Allah, Exalted is He, said: "The lightning nearly snatches away their sight" (2:20).

Page 263
"Al-akhdh" (seizing) is a metaphor for a destructive strike, because it is a contact with the one destroyed that removes him from life, so it is as if it were a seizing by the hand.

"Al-sa'iqah" (the thunderbolt): the cry that arises from the electrical charge of the water-bearing cloud, whereby fire is struck out of it that destroys whatever it strikes. The annexation of "sa'iqah" to "al-'adhab" (the punishment) serves to indicate that it is a thunderbolt defined by way of annexation, since a thing is defined by annexation only through what it is annexed to, meaning a thunderbolt that breaks the customary pattern of thunderbolts. It is thus a thunderbolt subjected by Allah to the punishment of Thamud, for the original sense of the annexation is that it implies the particle of possession (lam al-ikhtisas), so the definiteness of the annexed noun has no way except by showing its exclusive connection to the noun it is annexed to.

"Al-'adhab" is: destruction by the thunderbolt. It is described as "al-hun" (humiliating), just as the punishment is described as "al-khizy" (disgrace) in His saying: "That We may make them taste the punishment of disgrace" (41:16), i.e., the punishment which is the cause of humiliation. "Al-hun" means "al-hawan," which is abasement and humiliation. The reason it is abasement is that it is a destruction containing degradation, as they were uprooted root and branch and left prostrate on the face of the earth, as we explained regarding the destruction of 'Ad.

That is: the thunderbolt seized them because of their earning, in their choosing to remain upon misguidance by turning away from the call of their Messenger and from the indication of his signs.

It is known from His saying regarding 'Ad, "And the punishment of the Hereafter is more humiliating" (41:16), that Thamud also has a punishment in the Hereafter, because the two nations were alike in disbelief; so that was not mentioned here, being sufficient with its mention in what preceded. This is the embellishment of brevity (muhassin al-iktifa'), and it is an embellishment that returns to conciseness (al-ijaz).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 41, verse 18:

﴿And We saved those who believed and used to be God-fearing.﴾

The more apparent view is that this is a conjunction (ʿatf) with the detailed account in His words ﴿As for ʿAd, they waxed arrogant﴾ [Fussilat: 15], and what is conjoined to it, His words ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them﴾ [Fussilat: 17]. This is because the position of this sentence, which includes the deliverance of the believers from the punishment after the punishment of ʿAd and the punishment of Thamud has been mentioned, indicates that the meaning is the deliverance of those who believed from the people of ʿAd and the people of Thamud. Thus the content of this sentence carries the sense of an exception from the generality of the two nations of ʿAd and Thamud, and so it has the ruling of the exception that follows a series of successive sentences: that it refers back to all of them.

The two detailed sentences are the intended subject, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿So when Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him by mercy from Us﴾ [Hud: 58], and He said: ﴿So when Our command came, We saved Salih and those who believed with him by mercy from Us﴾ [Hud: 66]. We have already explained in Surat Hud how God saved Hud and those who believed with him, and Salih and those who believed with him.

His words (﴿and used to be God-fearing﴾) mean: their custom was guarding against God and considering what would save them from His wrath and His punishment. This is more eloquent in description than saying "and the God-fearing" (al-muttaqin).

[p. 265 begins mid-passage]

When [Ibn 'Ashur] finished admonishing the polytheists with the condition of the peoples before them who denied their messengers, and warning them of a punishment that would befall them in this world as it befell those peoples, so that this would serve them as a lesson (ʿibrah), since invoking examples and parallels (al-mathal wa-l-naẓāʾir) has an effect on the soul by which it takes heed in a way it does not through the description of abstract meanings, he moved on to warn them about what would befall them in the Hereafter. The clause ﴿And [mention] the Day when We gather the enemies of Allah to the Fire, and they will be driven in ranks﴾ and what follows is coordinated (maʿṭūfah) upon the clause "Say: I have warned you of a thunderbolt" and so on. The implied sense is: "And warn them of the Day when We gather the enemies of Allah to the Fire." This implied element is indicated by his saying "I have warned you of a thunderbolt," etc., meaning: "And warn them of the Day of the punishment of the Hereafter."

The "enemies of Allah" are the polytheists of Quraysh, because they are the enemies of His Messenger ﷺ. Allah says: ﴿O you who believe, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [60:1], meaning the polytheists, as is shown by His words that follow: ﴿they expel the Messenger and yourselves﴾ [60:1]. It is also because that verse was revealed concerning the affair of the letter of Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah to Quraysh, informing them of the Prophet's ﷺ preparations to invade Makkah; and because of His words at the end of these verses: ﴿That is the recompense of the enemies of Allah﴾ [41:28], after His words: ﴿And those who disbelieve say: Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it, that perhaps you may prevail﴾ [41:26].

It is not permissible for the intended meaning of "enemies of Allah" to be all the disbelievers of the nations, in such a way that the polytheists of Quraysh would enter it as part of the general category, because that interpretation would not have an elegant placement in this context. The purpose of mentioning what befell ʿAd and Thamud is to threaten the polytheists of Makkah with the descent of a punishment like theirs in this world, since they already knew of it and saw its traces; so a threat with its like has a force that they cannot ignore. As for the punishment of ʿAd and Thamud in the Hereafter, it is promised for the future, and they do not believe in it; therefore it is not fitting to make it an admonition to Quraysh. Rather, it is more appropriate that the warning to Quraysh be stated directly with a punishment they will suffer in the Hereafter. For this reason its description was lengthened to magnify its terror, more than was lengthened with its like when the punishment of ʿAd in the Hereafter was mentioned in the words: ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is more disgraceful﴾ [41:16], which sufficed without mention of the punishment of Thamud. Therefore there is no explicit noun in the place of a pronoun in His words "the enemies of Allah" (in place of a pronoun referring to ʿAd and Thamud).

It is also possible that "﴿And [mention] the Day when We gather the enemies of Allah﴾" is an object (mafʿūl) of an omitted verb "uthkur" (remember), like its many counterparts.

Al-ḥashr (gathering) is: bringing people together in a place for a purpose.

The phrase "to the Fire" is connected to "We gather," with "We gather" construed to include the meaning of "We send," i.e., We send them to the Fire.

The fāʾ in His words ﴿so they will be driven in ranks﴾ is coordinating and consequential upon "We gather," because gathering (customarily) requires driving them, as it is one of its necessary implications: gathering entails a great number of those gathered, and a great number entails confusion and some of them mixing with others, so they have no need to be driven and sorted, and some of them to be turned back from others.

Al-wazʿ (driving/restraining) is: restraining some of them from others and preventing them from disorder. It was discussed in Surat al-Naml. It is a metonymy for the great number of those gathered.

Nāfiʿ and Yaʿqūb read "naḥshuru" with the first-person plural of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓamah), in the active voice, and with "aʿdāʾa" in the accusative. The rest read it with the third-person masculine (yāʾ al-ghāʾib), in the passive voice.

Ḥattā here is ibtidāʾiyyah (introducing a new clause), and it conveys the sense of a limit (ghāyah), so it is a particle of termination in meaning and a particle of beginning in form; that is, what follows it is a new, resumed sentence (jumlah mustaʾnafah).

[p. 266]

"Idhā" is a temporal adverb for the future that includes the meaning of a conditional, and it is connected to its response. "Mā" is an emphatic addition after "idhā," which emphasizes the connection of "idhā" with the verb that follows it, whether it is conditional, as in this verse, or merely temporal, as in His words: ﴿and when they become angry, they forgive﴾ [42:37]. It appears that the occurrence of "mā" after "idhā" strengthens the conditional meaning of "idhā," and perhaps the conditional meaning in this case is explicitly intended as a possibility.

The feminine third-person pronoun in "jāʾūhā" refers to the Fire, meaning: when they reach Jahannam.

The clause ﴿their hearing, their sight and their skins will testify against them﴾ and so on: the statements of the exegetes imply that it is the response to "idhā," so the connection between its condition and its response and the linking of it with the verb of the response required this. They sensed that the testimony against them would occur before they were brought to the Fire, so they supposed an omitted verb, its estimate being: "They were asked about what they used to do, and they denied it, so their hearing, sight and skins testified against them," meaning: the keepers of the Fire asked them.

Better than that, we may say: the response to "idhā" is omitted for the sake of terrifying effect, and omission of its like is frequent in the Qur'an, and the clause "their hearing will testify against them" through its end is a resumptive sentence of explanatory resumption (istiʾnāf bayānī), arising from the meaning of the limit conveyed by "ḥattā," because the questioner seeks what happened between their being gathered to the Fire and their presence at the Fire. He is answered that their hearing, sight and skins testified against them, up to His words "who made every thing speak." This implies that they were held to account for their deeds, and they denied them, so their limbs and bodies testified against them.

Or the response to "idhā" is His words: ﴿So if they endure, the Fire is their abode﴾ [41:24], and so on.

The clause ﴿their hearing and their sight testified against them﴾ and what is conjoined to it is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ) between the condition and its response.

The testimony of their limbs and skins against them is a testimony of rebuke and exposure, because the fact that it is testimony implies that when they saw the Fire, they excused themselves by denying some of their sins, hoping to lighten the punishment; otherwise, Allah knows what they were doing, and the guardians (al-ḥafaẓah) testified to it, and their book was read to them, and they were brought to the Fire only after their condemnation had been established. So the testimony of their limbs was nothing but an increase in their disgrace, regret, and remorse over their bad belief in the vastness of Allah's knowledge.

The specification of hearing, sight and skins for testimony against these people, rather than the rest of the limbs, is because hearing has a particular relation to receiving the Prophet's ﷺ call and receiving the verses of the Qur'an. So their hearing testifies against them that they used to turn it away from hearing that, as Allah related of them in His words: ﴿and in our ears is deafness﴾ [41:5]. And because sight has a particular relation to observing the signs in created things, which indicate that Allah the Exalted alone creates and governs, and that is the proof of His oneness in divinity. And the testimony of the skins is because the skin encompasses the whole body, so the testimony of the skins against them is a testimony against themselves, so that their deserving of burning in the Fire becomes evident for the rest of the bodies, without being limited to burning the place of hearing and sight.

For this reason they limited the blame directed at them to their skins, because the skins contain all the senses and limbs. By this the reason for limiting the testimony to hearing, sight and skins here becomes clear, unlike the verse in Surat al-Nur: ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands and their feet will testify against them concerning what they used to do﴾ [24:24], because the verse of al-Nur describes those who accuse chaste women, who were the ones who fabricated the slander of the lie and walked in gatherings spreading it among people, pointing with their hands at the one they falsely accused.

They said "to their skins: Why did you testify against us?" rather than saying it to their hearing and sight, because the skins are what faces them, and they turn to them with blame.

The use of the pronouns of hearing, sight and skins with the forms of the plural pronoun for rational beings is because addressing them as interlocutors made them like rational beings on that day. Among the strange interpretations is the view of those who claimed that "the skins" means the private parts, attributed to al-Suddi and al-Farra', and this is an obstinate reading of the verse for which there is no justification at all. On this interpretation Ahmad al-Jurjani built in his book Kinayat al-Udaba' (Metonymies of the Men of Letters), counting "skins" among the metonymies for private parts, attributing it to the exegetes, and he overreached in his expression.

The interrogative in their words ﴿Why did you testify against us?﴾ [41:21] is used in the sense of blame, and they assume that

[p. 268]

their skins, being part of them, have no right to testify against them, because it draws punishment toward them.

The use of an interrogative about the reason in the context of reproach is common, as in His words: ﴿Why do you argue about what you have no knowledge of?﴾ [3:66].

The skins' saying ﴿Allah made us speak﴾ [41:21] is an excuse that the testimony came from them without their choice.

This speech is one of the extraordinary events, as is the nature of the otherworldly realm. Their saying ﴿who made every thing speak﴾ [41:21] is a glorification of Allah the Exalted, and it has no connection with the excuse. The meaning is: the One who made every thing that has speech among the animals speak, and the variation in the significance of their sounds indicates their feelings. So the generality of "every thing" is restricted by custom.

When [Ibn 'Ashur] finished admonishing the polytheists with the condition of the peoples before them who denied their messengers, and warning them of a punishment that would befall them in this world as it befell those peoples, so that this would serve them as a lesson (ʿibrah), since invoking examples and parallels (al-mathal wa-l-naẓāʾir) has an effect on the soul by which it takes heed in a way it does not through the description of abstract meanings, he moved on to warn them about what would befall them in the Hereafter. This implied element is indicated by his saying "I have warned you of a thunderbolt," etc., meaning: "And warn them of the Day of the punishment of the Hereafter."

Allah says: ﴿O you who believe, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [60:1], meaning the polytheists, as is shown by His words that follow: ﴿they expel the Messenger and yourselves﴾ [60:1]. It is also because that verse was revealed concerning the affair of the letter of Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah to Quraysh, informing them of the Prophet's ﷺ preparations to invade Makkah; and because of His words at the end of these verses: ﴿That is the recompense of the enemies of Allah﴾ [41:28], after His words: ﴿And those who disbelieve say: Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it, that perhaps you may prevail﴾ [41:26].

It is not permissible for the intended meaning of "enemies of Allah" to be all the disbelievers of the nations, in such a way that the polytheists of Quraysh would enter it as part of the general category, because that interpretation would not have an elegant placement in this context. The purpose of mentioning what befell ʿAd and Thamud is to threaten the polytheists of Makkah with the descent of a punishment like theirs in this world, since they already knew of it and saw its traces; so a threat with its like has a force that they cannot ignore. As for the punishment of ʿAd and Thamud in the Hereafter, it is promised for the future, and they do not believe in it; therefore it is not fitting to make it an admonition to Quraysh. Rather, it is more appropriate that the warning to Quraysh be stated directly with a punishment they will suffer in the Hereafter. For this reason its description was lengthened to magnify its terror, more than was lengthened with its like when the punishment of ʿAd in the Hereafter was mentioned in the words: ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is more disgraceful﴾ [41:16], which sufficed without mention of the punishment of Thamud. Therefore there is no explicit noun in the place of a pronoun in His words "the enemies of Allah" (in place of a pronoun referring to ʿAd and Thamud).

It is also possible that "﴿And [mention] the Day when We gather the enemies of Allah﴾" is an object (mafʿūl) of an omitted verb "uthkur" (remember), like its many counterparts.

Al-ḥashr (gathering) is: bringing people together in a place for a purpose.
