Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 41, verse 22–23:

﴿And you did not conceal yourselves lest your hearing and your sight and your skins should testify against you, but you thought that Allah does not know much of what you do.﴾ ﴿And that was your assumption which you assumed about your Lord; it has ruined you, and you have become among the losers.﴾

Few of the exegetes have undertaken to explain the connection of these three verses with what precedes them, and those who have undertaken it have not offered anything convincing. The most fitting statement on this is that of Ibn 'Atiyya, but it is concise and not well-edited. Some exegetes also mentioned a cause of revelation for them, and by doing so they added difficulty and did not clarify the disconnection. Let us begin with what the structure of the speech requires, and then come to what has been related regarding the cause of their revelation, in a manner that does not lead to a break.

It is permissible that the clause ﴿And you did not conceal yourselves﴾ in its entirety be coordinated (ma'tuf) upon the clause ﴿And He it is who created you the first time﴾ etc., so that it is included within the parenthetical insertion (i'tirad) connected to what precedes it, on both of the two interpretations previously mentioned concerning what precedes it.

It is also permissible that it be independent of it: either coordinated upon the clause ﴿And [mention] the Day when the enemies of Allah will be gathered to the Fire﴾ [Fussilat: 19] etc., or a parenthetical insertion between that clause and the clause ﴿So if they are patient, the Fire is their residence﴾ [Fussilat: 24], with the waw being parenthetical (i'tiradiyya). The reason for the parenthetical insertion is the mention that has occurred of the testimony of their hearing, their sight and their skins against them. Then the address is to all the living polytheists in this world, or to the polytheists on the Day of Resurrection.

On these aspects the meaning is: in this world you did not hide your polytheism and conceal it from others; rather you used to proclaim it openly and boast of following it. So what blame is there upon your limbs and bodies for testifying against you with that, since it was a well-known matter? Thus the word "istitar" (concealment) is used in the sense of informing, metaphorically,

Page 270

because the true meaning of istitar is concealing the essences, whereas what their limbs testified to is the belief in polytheism and the statements that call to it. The particle ma is a negation, by the indication of his saying after it "but you thought that Allah does not know" etc. A preposition that the verb (tastatirun) transmits to (an yashhada) must be assumed, and it is omitted in the well-known manner of omitting a preposition before "an", and its estimate is according to what the speech indicates; here the preposition min is estimated, meaning: you did not conceal yourselves from the testimony of your hearing, your sight and your skins, i.e., you were not screened from those witnesses, and you did not guard against their testimony, since you did not reckon that what you were upon would harm you, as you did not believe in the occurrence of the Day of Reckoning.

As for what has been transmitted regarding the cause of the revelation of the verse, it is the hadith in the two Sahihs and in the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi, with chains of narration some of which exceed others, traced to 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: "I was concealed behind the curtains of the Ka'ba when three men came: two Qurashis and a Thaqafi, or two Thaqafis and a Qurashi, few in understanding of their hearts, abundant in the fat of their bellies. They spoke words I did not understand. One of them said: 'Do you think Allah hears what we say?' The other said: 'He hears if we speak aloud, and does not hear if we conceal.' And another said: 'If He hears when we speak aloud, then He hears when we conceal.' 'Abd Allah said: 'I mentioned that to the Prophet ﷺ, and Allah the Exalted revealed ﴿And you did not conceal yourselves lest your hearing and your sight…﴾ to His saying ﴿…you have become among the losers.﴾" Taken at face value, this indicates that the one addressed is a specific group of people in a particular matter, while being fit to include whoever might have produced this same kind of act, because of the equality in thinking.

Its placement between the verses before and after it is considered strange. It is permissible that its revelation coincided with the time immediately following the revelation of the verse before it; and it is permissible that it was revealed at another time, and that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered it to be placed in this position for the sake of the connection with what is in the preceding verse of their hearing and their sight testifying.

Nevertheless, it is a Meccan verse, since the exegetes did not differ that the whole surah is Meccan. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It seems that this occurred after the conquest of Mecca, so the verse is Madani; and it seems that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited the verse as an illustration when 'Abd Allah informed him." End of quote. In his first statement there is a contradiction to what he and the other exegetes asserted decisively, that the whole surah is Meccan. How can his statement be sound when others have mentioned that the three men were: 'Abd Yalil al-Thaqafi, and Safwan and Rabi'a, the two sons of Umayya ibn Khalaf? As for 'Abd Yalil, he embraced Islam and had companionship according to Ibn Ishaq and a group; likewise Safwan ibn Umayya. As for Rabi'a ibn Umayya, no Islam is known for him, so it does not fit that the verse was revealed after the conquest of Mecca. The best part of Ibn 'Atiyya's statement is its second part, that the Prophet ﷺ recited the verse as an illustration, for that explains Ibn Mas'ud's saying "then Allah revealed the verse," and clarifies the aspect of the Prophet's ﷺ recitation of it when Ibn Mas'ud informed him: that he recited it to establish one example of the forms of the verse's meaning, namely that such a group are among those upon whom their hearing, sight and skins testify; and that indicates that these men were polytheists at that time, and the verse binds whoever of them died as a disbeliever, such as Rabi'a ibn Umayya ibn Khalaf.

On some of the possibilities of this interpretation, the verb tastatirun is used in its literal sense, i.e., you conceal your deeds from your hearing, sight and skins; and that is rebuke by way of kinaya (allusion) to the fact that they did not see what they were upon as ugly so as to hide from it.

On some of the possibilities mentioned, the verb tastatirun is used both in its literal and metaphorical sense, and there is no difficulty in distributing these categories of possibilities with one another in every estimate you propose.

The summary of the verse's meaning upon all the possibilities is: Allah is All-Knowing of your deeds and intentions; nothing of them is hidden from Him, whether you speak aloud or conceal; and Allah has no need of the testimony of your limbs against you. What brought you to this harm was nothing but your evil assumption about the majesty of Allah.

"And that was your assumption" — the demonstrative refers to the assumption derived from the verb ﴿you thought that Allah does not know much of what you do﴾. Pointing to it conveys its distinguishing with the utmost clarity and the exposure of its ugliness, as a proclamation of their error.

He followed the demonstrative with the apposition "your assumption" to increase its clarification, so that what follows of the predicate may settle firmly. The predicate is the verb "it has ruined you" and what branches from it.

"which you assumed about your Lord" is a relative clause qualifying "your assumption." The use of the relative pronoun, for what is in the relative clause of an indication to the reason for constructing the predicate, namely "it has ruined you" and what branches from it, i.e., the assumption you assumed about your Lord, a false assumption.

The turning away from the proper name Allah to "your Lord" is to draw attention to the error of their assumption, since they assumed that some of their deeds were hidden from His knowledge, although He is their Lord and Creator. How could He create them and their deeds be hidden from Him? This alludes to His saying ﴿Should He not know who created? And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾ [al-Mulk: 14], so in the description "your Lord" there is an allusion to this meaning.

"Irda'" (ruin) means destruction; it is said: radiya, like radiya (the same pattern), when he perished, i.e., died. Irda' is used metaphorically for casting into a bad condition, to the point of making them like the dead, for that is the furthest that is commonly understood among people as a bad condition. In the use of the predicate as a verb there is a restrictive force, i.e., nothing ruined you except your assumption of that, and this is a relative restriction: your assumption that Allah does not know your deeds ruined you, not the testimony of your limbs such that you would blame them; rather your assumption that Allah does not know your deeds ruined you, so you did not fear His punishment.

His saying ﴿so you have become among the losers﴾ is an image of their state, when they reckon that they have reached knowledge of what they should know of the affairs of Allah and felt secure in securing their happiness, while they did not know Allah with the knowledge due to Him; so they treated Allah in a manner He does not approve, and deserved the punishment from the very place they assumed salvation. Their state is thus likened to the state of the merchant who prepared for profit and then fell into loss.

The meaning is: he censured them for their faulty reasoning and corrupt analogy in divine matters, and for their analogizing the unseen upon the seen. These are the principles that lured them into error: they denied the mission of human beings from Allah, denied the resurrection, then affirmed partners with Allah in divinity; and there branched out for them from all of that the severing of their attention from what lies beyond the worldly life and their sense of security from consequences in the worldly life. That is the sum of His saying the Exalted: ﴿And that was your assumption which you assumed about your Lord; it has ruined you, and you have become among the losers.﴾

Know that the causes of error in all beliefs come upon people only from corrupt reflection, hastiness in certainty, and failure to distinguish between sound proofs and resembling proofs; and all of that leads to delusion, expressed by the evil or false assumption.

Allah has mentioned something similar concerning the hypocrites, that their assumption is the assumption of the people of ignorance, saying ﴿They assume about Allah other than the truth, the assumption of ignorance﴾ [Al 'Imran: 154]. So let the believers beware of falling into such delusions, lest they suffer some of what was censured in the worshippers of idols.

The Prophet ﷺ has said: "Beware of assumption, for assumption is the most false of speech," meaning the assumption for which there is no proof.

And "you have become" (asbahtum) means "you became" (sirtum), because asbaha frequently comes in the sense of sara (to become).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 41, verse 22–23:

﴿And you did not conceal yourselves lest your hearing and your sight and your skins should testify against you, but you thought that Allah does not know much of what you do.﴾ ﴿And that was your assumption which you assumed about your Lord; it has ruined you, and you have become among the losers.﴾

Few of the exegetes have undertaken to explain the connection of these three verses with what precedes them, and those who have undertaken it have not offered anything convincing. The most fitting statement on this is that of Ibn 'Atiyya, but it is concise and not well-edited. Some exegetes also mentioned a cause of revelation for them, and by doing so they added difficulty and did not clarify the disconnection. Let us begin with what the structure of the speech requires, and then come to what has been related regarding the cause of their revelation, in a manner that does not lead to a break.

It is permissible that the clause ﴿And you did not conceal yourselves﴾ in its entirety be coordinated (ma'tuf) upon the clause ﴿And He it is who created you the first time﴾ etc., so that it is included within the parenthetical insertion (i'tirad) connected to what precedes it, on both of the two interpretations previously mentioned concerning what precedes it.

It is also permissible that it be independent of it: either coordinated upon the clause ﴿And [mention] the Day when the enemies of Allah will be gathered to the Fire﴾ [Fussilat: 19] etc., or a parenthetical insertion between that clause and the clause ﴿So if they are patient, the Fire is their residence﴾ [Fussilat: 24], with the waw being parenthetical (i'tiradiyya). The reason for the parenthetical insertion is the mention that has occurred of the testimony of their hearing, their sight and their skins against them. Then the address is to all the living polytheists in this world, or to the polytheists on the Day of Resurrection.

On these aspects the meaning is: in this world you did not hide your polytheism and conceal it from others; rather you used to proclaim it openly and boast of following it. So what blame is there upon your limbs and bodies for testifying against you with that, since it was a well-known matter? Thus the word "istitar" (concealment) is used in the sense of informing, metaphorically,

Page 270

because the true meaning of istitar is concealing the essences, whereas what their limbs testified to is the belief in polytheism and the statements that call to it. The particle ma is a negation, by the indication of his saying after it "but you thought that Allah does not know" etc. A preposition that the verb (tastatirun) transmits to (an yashhada) must be assumed, and it is omitted in the well-known manner of omitting a preposition before "an", and its estimate is according to what the speech indicates; here the preposition min is estimated, meaning: you did not conceal yourselves from the testimony of your hearing, your sight and your skins, i.e., you were not screened from those witnesses, and you did not guard against their testimony, since you did not reckon that what you were upon would harm you, as you did not believe in the occurrence of the Day of Reckoning.

As for what has been transmitted regarding the cause of the revelation of the verse, it is the hadith in the two Sahihs and in the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi, with chains of narration some of which exceed others, traced to 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: "I was concealed behind the curtains of the Ka'ba when three men came: two Qurashis and a Thaqafi, or two Thaqafis and a Qurashi, few in understanding of their hearts, abundant in the fat of their bellies. They spoke words I did not understand. One of them said: 'Do you think Allah hears what we say?' The other said: 'He hears if we speak aloud, and does not hear if we conceal.' And another said: 'If He hears when we speak aloud, then He hears when we conceal.' 'Abd Allah said: 'I mentioned that to the Prophet ﷺ, and Allah the Exalted revealed ﴿And you did not conceal yourselves lest your hearing and your sight…﴾ to His saying ﴿…you have become among the losers.﴾" Taken at face value, this indicates that the one addressed is a specific group of people in a particular matter, while being fit to include whoever might have produced this same kind of act, because of the equality in thinking.

Its placement between the verses before and after it is considered strange. It is permissible that its revelation coincided with the time immediately following the revelation of the verse before it; and it is permissible that it was revealed at another time, and that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered it to be placed in this position for the sake of the connection with what is in the preceding verse of their hearing and their sight testifying.

Nevertheless, it is a Meccan verse, since the exegetes did not differ that the whole surah is Meccan. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It seems that this occurred after the conquest of Mecca, so the verse is Madani; and it seems that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited the verse as an illustration when 'Abd Allah informed him." End of quote. In his first statement there is a contradiction to what he and the other exegetes asserted decisively, that the whole surah is Meccan. How can his statement be sound when others have mentioned that the three men were: 'Abd Yalil al-Thaqafi, and Safwan and Rabi'a, the two sons of Umayya ibn Khalaf? As for 'Abd Yalil, he embraced Islam and had companionship according to Ibn Ishaq and a group; likewise Safwan ibn Umayya. As for Rabi'a ibn Umayya, no Islam is known for him, so it does not fit that the verse was revealed after the conquest of Mecca. The best part of Ibn 'Atiyya's statement is its second part, that the Prophet ﷺ recited the verse as an illustration, for that explains Ibn Mas'ud's saying "then Allah revealed the verse," and clarifies the aspect of the Prophet's ﷺ recitation of it when Ibn Mas'ud informed him: that he recited it to establish one example of the forms of the verse's meaning, namely that such a group are among those upon whom their hearing, sight and skins testify; and that indicates that these men were polytheists at that time, and the verse binds whoever of them died as a disbeliever, such as Rabi'a ibn Umayya ibn Khalaf.

On some of the possibilities of this interpretation, the verb tastatirun is used in its literal sense, i.e., you conceal your deeds from your hearing, sight and skins; and that is rebuke by way of kinaya (allusion) to the fact that they did not see what they were upon as ugly so as to hide from it.

On some of the possibilities mentioned, the verb tastatirun is used both in its literal and metaphorical sense, and there is no difficulty in distributing these categories of possibilities with one another in every estimate you propose.

The summary of the verse's meaning upon all the possibilities is: Allah is All-Knowing of your deeds and intentions; nothing of them is hidden from Him, whether you speak aloud or conceal; and Allah has no need of the testimony of your limbs against you. What brought you to this harm was nothing but your evil assumption about the majesty of Allah.

"And that was your assumption" — the demonstrative refers to the assumption derived from the verb ﴿you thought that Allah does not know much of what you do﴾. Pointing to it conveys its distinguishing with the utmost clarity and the exposure of its ugliness, as a proclamation of their error.

He followed the demonstrative with the apposition "your assumption" to increase its clarification, so that what follows of the predicate may settle firmly. The predicate is the verb "it has ruined you" and what branches from it.

"which you assumed about your Lord" is a relative clause qualifying "your assumption." The use of the relative pronoun, for what is in the relative clause of an indication to the reason for constructing the predicate, namely "it has ruined you" and what branches from it, i.e., the assumption you assumed about your Lord, a false assumption.

The turning away from the proper name Allah to "your Lord" is to draw attention to the error of their assumption, since they assumed that some of their deeds were hidden from His knowledge, although He is their Lord and Creator. How could He create them and their deeds be hidden from Him? This alludes to His saying ﴿Should He not know who created? And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾ [al-Mulk: 14], so in the description "your Lord" there is an allusion to this meaning.

"Irda'" (ruin) means destruction; it is said: radiya, like radiya (the same pattern), when he perished, i.e., died. Irda' is used metaphorically for casting into a bad condition, to the point of making them like the dead, for that is the furthest that is commonly understood among people as a bad condition. In the use of the predicate as a verb there is a restrictive force, i.e., nothing ruined you except your assumption of that, and this is a relative restriction: your assumption that Allah does not know your deeds ruined you, not the testimony of your limbs such that you would blame them; rather your assumption that Allah does not know your deeds ruined you, so you did not fear His punishment.

His saying ﴿so you have become among the losers﴾ is an image of their state, when they reckon that they have reached knowledge of what they should know of the affairs of Allah and felt secure in securing their happiness, while they did not know Allah with the knowledge due to Him; so they treated Allah in a manner He does not approve, and deserved the punishment from the very place they assumed salvation. Their state is thus likened to the state of the merchant who prepared for profit and then fell into loss.

The meaning is: he censured them for their faulty reasoning and corrupt analogy in divine matters, and for their analogizing the unseen upon the seen. These are the principles that lured them into error: they denied the mission of human beings from Allah, denied the resurrection, then affirmed partners with Allah in divinity; and there branched out for them from all of that the severing of their attention from what lies beyond the worldly life and their sense of security from consequences in the worldly life. That is the sum of His saying the Exalted: ﴿And that was your assumption which you assumed about your Lord; it has ruined you, and you have become among the losers.﴾

Know that the causes of error in all beliefs come upon people only from corrupt reflection, hastiness in certainty, and failure to distinguish between sound proofs and resembling proofs; and all of that leads to delusion, expressed by the evil or false assumption.

Allah has mentioned something similar concerning the hypocrites, that their assumption is the assumption of the people of ignorance, saying ﴿They assume about Allah other than the truth, the assumption of ignorance﴾ [Al 'Imran: 154]. So let the believers beware of falling into such delusions, lest they suffer some of what was censured in the worshippers of idols.

The Prophet ﷺ has said: "Beware of assumption, for assumption is the most false of speech," meaning the assumption for which there is no proof.

And "you have become" (asbahtum) means "you became" (sirtum), because asbaha frequently comes in the sense of sara (to become).

This is a continuation of the same argument as the previous section: the phrase ﴿فالنار مثوى﴾ and the rest of the verse, and the passage ends where the commentary ends.

**Translation:**

A continuation (*tafri'*) on the answer to *idha* (the conditional particle) in both of the two preceding interpretations, or a continuation on the sentence ﴿And they will say to their skins, "Why did you testify against us?"﴾ [Fussilat: 21], or it is the answer to *idha*, with what lies between them being a parenthetical interjection (*i'tiraD*) in accordance with what suits the interpretations previously mentioned.

The meaning, according to all the interpretations, is that the outcome of their situation is that they have already been thrown into the Fire. So if they endure and submit, they remain in the Fire; and if they offer excuses, the excuse will not benefit them, and no apology (*tanassul*) will be accepted from them.

His saying ﴿so the Fire is their abode﴾ serves as the answer to the condition (*dalil jawab al-sharT*), because the Fire being their abode is not a consequence of their enduring. Rather, it is of the type of the saying, "If that is accepted, then so be it," meaning: then it is in that state. So the implied sense is: "If they endure, then they have no choice but to endure, because the Fire is their abode."

The meaning of ﴿and if they ask to be pleased (*yasta'tibu*)﴾ is: if they ask for *al-'utba* (restoration of goodwill), with the 'ayn vowelled with a *damma* and the *ba'* with a *fatha*, as a short form (*maqsur*), the verbal noun of *al-i'tab*, which is the return of the one who has been blamed to what pleases the one who blames.

[Page 274]

There is a proverb: "The one who restores goodwill is not a wrongdoer" (*ma musi' man a'tab*), meaning: whoever returns from what he has done wrong, it is as if he had not done wrong. They rarely used the original verbal noun to mean "returning," relying instead on the verbal noun of the form (*ism al-masdar*), which is *al-'utba*. The one who blames (*al-'atib*) is the one who censures, and the *sin* and *ta'* in it indicate a request, because a person does not ask someone to blame him; rather, he asks him to stop blaming him, that is, he asks him to pardon him. When he accepts that from him, it is said *a'tabahu* as well. This is one of the strange derivations (*tasarif*) of this root in the language. For this reason they almost caused the verbal noun of *a'taba* in the sense of "returned" to die out, and kept it in the sense of "accepted the restoration of goodwill." This is the meaning intended in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿so they are not among those who are pleased﴾, that is, God does not grant them pleasure, meaning He does not accept from them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 41, verse 25:

﴿And We appointed for them companions who made attractive to them what was before them and what was behind them, and the word came true against them, among nations that had passed away before them of jinn and men. Indeed, they were losers.﴾

This is conjoined to the clause "﴿And [mention] the Day when We gather the enemies of Allah﴾ [Fussilat: 19]", because their statement has been related, which indicates their aversion to reflecting upon the call to faith. Then their disbelief in the Creator of the universe was mentioned with His saying: "﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in He who created the earth in two days?﴾ [Fussilat: 9]."

Then their final destination in the Hereafter was mentioned with His saying: "﴿And [mention] the Day when We gather the enemies of Allah﴾ [Fussilat: 19]." Then He followed that with mention of the cause of their misguidance, from which their conditions arose, with His saying "and We appointed for them companions." Between what is there and what is here came various admonitions, proofs, favours, instructions, startling warnings and awakenings.

Qayyada (appointed) means: to make something available and prepared for something to act upon another. Qurana' is the plural of qarin, which is the constant companion. The qurana' here are those who constantly accompany them in misguidance: either outwardly, such as the callers to disbelief and its leaders, or inwardly within the souls, such as the devils of whispering, concerning whom Allah said: "﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a devil, and he is to him a companion﴾," which will come in Surat al-Zukhruf.

The meaning of His appointing them for them is His decreeing them for them, i.e., the creation of the circumstances by which the togetherness of some of them with others is caused, to match the ideas of the callers and the receptive, as the wise say: the receptive's benefit from the source depends on the correspondence between them. Thus taqyid in the sense of decreeing is a comprehensive expression for the various influences and gatherings which necessitate affinity and mutual love among groups, and for the various natures formed in the souls of some people, so that some of them require the attraction of devils to them and the arising of evil thoughts within them. To encompass this meaning, the expression qayyadna was preferred here over its equivalents such as ba'athna (We sent) and arsalna (We dispatched).

Tazyin (making attractive) means embellishment, and it implies that what is made attractive is not good in itself. "What is before them" is used metaphorically for observable matters, and "what is behind them" is used metaphorically for unseen matters.

What is meant by "﴿what is before them﴾" is the affairs of this world, i.e., they made attractive to them what they do in this world of corruption, such as the worship of idols, killing a soul without right, consuming wealth, transgressing against people by hand and tongue, gambling, committing abominations, and burying daughters alive. They accustomed them to deeming all of that good, because it agrees with passing desires and fleeting appetites of short duration, and they diverted them from considering the lasting intrinsic corruptions surrounding those deeds.

What is meant by "what is behind them" is the matters hidden from the senses concerning the attributes of Allah and the matters of the Hereafter, such as associating partners with Allah and ascribing offspring to Him, their supposition that what is concealed of their deeds is hidden from Him, their denial of the sending of messengers, and their denial of resurrection and recompense.

The meaning of their making this attractive to them is their instilling those beliefs through sophistic proofs, such as analogizing the unseen to the seen, and negating realities that do not fall under sensory perception, as in their saying: "(﴿When we are dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 47] ﴿and our first forefathers?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 48])."

"And the word came true against them" means the saying was fulfilled concerning them, and the saying is Allah's threat to them of the Fire for disbelief. The definite article in "al-qawl" is for a known reference. In this reference there is some generality, because although the Qur'an contains what is known to express this saying, such as His saying "﴿Is then he upon whom the word of punishment has been justified﴾ [al-Zumar: 19] and His saying "﴿So the word of our Lord has come into effect upon us; indeed, we will taste [it]﴾ [al-Saffat: 31], it is possible that the verses mentioned had not preceded this verse.

His saying "among nations" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "'alayhim", i.e., the word came true against them while they were among nations like them who had preceded them.

The adverbial sense (zarfiyya) here is metaphorical, and it has the meaning of partition (tab'id), i.e., they are of nations that passed away before them, upon whom the word came true. A similar usage is the saying of 'Amr ibn Udhayna:

"If you are turned away from the best of conduct, then among others who have been led astray from it [you are not alone]."
i.e., you are among a group of others who have been turned away from the best conduct.

The "min" in His saying "﴿of jinn and men﴾" is explicative (bayaniyya). It may be an explanation of "nations," i.e., of nations of humans and of devils, as in His saying "﴿He said: The truth I say, and the truth I speak﴾ [Sad: 84] ﴿Surely I will fill Hell with you and those who follow you among them, all together﴾ [Sad: 85], and His saying "﴿He said: Enter among nations that have passed away before you, of jinn and men, into the Fire﴾" [al-A'raf: 38]. It may also be an explanation of "qurana'", i.e., constant companions to them in a hidden companionship, which is the constancy of devils with them through whispering and the constancy of leaders of disbelief with them through legislating for them what Allah did not permit.

The clause "﴿Indeed, they were losers﴾" may be an explanation of the saying, like its counterpart "﴿So the word of our Lord has come into effect upon us; indeed, we will taste [it]﴾" [al-Saffat: 31] in Surat al-Saffat. It may also be a resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani) arising from the clause "﴿And the word came true against them among nations﴾". The two meanings are close.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 41, verse 26:

﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it, that perhaps you may prevail."﴾

It is conjoined to the sentence ﴿And they say: "Our hearts are in coverings from what you call us to"﴾ [Fussilat: 5], being a conjunction of narrative upon narrative. The occasion for transitioning to it is that this saying arises from the adornment of their companions among mankind, or it is conjoined to the sentence (﴿So they made attractive to them﴾ [Fussilat: 25]).

This is a report of another state of their aversion to the Muhammadan call. After describing their aversion within themselves, he moved to describing their instructing the people in the methods of aversion. Those who disbelieve here are the leaders of disbelief, who say to their common folk: "Do not listen to this Qur'an," for they knew that the Qur'an is a speech that is the most perfect of speech, noble in meanings, eloquent in composition and excellent in expression, and they were certain that anyone who hears it and in whose soul the solidity of its words and the loftiness of its aims penetrates, his understanding judges that following it is true. They had perceived this within themselves, but the love of continuing in the sovereignty of their people overcame them, so they conspired and devised a scheme to prevent the people from listening to it, out of fear that their hearts would soften upon hearing the Qur'an, so they turned them away from hearing it.

This is the manner of the callers to misguidance and falsehood: to silence the mouths of those who speak the truth and the proof, by whatever they can of intimidation and enticement, and of frightening and encouraging, and they do not let the people debate by proof or refer to evidence, because they are certain that the proof of their opponents is more forceful. So they conceal it and repel it not with its like, but with methods of slander and misleading. When their tricks fail them and they see the flashes of truth faltering, they fear that its light will spread among the people who retain some remnant of good and right guidance, so they turn to idle talk and blow into the trumpets of nonsense and clamour, perhaps they may prevail thereby over the proofs of truth and overwhelm the good saying with idle talk. Such is the manner of these people.

Their saying ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an﴾ is a warning and a mockery of the Qur'an. The demonstrative "this" is used in the sense of belittling, as in what is related of them: ﴿Is this the one who mentions your gods?﴾

Their naming it "the Qur'an" is a report of what is current on the tongues of the Muslims of calling it by that name.

The verb "tasma'u" (listen) is construed with the preposition "li-" (for/to) because it is made to include the meaning of "tatma'innu" (be at ease) or "tarkanu" (incline toward).

Al-laghw: speech that has no benefit in it; speech with no use is called laghw. It is a verb with a waw as its third radical. The root of "walghaw" is "walghuw": the damma was made heavy on the waw, so it was deleted, two sakins met, so the first was deleted, and the second waw became living-sukun, the waw being the sign of the plural. This is what runs on the apparent wording of al-Sihah and al-Qamus; and in al-Kashshaf it is said: laghiya yalgha, as one says laghā yalghū, so it is then both waw-based and ya-based.

So the meaning of "walghaw fihi" is: say sayings that have no meaning, or speak words not intended to convey anything, or the aim is to produce sounds that overwhelm the voice of the Prophet ﷺ with the Qur'an. Since the aim of interspersing their sounds is the voice of the reciter, so that the listeners do not understand it, the laghw is construed with the preposition "fi" of location, to indicate the placing of their idle talk within the interstices of the reciter's voice, the containment of the contained within the container in a figurative sense.

The preposition of location was attached to the name "the Qur'an" and not to the name of some aspect of it such as "voice" or "speech," so as to include everything that obscures the words of the Qur'an, or casts doubt on their meanings, or the like. This is an arrangement that has a place in eloquence.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "The Prophet ﷺ, while in Makkah, when he recited the Qur'an, would raise his voice, so Abu Jahl and others would drive the people away from him and say to them: 'Do not listen to him, and make noise during it.' They would come with whistling, clapping, shouting, reciting poetry and rajaz, and whatever sayings came to them with which they would clamour." It is recorded in the Sahih that when they heard the recitation of Abu Bakr, who was tender in his recitation, they said: "We fear that he will tempt our sons and our women."

The meaning of ﴿perhaps you may prevail﴾ is: hoping that you will overcome Muhammad by diverting those who are expected to follow him when they hear his recitation. This indicates that they found the Qur'an dominant over them, since those who heard it would penetrate their hearts and they would believe, i.e., if you do not do this, then it will overcome you.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 41, verses 27–28:

﴿So We will surely make those who disbelieve taste a severe punishment, and We will surely recompense them with the worst of what they used to do.﴾ ﴿That is the recompense of the enemies of Allah: the Fire; for them therein is the abode of eternity, as a recompense for what they used to deny of Our signs.﴾

The fa' (fa') indicates that what follows is a consequence (mufarra') of what precedes it. It may be a consequence of the last thing mentioned, which is His saying ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Do not listen to this Qur'an"﴾ [Fussilat: 26], and so on; or it may be a consequence of everything mentioned previously, beginning from His saying ﴿And they say: "Our hearts are in coverings from that to which you call us"﴾ [Fussilat: 5], and so on; and His saying ﴿But if they turn away﴾ [Fussilat: 13], and so on; and His saying ﴿And the Day when the enemies of Allah are gathered to the Fire﴾ [Fussilat: 19], and so on; and His saying ﴿And We appointed for them companions﴾ [Fussilat: 25], and so on; and His saying ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Do not listen"﴾ [Fussilat: 26], etc.

In both cases, the intended meaning of ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ here is necessarily the polytheists about whom the discourse is.

So the use of ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ (idhhar) in place of a pronoun (idmar) is to intend what the relative clause implies of an indication to the cause of making them taste the punishment, i.e., because of their disbelief, part of which has been related previously.

"Making them taste the punishment" means punishing them; the word "taste" is used for it metaphorically (isti'arah makniyyah takhyiliyyah). As for "the severe punishment," it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it is the punishment of the Day of Badr, and so it is the punishment of this world.

As for the conjunction ﴿and We will surely recompense them with the worst of what they used to do﴾, it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "We will surely recompense them with the worst of what they used to do" in the Hereafter.

"The worst of what they used to do" is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition. The sense is: "for the worst of what they used to do." Or you may take it as accusative as a substitute for the absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), its estimated sense being: "a recompense equal to the worst of what they used to do."

"Asw'a" (worst) is an elative form (ism tafdil) stripped of comparison; it is intended only to mean "bad," and it is put in the elative form for emphasis on its badness. Its being annexed to "what they used to do" is an annexation of part to whole, not an annexation of an elative to the thing it is compared with.

The indication in ﴿That is the recompense of the enemies of Allah﴾ refers to what preceded, namely the recompense and the severe punishment for the worst of their deeds. "The enemies of Allah" are the polytheists whose mention preceded in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And the Day when the enemies of Allah are gathered﴾ [Fussilat: 19].

"Al-nar" (the Fire) is an explicative apposition (atf bayan) to "the recompense of the enemies of Allah."

"Dar al-khuld" (the abode of eternity) is the Fire. His saying ﴿for them therein is the abode of eternity﴾ uses the adverbial form, by treating the Fire as if it were a place (zarf) for "the abode of eternity," though the abode of eternity is nothing other than the Fire itself. This is of the style of tajrid (abstraction), to convey the intensification of the meaning of eternity within the Fire. It is counted among the embellishments of rhetoric (muhassinat badi'iyyah), and of it is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed there has been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example﴾ [al-Ahzab: 21], and the saying of Abu Hamid al-'Attabi:

Verse 206

"And in the Most Merciful is a sufficiency for the weak"
That is: "and the Most Merciful is sufficient for the weak."

"Al-khuld" means long duration, and in the terminology of the Qur'an it is applied to the everlasting endless duration that has no end.

"Jaza'" (recompense) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from "dar al-khuld," and the ba' is causal. And ma is verbal-masdar (masdariyyah), meaning: a recompense because of their denying Our signs.

The form of the present tense in "yajhadun" indicates the renewal of denial moment by moment and its repetition. The verb "yajhadun" is transitive with the ba' because it is implicitly construed with the meaning of "yakdhibun" (they deny). The fronting of "bi-ayatina" is for emphasis and for care, placed before the verse-ending (fasilah).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 41, verses 27–28:

﴿So We will surely make those who disbelieve taste a severe punishment, and We will surely recompense them with the worst of what they used to do.﴾ ﴿That is the recompense of the enemies of Allah: the Fire; for them therein is the abode of eternity, as a recompense for what they used to deny of Our signs.﴾

The fa' (fa') indicates that what follows is a consequence (mufarra') of what precedes it. It may be a consequence of the last thing mentioned, which is His saying ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Do not listen to this Qur'an"﴾ [Fussilat: 26], and so on; or it may be a consequence of everything mentioned previously, beginning from His saying ﴿And they say: "Our hearts are in coverings from that to which you call us"﴾ [Fussilat: 5], and so on; and His saying ﴿But if they turn away﴾ [Fussilat: 13], and so on; and His saying ﴿And the Day when the enemies of Allah are gathered to the Fire﴾ [Fussilat: 19], and so on; and His saying ﴿And We appointed for them companions﴾ [Fussilat: 25], and so on; and His saying ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Do not listen"﴾ [Fussilat: 26], etc.

In both cases, the intended meaning of ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ here is necessarily the polytheists about whom the discourse is.

So the use of ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ (idhhar) in place of a pronoun (idmar) is to intend what the relative clause implies of an indication to the cause of making them taste the punishment, i.e., because of their disbelief, part of which has been related previously.

"Making them taste the punishment" means punishing them; the word "taste" is used for it metaphorically (isti'arah makniyyah takhyiliyyah). As for "the severe punishment," it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it is the punishment of the Day of Badr, and so it is the punishment of this world.

As for the conjunction ﴿and We will surely recompense them with the worst of what they used to do﴾, it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "We will surely recompense them with the worst of what they used to do" in the Hereafter.

"The worst of what they used to do" is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition. The sense is: "for the worst of what they used to do." Or you may take it as accusative as a substitute for the absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), its estimated sense being: "a recompense equal to the worst of what they used to do."

"Asw'a" (worst) is an elative form (ism tafdil) stripped of comparison; it is intended only to mean "bad," and it is put in the elative form for emphasis on its badness. Its being annexed to "what they used to do" is an annexation of part to whole, not an annexation of an elative to the thing it is compared with.

The indication in ﴿That is the recompense of the enemies of Allah﴾ refers to what preceded, namely the recompense and the severe punishment for the worst of their deeds. "The enemies of Allah" are the polytheists whose mention preceded in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And the Day when the enemies of Allah are gathered﴾ [Fussilat: 19].

"Al-nar" (the Fire) is an explicative apposition (atf bayan) to "the recompense of the enemies of Allah."

"Dar al-khuld" (the abode of eternity) is the Fire. His saying ﴿for them therein is the abode of eternity﴾ uses the adverbial form, by treating the Fire as if it were a place (zarf) for "the abode of eternity," though the abode of eternity is nothing other than the Fire itself. This is of the style of tajrid (abstraction), to convey the intensification of the meaning of eternity within the Fire. It is counted among the embellishments of rhetoric (muhassinat badi'iyyah), and of it is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed there has been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example﴾ [al-Ahzab: 21], and the saying of Abu Hamid al-'Attabi:

Verse 206

"And in the Most Merciful is a sufficiency for the weak"
That is: "and the Most Merciful is sufficient for the weak."

"Al-khuld" means long duration, and in the terminology of the Qur'an it is applied to the everlasting endless duration that has no end.

"Jaza'" (recompense) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) from "dar al-khuld," and the ba' is causal. And ma is verbal-masdar (masdariyyah), meaning: a recompense because of their denying Our signs.

The form of the present tense in "yajhadun" indicates the renewal of denial moment by moment and its repetition. The verb "yajhadun" is transitive with the ba' because it is implicitly construed with the meaning of "yakdhibun" (they deny). The fronting of "bi-ayatina" is for emphasis and for care, placed before the verse-ending (fasilah).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 41, verse 29:

﴿And those who disbelieve will say: "Our Lord, show us the two who led us astray, of the jinn and mankind, and we will place them beneath our feet so that they may be among the lowest."﴾

This is coordinated with the sentence ﴿For them therein is the abode of eternity﴾ [Fussilat: 28], meaning: and they will say in Hell. He turned from the future form to the past form to indicate the certainty of the occurrence of this statement, and it has the same meaning as His, the Exalted, saying ﴿Until, when they have all overtaken one another therein, the last of them will say of the first of them, "Our Lord, these are the ones who led us astray, so give them a double punishment of the Fire"﴾ [al-A'raf: 38]. So the sayers of "Our Lord, show us the two who led us astray" are the general body of polytheists, as His saying "the two who led us astray" indicates.

The meaning of "show us" (arina) is "designate for us," and it is a metonymy for the intention to take vengeance upon them. For this reason (naj'alhuma) is in the jussive mood as the answer to the imperative, on the assumption: if You show us them, we will place them beneath our feet.

Placing beneath the feet means trampling with the feet and stamping on them, i.e., we will place their individuals beneath the feet of the individuals of our group, for the common folk are more numerous than the leaders, so vengeance upon them will not be lacking. Trampling with the feet was among the manners of vengeance and humiliation. Ibn Wa'la al-Jarmi said:

"And we trampled them in rage, the trampling of one fettered, upon the growing hair of the old."

They only asked to see them because the misleaders were in deeper levels of the Fire, lower than the levels of their followers, so for this reason they did not know where they were.

The clause "so that they may be among the lowest" is a preface to God's granting their request to show them both, because they knew from God's wrath against them that He was more wrathful against the two misleading groups; so they sought, by their resolve to take vengeance upon them, to facilitate their being empowered to take vengeance upon them.

"The lowest" are those who are more abject in lowliness than these who disbelieved, i.e., that they may be more debased than us in recompense for them. So "lowliness" is used metaphorically for humiliation and contemptibility.

Al-Jumhur read "arina" with a kasra on the ra'. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, al-Susi on the authority of Abu 'Amr, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim and Ya'qub read it with a sukun on the ra' for lightness, to ease the heaviness of the kasra, as they said: "fakhdh" for "fakhidh." On the authority of al-Khalil: when you say "arini thawbaka" with a kasra on the ra', the meaning is "show me it" (rassirnihi); and when you say it with a sukun on the ra', it is a request for giving, meaning "give it to me." On this basis, the meaning of the reading of Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, and those who agree with them is: "Empower us against the two who led us astray, so that we may place them beneath our feet," i.e., grant us permission to humiliate them and disgrace them.

Ibn Kathir read "alladhayni" with a shadda on the nun of the relative pronoun, which is a dialectal form, and it was mentioned in His saying, "And the two (alladhani) of you who commit it" [al-Nisa': 16], in Surat al-Nisa'.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 41, verses 30–32 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast, the angels will descend upon them, [saying], "Do not fear and do not grieve, but rejoice in Paradise, which you were promised."﴾ ﴿We are your allies in the life of this world and in the Hereafter. And for you therein is whatever your souls desire, and for you therein is whatever you ask for.﴾ ﴿As a welcome gift from the Forgiving, the Merciful.﴾

After completing the discussion of what befell the earlier nations, the polytheists who denied, of the punishment of this world and of what has been prepared for them of the punishment of the Hereafter, which contains a lesson for the polytheists who denied Muhammad (ﷺ) by way of allusion, and after they were warned explicitly of what would befall them in the Hereafter and of some of its terrors, the listener became eager to know the portion of the believers and the description of their state. So His saying ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah"﴾ etc. came as an explanation of what was awaited and as good news to the one seeking it. Thus the sentence is a resumptive explanatory sentence (isti'naf bayani) arising from what preceded it, namely His saying "﴿And [mention] the Day when the enemies of Allah will be gathered to the Fire﴾ [Fussilat: 19]" up to His saying "﴿among the debased﴾ [Fussilat: 29]."

The opening of the sentence with the particle of emphasis (inna) takes into account the denial of the polytheists of that; so the emphasis of the statement includes additional suppression of them.

The meaning of ﴿they said, "Our Lord is Allah"﴾ is that they proclaimed it and did not fear anyone by declaring their monotheism. Their saying is therefore an expression of what is in their belief, because what is intended is that they said it out of conviction, for the原 principle in speech is truthfulness, which is the correspondence of the statement to the actual reality in external existence.

His saying ﴿Our Lord is Allah﴾ conveys restriction (hasr) through the definiteness of both the subject and the predicate, meaning: we have no lord except Allah. This comprises the root of correct belief, because affirming monotheism removes the obstacle to believing the Messenger (ﷺ) in what he brought, since the polytheists were not prevented from believing in what the Prophet (ﷺ) brought except that he commanded them to abandon the worship of other than Allah; and because they received the denial of resurrection from the proponents of polytheism.

Istiqamah (steadfastness) in its real sense is: the absence of crookedness and inclination; its sin and ta' are for intensification in straightening, so the real meaning of istaqama is: it stood upright, not inclined nor bent. Istiqamah is also used figuratively for what combines the meaning of good action and conduct upon truth and sincerity. Allah the Exalted said ﴿So be upright toward Him and seek His forgiveness﴾ [Fussilat: 6], and ﴿So remain upright as you have been commanded﴾ [Hud: 112]. It is said: the lands became upright for the king, i.e., they obeyed him, and from this is His saying the Exalted ﴿So as long as they are upright with you, be upright with them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 7].

So (istaqamu) here includes the meaning of fulfilling what they were charged with, and the first thing it includes of that is that they remain firm upon the root of monotheism, i.e., they do not change or turn away from it.

Among the meanings of this verse is what is related in Sahih Muslim from Sufyan al-Thaqafi, who said:
I said, "O Messenger of Allah, tell me in Islam a statement about which I will not ask anyone other than you." He said: "Say: I have believed in Allah, then be upright."

And from Abu Bakr concerning ﴿then remain upright﴾: they did not associate anything with Allah. And from 'Umar: they remained upright on the path to His obedience, then they did not dodge like the dodging of foxes. 'Uthman said: then they made their deeds sincere for Allah. And from 'Ali: then they performed the obligations. Thus the Four Caliphs—may Allah be pleased with them—undertook the interpretation of this verse. All these sayings return to the meaning of steadfastness in faith and its effects, and the concern of these four, the pillars of Islam, with explaining steadfastness points to its importance in the religion.

The definiteness of the subject through the relative pronoun (al-mawsuliyyah), rather than saying "the believers" and the like, is because of what the relative clause contains of faith, indicating that it is the cause of the predicate's attribution to the subject; so it conveys that the descent of the angels upon them with that honor is a consequence of their saying "Our Lord is Allah" and their steadfastness, for correct belief and devotion to righteous action are the cause of success.

"Thumma" (then) here indicates gradation in rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), because steadfastness exceeds the affirmation of monotheism in rank, since it includes it and includes persistence upon it and acting in accordance with what it requires; and because steadfastness is evidence that their saying "Our Lord is Allah" was a statement issuing from inner conviction and true knowledge.

His saying ﴿They said, "Our Lord is Allah," then they remained upright﴾ combined the two foundations of Islamic perfection: His saying ﴿They said, "Our Lord is Allah"﴾ points to the perfection of the soul, which is knowledge of the truth in order to be guided by it, and knowledge of the good in order to act upon it. Perfection is then certain knowledge and righteous action; so knowledge of Allah in His divinity is the foundation of certain knowledge.

His saying "istaqamu" pointed to the foundation of righteous deeds, which is steadfastness upon the truth, i.e., that one be moderate, not inclining toward either extreme of excess or deficiency. Allah the Exalted said ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatihah: 6], and ﴿And thus We have made you a median nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. Moreover, the perfection of belief returns to steadfastness: correct belief is that one does not go to excess in negation to the point of nullification (ta'til), nor go to excess in affirmation to the point of likening (tashbih) and comparison, but rather walks the straight line that separates likening and nullification,
[p. 284]
and continues thus, separating between the determinist (jabri) and the free-will proponent (qadari), between hope and despair, and in deeds between exaggeration and negligence.

The descent of the angels upon the believers may be at the time of the gathering, as indicated by their saying ﴿which you were promised﴾ and as their speech to them suggests, because the apparent sense of the address is literal. This corresponds to His saying ﴿And [mention] the Day when the enemies of Allah will be gathered to the Fire, and they will be driven back﴾ [Fussilat: 19]: those are met by the angels with driving, while the believers are descended upon by the angels with security.

The mention of descent here is to honor the believers: the angels descend from their exalted abodes on their account, whereas the enemies of Allah find the angels present at the gathering driving them, and the angels do not descend for their sake. Thus there is established for the believers by this an honor like the honor of the prophets and messengers, when Allah sends the angels down to them. The meaning: upon every believer descend two angels, the guardians who used to record his deeds in this world. The particle "an" (that, explanatory) came after "tatanazzalu" because it includes the meaning of saying; so the implied sense is: they say, "Do not fear and do not grieve."

It is also possible that the descent of the angels upon them is in this world, a hidden descent known by the occurrence of its effects in the souls of the believers, and the address "Do not fear and do not grieve" is in the sense of their casting into their hearts what turns them away from fear and grief—the opposite of the whispering of the devils, the companions, with embellishment—i.e., they cast into the souls of the believers what diverts them from fear and grief and reminds them of Paradise, so tranquility settles upon them and their chests expand with confidence in its settling, and they cast into their souls the rejection of allegiance to those who are not of the party of Allah. This corresponds to His saying ﴿And We appointed for them companions﴾ [Fussilat: 25] and what follows, for that is an appointing in this world. This implies that the perfect believers do not fear other than Allah, do not grieve over what befalls them, are certain that everything is by decree, and rejoice in what they anticipate of the bounty of Allah.

On this meaning, His saying ﴿which you were promised﴾ — "kana" in it is regarded as superfluous for emphasis, and the present tense in "tu'adun" remains in its original usage for the present and future. His saying ﴿We are your allies in the life of this world and in the Hereafter﴾ is then a reassurance to them in this world and a promise of benefit to them in the Hereafter.

[p. 285]
"La" (do not) is a prohibition, and what is intended by the prohibition of fear is the prohibition of its cause, which is the expectation of harm, i.e., do not suppose that Allah is punishing you. So the prohibition is a metonymy (kinayah) for security from Allah the Exalted, because when they realize security, their fear disappears; and this is reassurance from the angels to the souls of the believers.

Fear (khawf) is distress in the soul arising from the supposition of the occurrence of a severe displeasing thing.

Grief (huzn) is distress in the soul arising from the occurrence of something displeasing, through the loss of a benefit or the occurrence of harm.

They attached good news to their reassurance, because the impact of blessing upon the soul has the effect of joy when it is not mixed with the expectation of something displeasing.

The description of Paradise as ﴿which you were promised﴾ is a reminder to them of the deeds for which they were promised Paradise, and a hastening of the joy of success through the good pleasure of Allah, and a confirmation of His promise, i.e., which you were promised in this world.

In the mention of the verb "kana" there is an indication that they are firmly rooted in the promise of Paradise, and that is because of their earlier faith and deeds.

In the use of the present tense in "tu'adun" is the indication that their promise of it has been repeated, through the repetition of the deeds for which it was promised and through the repetition of the promise in occasions of reminder and glad tidings.

The saying of the angels ﴿We are your allies in the life of this world and in the Hereafter﴾ is an introduction of themselves to the believers, to make them feel at ease.

For knowing that the one being met is an old companion increases the arriving person's ease and gladness and removes from him the bewilderment of arrival; it lightens from him the formality of hospitality and removes from him the loneliness of estrangement. That is: we are those who were in your company in the world, when they used to record your good deeds and bear witness before Allah to your prayers, as in the hadith: "Angels succeed one another among you by night and angels by day, and their Lord asks them—and He is most knowing of them—'How did you leave My servants?' They say, 'We came to them while they were praying, and we left them while they were praying.'" And they kept the covenant, so they were allies of the believers in the Hereafter. This saying has been placed in an intervening position between the attributes of Paradise,
[p. 286]
so that the believers may realize that their good news of Paradise is the good news of one who loves, who rejoices for his beloved in goodness and strives to increase it for him.

Know that His saying ﴿in the life of this world﴾ is an indication contrasting His saying about the polytheists ﴿And We appointed for them companions﴾ [Fussilat: 25]. Just as He appointed for the disbelievers companions in the world, He appointed for the believers angels with praise of the believers.

This verse implies that this class of angels is specific to the companionship and allegiance of the believers, and the disbelievers have no share in them. If the guardians are among the особенностей of the believers, as Ibn Naji related in his commentary on the Risalah, then the meaning of their allegiance to the believers is clear. And if the guardians are appointed over both believers and disbelievers, as the majority maintain, and as is the apparent sense of His saying the Exalted ﴿Nay, but you deny the Judgment. And indeed, over you are guardians, noble, writing, who know what you do﴾ [al-Infitar: 9–12], then this is a class of angels appointed to guard the believers in this world, and they are other than the guardians. This class may be the one called "al-mu'aqqibat" in His saying the Exalted ﴿For him are successive [angels] before him and behind him, who protect him by the command of Allah﴾ [al-Ra'd: 11], according to what has preceded in Surat al-Ra'd.

Several reports of varying acceptability have indicated that the angels who have a connection with people in general or with believers in particular are many kinds. It is related from 'Uthman that "he asked the Prophet (ﷺ): How many angels are there over a human being? So he mentioned to him twenty angels." Perhaps the description of the descending angels as "allies" implies that their work with the believer is work of righteousness and support, such as inspiring acts of obedience, combating the devils, and the like; and by this the correspondence of their descent upon the believers is completed with the mention of the appointing of companions for the disbelievers. This is the better view.

His saying ﴿And for you therein is whatever your souls desire﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) upon ﴿which you were promised﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical sentence, as I explained just now.

The meaning of ﴿whatever you ask for﴾ (ma tadda'un): what you wish for. It is said: "idda'a," i.e., "tamanna" (wished). This was mentioned earlier at His saying the Exalted ﴿and for them is whatever they ask for﴾ [Ya-Sin: 57] in Surat Ya-Sin.
[p. 287]
The meaning: for you therein is what you desire of what falls under the senses, and what you wish in your souls of everything that occurs to the mind, of what passes through the imagination; so what they ask for is nothing other than what their souls desire.

The following translation is provided in the required form.

This difference is the reason the phrase "for you" (lakum) is repeated, to signal that this promise is independent of the preceding one, so it is not supposed that the conjunction is an explanatory conjunction (ʿaṭf tafsīr) or a general term conjoined to a specific one (ʿaṭf ʿāmm ʿalā khāṣṣ).

Nuzul, with a damma on the nun and a damma on the zay, is what is prepared for a guest of hospitality (qirā), and it is derived from nuzul (descending/lodging), because it is the honour of the one who lodges (nazil). Here it is used metaphorically for what they are given of desirable things, whether it is provision or otherwise. The point of resemblance is the speed of its provision, as if it had been prepared before they desired it or wished for it.

The phrase ﴿ghafūrin raḥīmin﴾ is an attributive description of nuzulan, and min is the min of origin (ibtidaʾiyyah).

Nuzulan is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of ﴿mā tashtahī anfusukum﴾ and "what you request": that is, they are given it in the way that the prepared hospitality is given to a guest.

The two attributes, ghafūr and raḥīm, are chosen here to indicate that God has forgiven them, or most of them, the minor sins (al-lamam) and what they repented of, and that He is merciful to them because they loved Him, feared Him, and supported His religion.

[p. 287]

And for you therein is whatever your souls desire, and for you therein is whatever you ask for.﴾ ﴿As a welcome gift from the Forgiving, the Merciful.﴾

After completing the discussion of what befell the earlier nations, the polytheists who denied, of the punishment of this world and of what has been prepared for them of the punishment of the Hereafter, which contains a lesson for the polytheists who denied Muhammad (ﷺ) by way of allusion, and after they were warned explicitly of what would befall them in the Hereafter and of some of its terrors, the listener became eager to know the portion of the believers and the description of their state. Thus the sentence is a resumptive explanatory sentence (isti'naf bayani) arising from what preceded it, namely His saying "﴿And [mention] the Day when the enemies of Allah will be gathered to the Fire﴾ [Fussilat: 19]" up to His saying "﴿among the debased﴾ [Fussilat: 29]."

The opening of the sentence with the particle of emphasis (inna) takes into account the denial of the polytheists of that; so the emphasis of the statement includes additional suppression of them.

The meaning of ﴿they said, "Our Lord is Allah"﴾ is that they proclaimed it and did not fear anyone by declaring their monotheism. Their saying is therefore an expression of what is in their belief, because what is intended is that they said it out of conviction, for the原 principle in speech is truthfulness, which is the correspondence of the statement to the actual reality in external existence.

His saying ﴿Our Lord is Allah﴾ conveys restriction (hasr) through the definiteness of both the subject and the predicate, meaning: we have no lord except Allah. This comprises the root of correct belief, because affirming monotheism removes the obstacle to believing the Messenger (ﷺ) in what he brought, since the polytheists were not prevented from believing in what the Prophet (ﷺ) brought except that he commanded them to abandon the worship of other than Allah; and because they received the denial of resurrection from the proponents of polytheism.

Istiqamah (steadfastness) in its real sense is: the absence of crookedness and inclination; its sin and ta' are for intensification in straightening, so the real meaning of istaqama is: it stood upright, not inclined nor bent. Istiqamah is also used figuratively for what combines the meaning of good action and conduct upon truth and sincerity. Allah the Exalted said ﴿So be upright toward Him and seek His forgiveness﴾ [Fussilat: 6], and ﴿So remain upright as you have been commanded﴾ [Hud: 112]. It is said: the lands became upright for the king, i.e., they obeyed him, and from this is His saying the Exalted ﴿So as long as they are upright with you, be upright with them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 7].

I said, "O Messenger of Allah, tell me in Islam a statement about which I will not ask anyone other than you." He said: "Say: I have believed in Allah, then be upright."

And from 'Ali: then they performed the obligations. Thus the Four Caliphs—may Allah be pleased with them—undertook the interpretation of this verse. All these sayings return to the meaning of steadfastness in faith and its effects, and the concern of these four, the pillars of Islam, with explaining steadfastness points to its importance in the religion.
