This is not part of the speech of the angels to the believers in the Hereafter. Rather, it is addressed from God. The most apparent reading is that it completes the praise of those who said, "Our Lord is God, and then they were upright," and it indicates that they deserve that noble treatment. It also suppresses the polytheists, since it strikes their ears, meaning: how could they not be in that station, when they have spoken the best speech and done the best deed? Mentioning this praise of them for the goodness of their speech, right after mentioning the blame of the polytheists and the warning against their evil speech, that "Do not listen to this Qur'an," inevitably indicates that there is a great gulf between the two groups. Its two extremes are the explicitly stated goodness and the implied worst, by contrast. That is, those who said the best speech and did the most righteous deed are not equal to those who said the worst speech and did the worst deed. For this reason, it is followed by His words, ﴿Good and evil are not equal﴾ [Fussilat: 34].

[Page 288 continued]

The waw (و) is either conjunctive, coordinating with the clause ﴿Indeed, those who said, "Our Lord is God"﴾ [Fussilat: 30], or circumstantial (ḥāliyya), relating to the subject of "those who said." The meaning is that they attained that because there is no one better than them in speech and deed.

The "man" (مَن) is interrogative used in the sense of negation, meaning: no one is better in speech than this group, like His words, ﴿And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to God﴾ [an-Nisa': 125], the verse in Surat an-Nisa'.

"Whoever calls to God" refers to anyone for whom the content of this relative clause (ṣila) holds. Calling to something means commanding another to turn toward something. From this is the saying "the Abbasid call (da'wa)" and "the Alid call," and the naming of the preacher among the Banu 'Ubayd as "the caller (dā'ī)," because he calls to adherence to the party of the family of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. Thus, "calling to God" is an image of the state of one who commands the singling out of God in worship and the rejection of associating partners, by analogy with one who calls someone to turn toward a person. This is the state of the believers when they proclaimed monotheism, which is what they were described with earlier in His words, ﴿Indeed, those who said, "Our Lord is God"﴾ [Fussilat: 30], as you know. The believers used to call the polytheists to the monotheism of God, and the master of those who call to God is Muhammad (ﷺ).

His words "whoever calls to God," with "man" (مَن) here, are comparative (tafḍīliyya) relative to the word "better" (aḥsan), and the statement involves the ellipsis of a noun (ḥadhf muḍāf), its estimate being: "than the speech of (whoever calls to God)." This ellipsis is like that in the verse of al-Nabigha:

"I have feared so much that my fear does not exceed
The fear of a wild goat, intelligent, in the rugged ground."

That is, my fear does not exceed the fear of a wild goat. From this is His words, Exalted is He, ﴿But righteousness is [in] one who believes in God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177], the verse in Surat al-Baqarah.

"Righteous deed" (al-'amal al-ṣāliḥ) is the deed that makes its doer righteous in his religion and his worldly life, a righteousness not mixed with corruption. That deed is the one performed in accordance with what religion has brought. Thus the righteous deed is what the believers were described with earlier in His words, ﴿Then they remained steadfast﴾ [Fussilat: 30].

As for ﴿and said, "Indeed, I am of the Muslims"﴾, it is praise of the Muslims in that they took pride in Islam and were proud of it among the polytheists, and did not conceal their Islam.

Pride in religion is a righteous deed, but it was singled out for mention because it is intended to enrage the disbelievers. An example of this is what occurred on the day of Uhud, when Abu Sufyan shouted, "Hubal is high!" The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "Say: 'God is most high and most majestic.'" Abu Sufyan said, "We have al-'Uzza, and you have no 'Uzza." The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "Say: 'God is our Master, and you have no master.'"

The reason this statement is not mentioned in the relative clause that indicates the cause of the descent of the angels upon the believers with honor, which is ﴿Those who said, "Our Lord is God," then remained steadfast﴾ [Fussilat: 30], is that the purpose of mentioning it here is to praise them for their boasting over the polytheists in the might of Islam. That is among the effects of that relative clause, so there is no need to mention it there, unlike its placement here.

In this verse there is a great basis for the excellence of the scholars of religion who clarified the sunan, explained the rulings of the Shari'a, and strove to reach what God, Exalted is He, intends from His religion and from His character.

In it there is also a subtle basis for supporting the view of al-Maturidi and a group of the scholars of Qayrawan, headed by Muhammad ibn Sahnun, that the Muslim says, "I am a believer," and does not say, "If God wills." This is in contrast to the view of al-Ash'ari and a group of the scholars of Qayrawan, headed by Muhammad ibn 'Abdus, for it is reported that he used to say, "I am a believer, if God wills." The sparks of this disagreement flew among the scholars of Qayrawan for a period of a century. The truth is that it is a verbal disagreement, as Shaykh Abu Muhammad ibn Abi Zayd explained, and 'Iyad transmitted it in al-Madarik and agreed with it. We have discussed the issue in detail at His words, ﴿It is not for us to return to it unless God, our Lord, wills﴾ [al-A'raf: 89], in Surat al-A'raf. Accordingly, there is no proof in this verse for either side; the proof is rather in the verse of Surat al-A'raf against al-Maturidi and Muhammad ibn Sahnun.

The discussion of His words, ﴿and said, "Indeed, I am of the Muslims"﴾, is like the discussion of ﴿Indeed, those who said, "Our Lord is God"﴾ [Fussilat: 30].

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 41, verse 34:**

﴿Good and evil are not equal. Repel [evil] with that which is better, and then the one between whom and you there is enmity will become as if he were a close friend.﴾

The conjunction of this sentence has a remarkable placement, for it may be conjoined (*'atf*) to the sentence ﴿And who is better in speech than one who calls to Allah﴾ (Fussilat, 33), etc., as a complement to it. The sentence it is conjoined to contains praise of the believers immediately after the threat and censure of the polytheists.

[Page 290]

This sentence explains the disparity between the rank of the believers and the condition of the polytheists. The word *hasanah* (good) is a noun transferred from the adjective, so the notion of the adjective is inherent in it. Thus *al-hasanah* refers to the condition of the believers and *al-sayyi'ah* (evil) to the condition of the polytheists. The meaning is like the meaning of many verses of this kind, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The blind and the seeing are not alike, nor are those who believe and do righteous deeds and the wrongdoer﴾ (Ghafir, 58). On this interpretation, the conjunction of this sentence to the one before it is a conjunction of sentences that share one purpose, and not a conjunction of one purpose to another.

It may also be conjoined to the sentence ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it, that you may overcome"﴾ (Fussilat, 26), which follows the sentence ﴿And they say: "Our hearts are in coverings from that to which you call us"﴾ (Fussilat, 5), up to His saying ﴿So act, indeed we are acting﴾ (Fussilat, 5). That [sequence] stirs in the soul of the Prophet ﷺ distress at the persistence of the disbelievers in their disbelief and their non-response to the Prophet's ﷺ call to the truth. He was thus in a state where his capacity for patience was strained by the folly of those disbelievers. So Allah followed what preceded with that which removes this constriction from his soul, by His saying ﴿Good and evil are not equal﴾, to the end of the verse.

*Al-hasanah* encompasses all individual instances of its kind. The first to come to mind is the good of calling to Islam, because of its abundant benefits in the Hereafter and in this world. It also includes the quality of forgiving the harshness with which the polytheists meet the call of Islam, because forgiveness is a form of excellence. It involves leaving aside what would arouse their zeal for their religion and would bring about the softening of souls among those whose souls are gentle.

Thus the conjunction on this reading is a conjunction of one purpose to another, which is what is expressed as the conjunction of one narrative to another. It is a preparation and introduction to His saying after it ﴿Repel [evil] with that which is better﴾, to the end of the verse.

You have known more than once that the negation of equality and the like between two things usually intends the preference of one of them over its counterpart, according to the indication of the context. Examples are His saying ﴿Is one who was a believer like one who was a wicked person? They are not equal﴾ (al-Sajdah, 18), and the saying of al-A'sha:

*"That which is withheld, the niggardly, the one kept away from the rain-cloud's stormy course,*
*Is not made like the Euphrates when it rises and casts up its [foam] onto the Buṣiyy and the Māhir."*

[Page 291]

The apparent expectation would be that it be said ﴿Good and evil are not equal﴾ without repeating the negative particle *lā* after the second *wa*, as He, exalted is He, said ﴿The blind and the seeing are not equal﴾ (Fatir, 19). The repetition of the negative particle *lā* is then an emphasis for its earlier sister. A better approach than considering it emphasis is that there is an elision (*ḥadhf*) in the speech indicating an interlocking ellipsis (*iḥtibāk*). Its estimated form is: "Good and evil are not equal, nor are evil and good." The intended meaning of the first is the negation that the virtues of the good attain the level of the evil's deficiencies, and the intended meaning of the second is the negation that evil attains the nobility of the good. That is equality in qualities, and in it is an emphasis and reinforcement of the negation of equality, to show that it is a complete negation between the two genera, the genus of good and the genus of evil, with neither hyperbole nor metaphor in it. The discussion of its counterpart has already occurred in surah Fatir.

In using the expressions "good" and "evil" rather than "the doer of good" and "the doer of evil," there is an indication that each of these two groups has reached the extreme in the genus of its attribute, of goodness or evil, in the manner of description by the verbal noun. And so that the transition to the admonition of refining character in His saying ﴿Repel [evil] with that which is better﴾ may be facilitated, it seems that the choice of negating equality between good and evil is a preparation for the transition to His saying ﴿Repel [evil] with that which is better﴾.

His saying ﴿Repel [evil] with that which is better﴾ has its placement on the two aspects mentioned earlier regarding the conjunction of the sentence ﴿Good and evil are not equal﴾.

So the sentence, on the first of the two aspects of the placement of the sentence ﴿Good and evil are not equal﴾, is a transition from the purpose of preferring good over evil to the command to the moral quality of repelling [evil] with that which is better, because that repelling is among the effects of preferring good over evil. It is guidance from Allah to His Messenger and his community to adopt the character of repelling with the better.

On the second of the two aspects of the placement of the sentence ﴿Good and evil are not equal﴾, it stands in the position of the conclusion of an argument and the intended result of a premise, so its content arises from the content of the sentence before it.

Both of these considerations regarding the first sentence require that the sentence ﴿Repel [evil] with that which is better﴾ be separate and not conjoined.

[Page 292]

The Messenger ﷺ was commanded to do this because the furthest limit of human perfection is his character, as he said: "I was sent only to perfect noble character." 'A'ishah, when she was asked about his character, said: "His character was the Qur'an," because he was the most excellent of the wise.

Excellence (*ihsān*) is an intrinsic perfection, but leaving it may be praiseworthy in the case of the prescribed penalties (*ḥudūd*) and the like, and that is a particular meaning. Perfection is sought for its own sake, so one does not turn away from it as long as one is able, unless there is fear of missing a greater perfection. For this reason 'A'ishah said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ never took vengeance for himself at all, except when the sanctities of Allah were violated, and then he became angry for Allah's sake." The adoption of this character by the community is encouraged, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿The recompense for an evil is an evil like it, but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah﴾ (al-Shura, 40).

'Iyad related in al-Shifa, and it is among what Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, and Ibn Jarir in his tafsir: "When the saying of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿Take what is pardoned﴾ (al-A'raf, 199) was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ asked Jibril about its interpretation. He said: 'Let me ask the one who knows.' Then he came back and said: 'O Muhammad, indeed Allah commands you to join the one who cuts you off, to give to the one who withholds from you, and to pardon the one who wrongs you.'"

The object of *idfa'* (repel) is elided, indicated by the restriction of meaning between evil and good. When he was commanded that good be that with which evil is repelled, it became determined that what is repelled is evil. So the estimate is: "Repel evil with that which is better," as in His saying ﴿And they repel evil with good﴾ (al-Ra'd, 22) in surah al-Ra'd, and His saying ﴿Repel with that which is better the evil﴾ (al-Mu'minun, 96) in surah al-Mu'minun.

﴿That which is better﴾ (al-Isra', 53) is the good. It was formulated in the form of the comparative (*tafḍīl*) to encourage repelling evil with it, because that is hard upon the soul, for anger at bad treatment is a disposition of the soul, and it prompts a desire for revenge against the wrongdoer. So when the Messenger ﷺ was commanded to requite evil with good, the excellence of that was indicated. It has been reported in the description of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he did not repel evil with evil, but pardoned and forgave. It has been said that this is his description in the Torah.

Following upon this command is His saying ﴿Then the one between whom and you there is enmity will become as if he were a close friend﴾, to explain the good in that command, as a training toward adopting that noble character, namely that the soul becomes a source of excellence. Since good effects indicate the goodness of their source, and Allah commanded His Messenger ﷺ to repel with that which is better, He followed it with mention of some of its virtues,

[Page 293]

namely that the enemy becomes like a friend. The goodness of that is evident and accepted, so it must necessarily indicate the goodness of its cause.

Mention of the parable and the results immediately after the guidance has a notable function in establishing truths, especially those which souls may not accept because they are burdensome to them. Enmity is disliked, while friendship and allegiance are desired. Since excellence toward one who did wrong brings him closer to friendship or gains it for him, this is among the evidences for the benefit of the command to repel with that which is better.

*Idha* (then, suddenly) is for suddenness, and it is a metonymy for the speed with which the effect of repelling with what is better appears, in turning the enemy into a friend.

He turned away from mentioning the enemy defined by the article of genus to mentioning him by the relative pronoun, so that the indefiniteness of *'adawah* (enmity) can be used to denote the category (*nawʿiyyah*), which is the original purpose of indefiniteness. Thus it includes strong enmity and what is less than it, just as the adverbial phrase ﴿between you and him﴾ includes near and far separation, that is, the persistence of enmity or its occurrence.

This is a construction of the highest rank of eloquence, for it gathers the states of enmities. It makes known that excellence is effective in uprooting the enmity of the one who is treated well toward the one who treats him well, across the varying degrees of enmity in strength and weakness, firmness and remoteness. It also makes known that excellence toward the enemy should be strong in proportion to the firmness of his enmity, so that it may be more effective in uprooting it. Among the well-known sayings: souls are naturally inclined to love those who treat them well.

The comparison in His saying ﴿as if he were a close friend﴾ is a comparison in the disappearance of enmity and the mingling of traces of love. The point of resemblance is sincere closeness and nearness, and this is a meaning whose degrees vary, that is, it is predicated of its genus by gradation, according to the differing impact of excellence upon the soul and the differing strength of enmity before excellence. It does not reach the level of what it is compared to, for it is rare for an enemy to become an intimate friend. If he does, it is due to circumstances outside the meaning of rapidity which the sudden *idha* indicated.

The enmity between the polytheists and the Prophet ﷺ was enmity in religion, so the meaning is: "then the one between whom and you there is enmity because of his disbelief," [Page 294] and therefore the verse does not include those who believed after disbelief, whose enmity toward the Prophet ﷺ disappeared because of their faith, just as the enmity of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, disappeared after his Islam, to the point that he once said to the Prophet ﷺ: "You are dearer to me than my own soul that is between my two sides." And just as the enmity of Hind bint 'Utbah, wife of Abu Sufyan, disappeared when she said to the Prophet ﷺ: "There was no household tent more beloved to me than that its people should be humbled from among the people of your tent, and today there is no household tent more beloved to me than that its people should be honored from among the people of your tent." The Prophet ﷺ said to her: "And also," meaning: "and you will increase in love."

From Muqatil: he said: "This verse was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan, who was an enemy of the Prophet ﷺ in the Jahiliyyah, and after his Islam he became a loyal, sincere friend." Although this is as they say, I do not think the verse was revealed concerning that, because it was revealed concerning acquiring affection through excellence.

*Al-waliyy* (the ally, friend): a noun derived from *al-wilayah* (with the vowel *fatḥah* on the *waw*) and *al-walā'*, and it means the confederate and the helper. It is the opposite of the enemy, and it has been discussed in more than one verse of the Qur'an.

*Al-ḥamīm*: the near kinsman and the friend. The reason for combining ﴿a close friend﴾ is that it gathers two qualities, both of which cannot coexist with enmity: the qualities of allegiance and kinship.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 41, verse 35:

﴿And none is granted it except those who are patient, and none is granted it except one of great fortune.﴾

It is conjoined to the clause ﴿Repel [evil] with that which is better﴾ [Fussilat: 34], or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) relative to ﴿that which is better﴾ [al-Isra': 53]. The pronoun in yulaqqaha ("is granted it") refers to ﴿that which is better﴾ [al-Isra': 53], in consideration of its connection to the verb "repel" (idfa'), that is: with the dealing and repelling which is better. As for goodness in general, it may be attained by those other than those who are patient.

This is an exhortation to train oneself in this disposition, by showing that it requires strength of resolve and firmness of practice in patience, to refrain from the self's desire for revenge. In this there is also an honouring of its excellence, in that it is accompanied by the trait of patience, which in itself is a praiseworthy trait, and whose reward is abundant, as is known from several verses of the Qur'an. Sufficient for you is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [al-'Asr: 2] ﴿except for those who have believed and done righteous deeds and advised each other to truth and advised each other to patience﴾ [al-'Asr: 3].

The patient person is trained in bearing hardships, swallowing difficulties and restraining anger, so that leaving revenge becomes easy for him.

Yulaqqaha means "it is made to be encountered by them" (laqiyan lahā), like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He will give them radiance and happiness﴾ [al-Insan: 11]. This is used metaphorically for striving to attain it, because attaining something after effort and cultivating character resembles the striving to meet someone, so that one meets him.

The present tense is used for yulaqqaha in both places, in consideration of the fact that the one commanded to repel with what is better is commanded to acquire this disposition in the future. The past tense is used in the relative clause, "those who are patient," to indicate that patience is a prior disposition within them, which is the help in dealing with the wrongdoer with kindness. For this subtle point, it departed from saying "except the patient ones" (illa al-sabirun), because of the nuance that patience is a deeply rooted natural disposition in them.

Then the honouring of it is increased by saying that it is not attained except by one of great fortune.

Al-hazz (fortune) is one's share of a thing in general; it was said that it is specifically a share of good. The intended meaning here is a share of good, by context or by the indication of the lexical usage, that is: repelling evil with good is not attained except by one who possesses a great share of virtues, that is, of good character, guidance and piety.

From these two, it is concluded that acquiring patience is a condition for undertaking the excellence of repelling evil with what is better, and that it is not by itself the sole condition for it, but behind it are other conditions, gathered by His saying ﴿great fortune﴾, that is, of noble characteristics. Patience is part of the great fortune, because great fortune is more general than patience. Patience was singled out for mention only because it is its foundation, the head of its matter and its pillar.

In repeating the verb ﴿and none is granted it﴾ without relying on the conjunction alone, there is a display of heightened concern with this statement, such that nothing of its explicit meaning is hidden under the conjunction.

﴿One of great fortune﴾ conveys that great fortune in goodness is one's disposition and innate capacity, as the construction with dhu requires.

The sum of what the two clauses indicate is that someone like you, who receives this counsel, and it is not a matter easy for everyone.

[p. 297 begins at "...hadith of Ibn Masʿud in al-Tirmidhi"; page markers are preserved as given]

This is a conjunction on the phrase ﴿And none is granted it except those who are patient﴾ (Fussilat 41:35). After he guided to what helps attain this character trait that he was commanded to adopt, namely repelling evil with what is better, and after the benefit of acting by it was explained in His words ﴿and thereupon the one between whom and you there is enmity will become as if he were a close friend﴾ (Fussilat 41:34), He turned the reins here to warning against its obstacles, whose multiplicity is gathered in the reality of the incitement of Satan (nazgh al-shaytan). So he was commanded that if he finds in himself thoughts that divert him from that and call him to repel evil with its like, then that is an incitement from Satan, whose remedy is that you seek refuge in Allah from it. Allah has guaranteed that He will protect him when he seeks refuge, because He commanded him to do so. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ.

The benefit of this seeking of refuge is renewing the motive for infallibility (ʿișma) that is embedded in the soul of the Prophet ﷺ, because seeking refuge in Allah from Satan is seeking aid for infallibility and polishing that purifies the soul from the impurities that may approach it. This is a secret of the connection between the Prophet ﷺ and his Lord, and the saying of the Prophet ﷺ indicates it: «Indeed, my heart is veiled (yughān), and indeed I seek forgiveness from Allah a hundred times a day.» Through this his soul is kept safe from being covered by any of the impurities, and the righteous believers join him in this.

In the sacred hadith (ḥadīth qudsī) in al-Tirmidhi: «My servant does not cease to draw near to Me through voluntary acts until I love him. When I love him, I am his hearing with which he hears, his sight with which he sees, his hand with which he strikes, and his foot with which he walks. If he asks Me, I will surely give him, and if he seeks refuge in Me, I will surely protect him.»

Then the rest of the believers join with that, in their varying degrees, as indicated by the hadith of Ibn Masʿud in al-Tirmidhi. The Prophet ﷺ said: «Indeed, Satan has an influence (lamma) over the son of Adam, and the angel has an influence. As for the influence of Satan, it is a promise of evil and a denial of the truth; as for the influence of the angel, it is a promise of good and an affirmation of the truth. Whoever finds that, let him know that it is from Allah, and let him praise Allah. Whoever finds the other, let him seek refuge in Allah from Satan.»

Al-nazgh (incitement) means prodding (al-nakhs). Its reality is a strong touch to the skin with the tip of a stick or a finger. It is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and here it is used figuratively (mustaʿār) for the connection of the satanic force to the thoughts of a person, commanding him to evil and diverting him from good. Its occurrence in the words of the Most High ﴿And if an incitement from Satan incites you, then seek refuge in Allah; indeed, He is the Hearing, the Knowing﴾ (al-Aʿraf 7:200) was mentioned in Surat al-Aʿraf. The attribution of yanzaghannaka to nazgh is a rational metaphor (majāz ʿaqlī, a metaphor in the attribution of the act) of the type "jiddu jiddihi" (its very reality/its true self), and min is initial (ibtidāʾiyya, indicating origin).

It is possible that what is meant by nazgh here is the one who incites (al-nāzigh), who is Satan, described by the verbal noun for emphasis, and min is explicative (bayāniyya), meaning: "the inciter who is Satan will incite you." The emphasis is achieved under both interpretations, though the aspect of emphasis differs.

In this conditional clause, the particle "in" (inna) is used, whose original function is to leave open the non-certainty of the condition's occurrence, in order to elevate the rank of the Prophet ﷺ, for the incitement of Satan toward him is only supposed in the way that the impossible is supposed. Do you not see the words of the Most High ﴿Indeed, those who have feared Allah, when an impulse from Satan touches them, remember, and then they are seeing clearly﴾ (al-Aʿraf 7:201)? There, in that conditional clause, He used the particle "idhā," whose original function is the certainty of the condition's occurrence or the predominance of its occurrence.

The particle "mā" after the conditional particle is superfluous (zāʾida), to affirm the linkage between the condition and its response. It is not for confirming that the condition has occurred, for it is frequently added after "in" without indicating certainty of the occurrence of the conditional verb.

The pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl) in the words ﴿indeed, He is the Hearing, the Knowing﴾ is for strengthening the ruling. Here it is an implicit ruling (ḥukm kināʾī), because the intended meaning is the necessary implication of the attribute of the Hearing, the Knowing, which is the call to account of those from whom sayings and deeds proceed that harm the Prophet ﷺ and plot against him, from among those commanded to repel their evils with what is better.

The meaning is: If Satan embellishes for you not to deal with your enemies with good, and adorns for you retaliation, and says to you, "How will you do good to the enemies of the religion, when in retaliation against them is cutting off their plotting against the religion?", then do not follow his incitement. Take what We have commanded you, and seek refuge in Allah from Satan causing you to slip, for indeed nothing of the affair of your enemies is hidden from Allah, and He Himself will take charge of their recompense.

﴿And among His signs are the night and the day, and the sun and the moon. Do not prostrate to the sun or to the moon, but prostrate to God, who created them, if it is Him that you worship.﴾

This is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the sentence "﴿Say: Do you truly disbelieve in He who created the earth in two days?﴾ [Fussilat: 9]", as a narrative coordinated with another narrative. The purpose of mentioning the creation of the worlds is that they are proofs of God's exclusive divinity (ilahiyya). Therefore, here He informs that the things mentioned in this sentence are among God's signs, moving on to various modes of argumentation. This is a shift from arguing by the essences of His creatures to arguing by the conditions of those creatures. He begins with some heavenly conditions, namely the alternation of night and day and the rising of the sun and the moon, then after that mentions some earthly conditions with His saying: ﴿And among His signs is that you see the earth humbled﴾ [Fussilat: 39].

What indicates this shift is that the mode of address moves from the third person, in His saying: ﴿But if they turn away, say: I have warned you of a thunderbolt﴾ [Fussilat: 13], up to His saying: ﴿Good and evil are not equal﴾ [Fussilat: 34], to the mode of direct address to them, returning to the address found in His saying: ﴿Do you truly disbelieve in He who created the earth﴾ [Fussilat: 9].

The word "āyāt" (signs) means proofs, and its attribution to the pronoun of God is because they are evidence of His oneness and of His existence.

The alternation of night and day is one of the signs of power that no one other than God Most High performs. Therefore, it is certainly a proof of His exclusive act of creation, and so He alone is divine. The discussion of night and day has already occurred at His saying in Surat al-Baqara: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of night and day﴾ [al-Baqara: 164].

What is intended by the sun and the moon here, primarily, is their regular and continuous motion. As for their creation, it has already been known from the creation of the heavens and the earth, as mentioned just before in His saying: ﴿Then He completed them as seven heavens﴾ [Fussilat: 12]. The sun is one of the seven heavens, and the moon follows the sun. He did not mention anything indicating certain conditions of the sun and the moon, such as rising, setting, orbit, or the like, so that it would be suitable for argument by their conditions, which is the primary purpose. Their creation serves as an affirmation of what was derived from His saying: ﴿Then He completed them as seven heavens﴾ [Fussilat: 12], to increase the meanings.

Since reflection on the sun and the moon has taken place, and since among people there were groups who worshipped the sun and the moon, namely the Sabians (al-Sabiʾa), whose origin was in Iraq from the time of Abraham, peace be upon him, God has related their story in Surat al-Anʿam in His saying: ﴿So when the night covered him, he saw a star and said: This is my lord﴾ [al-Anʿam: 76], and so on. Then this religion appeared among Saba', who worshipped the sun, as God related in Surat al-Naml.

I have not found that among the Arabs at the time of the revelation of the Qur'an there were any who worshipped the sun and the moon. It appears from the words of al-Zamakhshari that he did not find this, since he says here: "Perhaps some people among them used to prostrate to the sun and the moon." End of quotation. However, the existence of sun worship in Yemen in the days of Saba', before they became Jews, requires that traces of it remained in some lands of the Arabs. It is also mentioned that among the idols of the Arabs there was an idol named Shams (the Sun), and by it they were named ʿAbd Shams (Servant of the Sun). Likewise, he counted among the names of the sun "the goddesses." Mayya bint Umm ʿUtba said:

"We went out from al-Laʿbaʾ in the afternoon, and we hurried the goddesses lest they return."

The idol named Shams was worshipped by Banu Tamim, Dabba, Tamim, ʿUkl, and Udd. I had also found that some of Kinana worshipped the moon.

In Talkhis al-Tafsir by al-Kawashi: "The people used to prostrate to the sun and the moon, claiming that they intended by that prostration to God, like the Sabians. So they were forbidden from that and were commanded to devote worship to Him, Most High." There is nothing in it indicating that these people were Arabs. Moreover, the guidance of the Qur'an is not restricted to the Arabs; rather, the spread of the religion of the Sabians in the lands neighboring them is sufficient as a warning against prostrating to the sun and the moon.

The Arabs used to think that the religion of Islam was the religion of the Sabians, so they would say to whoever embraced Islam: "He has become a Sabian (ṣabaʾa)," and they would describe the Prophet ﷺ as a Sabian. Therefore, if the prohibition in His saying: ﴿Do not prostrate to the sun or to the moon﴾ is not a prohibition of cessation with regard to those who prostrate to the sun and the moon, then it is a prohibition of warning to whoever does not prostrate to them, that they should not follow those who worship them.

The placement of His saying: ﴿But prostrate to God, who created them﴾ after the prohibition of prostration to the sun and the moon conveys the sense of restriction (ḥaṣr), because the prohibition has the status of negation, and the affirmation after it has the status of contrasting negation with affirmation. It has the status of negation and exception in conveying restriction, as you see in the verse of al-Samawʾal or ʿAbd al-Malik al-Harithi:

"Our souls flow on the edges of the swords, and they do not flow except on the swords."

So it is as if it were said: Do not prostrate except to God, that is, not to the sun or the moon.

So the sentence ﴿Do not prostrate to the sun﴾ up to His saying "you worship" is parenthetical (iʿtiraḍ) between the sentence ﴿And among His signs are the night and the day﴾ and the sentence ﴿But if they are arrogant﴾ [Fussilat: 38].

In this verse is a place of prostration of recitation (sujud al-tilawa). Mālik and his companions, except Ibn Wahb, said: the prostration is at His saying: ﴿if it is Him that you worship﴾. This is also the view of ʿAlī ibn Abi Talib and Ibn Masʿud, and it is reported from al-Shafiʿi. Abu Hanifa, al-Shafiʿi in the well-known report from him, and Ibn Wahb said: it is at His saying: ﴿and they are not weary﴾ [Fussilat: 38]. This is also reported from Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbas, and Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 41, verse 38:**

﴿Then if they are arrogant, those who are with your Lord glorify Him night and day, and they never tire.﴾

The fa' (فاء) here marks a consequence (tafri') of their being forbidden to prostrate to the sun and the moon and of their being commanded to prostrate to God alone. That is: "If they are arrogant" against following you and insist on prostrating to the sun and the moon; or "if they are arrogant" about acknowledging that the night and the day, the sun and the moon, point to God's sole divinity. In that case the pronoun in "they are arrogant" (istakbaru) encompasses all the polytheists, and God is independent of their worship of Him.

Al-istikbar (الاستكبار) means the intensity of takabbur (arrogance); the sin and ta' in it (as in the two letters used for intensification) are, in origin, the sin and ta' of reckoning (al-husban), meaning: they counted themselves as possessing great pride, out of the extreme excess of their arrogance.

The clause ﴿those who are with your Lord﴾ is the response (dalil jawab) to the conditional. The implied sense is: "If they are arrogant toward prostrating to God, then He is independent of their prostration, because He has servants more excellent than them who never cease glorifying Him with devotion and without weariness."

Al-tasbih (التسبيح, glorification) here means everything that indicates the exalted transcendence of God above what does not befit Him, by affirming the opposites of what does not befit Him or by negating what does not befit Him. This occurs by speech, as He said: ﴿And the angels glorify the praise of their Lord﴾ [al-Shura: 5], or by deeds, as He said: ﴿And to God prostrates whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of creatures, and the angels, and they are not arrogant. They fear their Lord above them and do what they are commanded﴾ [al-Nahl: 49]. This is what His saying ﴿and they never tire﴾ requires, namely that this glorification is both speech and action, not merely belief.

The "nearness" (al-'indiyyah) in His saying ﴿with your Lord﴾ is nearness of honor and dignity, like His saying in Surat al-A'raf: ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord are not too proud to worship Him; they glorify Him and prostrate to Him﴾ [al-A'raf: 206]. These are the angels who inhabit the higher worlds, which God made honored in that nothing occurs in them except excellence; thus they are more specifically related to Him, exalted is He, than other places, intentionally so as to honor them.

Al-sa'ama (السآمة) is boredom and weariness arising from fatigue. The mention of night and day here is for the purpose of encompassing all time, meaning: they glorify Him for all of time.

The clause ﴿and they never tire﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and it is more forceful than the sense of coordination (mahmal al-'atf); because the report about them being restricted to this circumstance more strongly displays the wondrous nature of their state, since it is the nature of constant action that its doer is spared from it.

[Page 302]

﴿And among His signs is that you see the earth barren, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells.﴾

This is coordinated with the clause ﴿And among His signs are the night and the day﴾ [Fussilat: 37]. It is an argument from this great act of creation that He, exalted is He, alone performs it, and so it is proof of His divinity to the exclusion of any other. For whoever does what no other can do is the true God. If that is the case, it is not possible for there to be more than one, because one who cannot do what He does lacks power, and deficiency contradicts divinity, as He said: ﴿Is He who creates like one who creates not?﴾ [al-Nahl: 17].

The address in His words "that you see" is to an unspecified addressee, so that it applies to every hearer.

Khushu' (humbling, submission) means abasement. It is used figuratively for the state of the earth when it is parched and has no vegetation on it, because its condition in that destitution is like the condition of one who is abased. This is an instance of rendering the perceptible in terms of the intelligible, based on what people imagine of the resemblance between the two states of dryness and fertility and the two states of abasement and exultation.

Ihtizaz (stirring, quivering) in its literal sense is the reflexive form of hazz, meaning that when one shakes a thing after it has been still, it moves. Here it is used figuratively for the swelling of the surface of the earth with vegetation. The state of its producing growth and rising, after it had been low and lifeless, through water and plants, is likened to stirring.

From the totality of this it is understood that this construction is a figurative representation (tamthil, an extended analogy). The state of the earth's dryness, then the sending down of water upon it, and its transformation from barrenness to fertility and beautiful growth, is likened to the state of a person who was downcast and shabbily dressed, then was given some wealth, so he put on finery and strutted in his gait with pride. For this reason it is said: "He shook his sides" when someone struts in his walk.

In His words "humbled" and "stirred" there is a metonymy (kinaya), in that the earth is likened to a person who was abased and then became one who shakes his sides. He alluded to the thing likened by means of these two, by mentioning their companions. This is among the finest kinds of figurative representation, and it is the kind that admits the separation of its parts into the parts of the comparison.

"And swells" is coordinated with "stirs" because the purpose of the stirring is the appearance of plants upon it and their movement. The meaning of swelling (rabw) is its inflating with water and its rising.

[Page 303]

Abu Ja'far read "ورَبَأتْ" (wa-rabaʾat) with a hamza after the letter ba, from "rabaʾa" with a hamza, meaning it rose up.

* * *

﴿Indeed, He who gave it life is surely the one who gives life to the dead. Indeed He has power over all things.﴾

This is an integration (idmaj, weaving one theme into another) of the affirmation of resurrection within the argument for His sole power over creation and governance. It occurs in accordance with the Qur'an's custom of varying its discourse and seizing opportunities for guidance toward the truth.

The sentence is a new independent statement (istinaf ibtida'i), and the connection is the resemblance between the two revivings. The emphatic particle is used to take into account the denial by the addressees of the revival of the dead.

The definition of the predicate's subject by the relative construction is because the relative clause contains the explanation of the predicate. The support of the earth by rainwater, which is the cause of the emergence of the seeds within it that become plants, is likened to the reviving of the dead. So the expression "He gave it life" is used for that by way of an indirect metaphor (isti'ara tab'iyya). Then it was elevated from that, which was called "giving life," to making that which is called giving life, because it resembles giving life, a proof of the possibility of reviving the dead by way of analogy by resemblance. This is what logic calls qiyas al-tamthil (analogy by resemblance), and it serves to bring the thing being analogized close to the thing it is analogized to. Argument by resemblance and analogy is not a decisive proof, but a persuasive one. Yet here it becomes a proof, because the thing analogized to, although weaker than the thing analogized, since the likened does not reach the strength of that to which it is likened, is such that its doer cannot perform it except the Creator, who is characterized by complete power in His essence. Thus both its strong and weak aspects are equal in it. They had been denying the revival of the dead on the basis of ordinary improbability. When the revival of the dead was compared with the revival of the earth, which was the thing likened, the persuasive proof was completed, suited to their persuasive doubt. This is indicated by the concluding statement: "Indeed He has power over all things."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 41, verse 40:

﴿Indeed, those who deviate concerning Our verses are not hidden from Us.﴾

This is an independent resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), intended to threaten those who neglected to reason from the signs of God toward His Oneness.

His saying ﴿are not hidden from Us﴾ is meant as a kinayah (allusion) for the threat, reminding them that God's knowledge encompasses every existing thing. Its meaning is connected to His saying shortly before: ﴿And you did not conceal yourselves lest your hearing and your sight and your skins should testify against you﴾ [Fussilat: 22], and so on.

The root meaning of ilhad (deviation) is turning away from uprightness. The "signs" (ayat) include the cosmic proofs mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in He who created the earth in two days?﴾ [Fussilat: 9], and His saying ﴿And among His signs are the night and the day﴾ [Fussilat: 37], etc. They also include the verbal signs mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿And those who disbelieve said: Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during its recitation﴾ [Fussilat: 26].

So deviation concerning the signs is used metaphorically for turning away from and diverting from the indication of the cosmic signs toward what they indicate. Deviation concerning the verbal signs is used metaphorically for turning away from listening to them, and for impugning their authenticity and diverting people from listening to them.

The particle fi (in) in His exalted saying ﴿concerning Our verses﴾ is for metaphorical spatial enclosure (zarfiyyah majaziyyah), to express that their deviation is firmly rooted, as though they were enclosed within God's signs wherever they are or whenever they hear them.

The meaning of the negation of their concealment is: the negation of the concealment of their deviation, not the concealment of their persons, since there is no purpose in knowing their persons themselves.

* * *

﴿Is then he who is thrown into the Fire better, or he who comes secure on the Day of Resurrection?﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of the threat in His saying ﴿are not hidden from Us﴾, to explain that the threat of the Fire of Jahannam is an indirect allusion to the polytheists, that they are destined for the Fire, and to the believers, that they are safe from that.

The interrogation is a consequence used to draw attention to the difference between the two ranks.

By His saying ﴿comes secure﴾ is alluded that this group's destination is Paradise, since the secure person has no end but to be in bliss. This is an allusive kinayah directed at those who deviate concerning the signs of God.

In the verse there is the embellishment of ihtibak (interweaving), in that the counterpart of ﴿he who is thrown into the Fire﴾ has been omitted, which is: he who enters Paradise; and the counterpart of ﴿he who comes secure﴾ has been omitted, which is: he who comes fearful, and they are the people of the Fire.

* * *

﴿Do what you will; indeed He is Seeing of what you do.﴾

The sentence is a tadhyil (appendix) to the sentence ﴿Indeed, those who deviate concerning Our verses﴾ etc., as indicated by His saying after it ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it has come to them﴾ [Fussilat: 41], etc., meaning: their deviation is not hidden from Us, nor is any other of their evil deeds. He specifically mentioned deviation first because it is the most abominable of their deeds and the source of their evils.

The imperative in His saying ﴿Do what you will﴾ is used for threat, or for incitement, which is an allusive expression for threat.

The sentence ﴿indeed He is Seeing of what you do﴾ is a threat of punishment for their deeds, by way of kinayah.

Its emphasis with (inna) is to affirm both its allusive and its explicit meanings, namely the affirmation that God's knowledge encompasses their deeds; for they were doubtful of that, as was mentioned in the story of the three men concerning whom His saying was revealed ﴿And you did not conceal yourselves lest your hearing and your sight should testify against you﴾ [Fussilat: 22], etc.

Al-Basir: the Knowing of things seen.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 41, verses 41–42:**

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it comes to them—and indeed, it is a mighty Book.﴾ ﴿Falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it; it is a revelation from the All-Wise, the Praiseworthy.﴾

After threatening them for their deviation (ilhad) regarding the signs of Allah in general, the verses turn to their deviation regarding the signs of the Qur'an in particular. This is the mention of the specific after the general, to highlight the qualities of the Qur'an and that it is not open to being disbelieved in. Rather, it is worthy of being accepted, through following it and being guided by its guidance. Thus this sentence is connected in meaning to the sentence "Indeed, those who deviate regarding Our signs" and connected in position to the sentence "Do whatever you wish."

صفحة ٣٠٦

The determination of these two connections has been disputed among the exegetes. On the basis of their disagreement about them, they also disagreed about its place in grammatical analysis (i'rab) and about the position of its parts, whether explicit or implied.

The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) made his statement "Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder" a substitute (badal) for his statement "Indeed, those who deviate regarding Our signs" [Fussilat: 40]. He meant that this is the substitution of a singular noun by a singular noun, either a corresponding substitute (badal mutabiq) or a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal). He also meant that this involves repeating the governing particle, which is the particle "inna," although repeating the governing word with a substitute is not well known except in the case of the prepositional particle, as al-Radi said. The words of al-Zamakhshari in al-Mufassal require the general application, although he gave two examples whose governing element is a prepositional particle.

On this view, no predicate (khabar) is posited, because the predicate of the substituted-from noun is a predicate of the substitute, which is his statement "they will not be hidden from Us."

From Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala', al-Kisa'i, and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd there is a report implying that they make the sentence "Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder" an independent sentence, because they made a predicate for "inna." As for Abu 'Amr, he said: the predicate of "inna" is his statement "Those will be called from a far place" [Fussilat: 44].

It is related that Bilal ibn Abi Burda was asked in the assembly of Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' about the predicate of "inna," and he said: "I have not found a way to it." Abu 'Amr said to him: "Indeed, it is near to you: 'Those will be called from a far place.'" This requires treating the sentences that lie between the subject of "inna" and its predicate as parenthetical sentences (jumal mu'taridah), and they number about seven.

As for al-Kisa'i and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, they posited a predicate for the subject of "inna." Al-Kisa'i said: the predicate is omitted and is indicated by his earlier statement "Is one who is thrown into the Fire better" [Fussilat: 40]; so we posit the predicate as: "They are thrown into the Fire," for example. 'Isa ibn 'Umar asked 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd about the predicate, and 'Amr said: "Its meaning is that those who disbelieved in the Reminder disbelieved in it, and indeed it is a mighty Book." 'Isa said: "You have done well, O Abu 'Uthman."

On the view of these scholars, it is possible for the sentence to be a substitute for the sentence "Indeed, those who deviate regarding Our signs" [Fussilat: 40], as a substitute of inclusion if by "signs" in his statement "regarding Our signs" is meant all signs in general, or as a corresponding substitute if by "signs" is meant the signs of the Qur'an.

It has also been said that the predicate is his statement "Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you" [Fussilat: 43]; that is, "Nothing is said to you about them except what We said to the messengers before you concerning their deniers," or "They say nothing except what the nations said to the messengers before you," and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion.

صفحة ٣٠٧

Disbelief in the Qur'an includes denying everything by which the Qur'an is described as being from Allah, and what it contains that opposes their belief and their religion of polytheism. This takes the form of the various accusations they made, such as their saying: "It is sorcery," "It is poetry," "It is the word of a soothsayer," "It is the word of a madman," "If We willed, We could say the like of this," "It is the fables of the ancients," and "Our hearts are in coverings, and in our ears is deafness" [Fussilat: 5].

The most apparent view is that the sentence "Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder" etc. occupies the position of a causal justification (ta'lil) for the threat of punishment in his statement "they will not be hidden from Us" [Fussilat: 40]. The meaning is: because they deserve punishment when they disbelieve in the signs, and these are the sign of the Qur'an in truth, and by the testimony of what was entrusted to the messengers before it.

The position of "inna" here is the position of the causal "fa'" (fa' al-ta'lil). The predicate of "inna" is omitted, and the context of the speech indicates it.

The best view is that its implied predicate should be what the situation indicates of the grandeur and preciousness of the Reminder. So the sense would be: "They lost this world and the Hereafter," or "They made fools of themselves," or something similar of what the mind of an eloquent listener inclines to. In this omission there is an abundance of meanings and a brevity of expression that stands in place of many sentences. The omission of the predicate of "inna," when it is indicated by a proof present in the speech, was permitted by Sibawayh in the chapter on which these five particles it is good to remain silent, and the majority followed him. Al-Farra' disagreed and made it conditional on the repetition of "inna." Among the omissions is the verse of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and bar from the way of Allah and the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Hajj: 25], in the surah of al-Hajj. Sibawayh also recited:

*Oh, would that the days of youth would return*

where "rawajiʿan" is related in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), so no predicate of "layta" is mentioned.

He also mentioned that the Arabs say: "Indeed wealth and indeed children," meaning "indeed for them," and the verse of al-A'sha:

*Indeed a dwelling place, and indeed a departure*

meaning: indeed for us in this world there is a dwelling, and for us a departure from it; since the rest of the line, which is his statement:

*And indeed in the journey, when they passed, a pause*

does not contain anything that can validly be the predicate of the first "inna."

Jamil said:

*They said: "We see her, O Jamil, changed,"*
*and the informer altered her, so I said: "Perhaps it is she."*

Al-Jahiz said in al-Bayan, in a section on what is omitted from speech: from al-Hasan, that the Emigrants said, "O Messenger of Allah, indeed the Helpers sheltered us and supported us." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do you know that for them?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Then indeed that [is so]." There is nothing in the hadith but this, meaning: "then indeed that is gratitude and reciprocation." End of quote. In the third-and-fortieth maqama [of al-Hariri] there is: "Enough, O shaykh, for I have recognized your identity, and have made clear that you are Abu Zayd." Al-Shalubin, in his commentary on al-Tashil, gave this verse as an example of the omission of the predicate of "inna."

The sentence "And indeed it is a mighty Book" etc. occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the Reminder, meaning: they disbelieved in it in this state of its. It is also permissible that the sentence be a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the sentence "Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder," on the basis of the implied predicate of "inna."

Six attributes have been ascribed to the Qur'an, each one of which is a great perfection.

The first attribute: it is a Reminder, meaning it reminds all people of what they are heedless of, and in that heedlessness is the loss of their success.

The second attribute, from the meaning of Reminder: it is a reminder for the Arabs and a fine reputation for them among the nations, which perpetuates for them a great glory, namely that it is in their language and was revealed among them, as the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 44]. And in his statement "when it came to them" there is an allusion to this second meaning.

The third attribute: it is a mighty Book. "Mighty" (aziz) means precious and noble. Its root is from "izza," which is protection, because a precious thing is defended and guarded from being cast aside. The Qur'an is between perfection of composition, loftiness of meanings, and clarity of proof, and something like this is mighty. Also, "aziz" means one who overcomes and is not overcome, and likewise are the proofs of the Qur'an.

صفحة ٣٠٩

The fourth attribute: falsehood cannot reach it, nor does it mix with its explicit or implicit meaning; that is, it does not contain falsehood in any way. This is illustrated by "from before it and from behind it," and the intended meaning is to encompass all directions, as an image of the state in which falsehood is absent from it in its outward form and in its interpretation, by analogy with an attacker who drives away a person in order to harm him: he comes to him from the front, and if he is repelled, he deceives him and comes at him from behind. This was mentioned in the Exalted's statement: ﴿Then I will come to them from before them and from behind them﴾ [al-A'raf: 17].

So the meaning of "falsehood cannot approach it" is that it is not found in it and does not enter into it, and the intention is not that falsehood is not claimed against it.

The fifth attribute: it contains wisdom, which is true knowledge, because it is a revelation from the All-Wise, and nothing but wisdom issues from the All-Wise: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269]. The speech of a wise person comes firm, perfected, and sound, and falsehood does not mix into it.

The sixth attribute: it is a revelation from the Praiseworthy. "Hamid" is one who is praised abundantly, meaning worthy of abundant praise. So the speech sent down from Him deserves praise. Speech is praised only when it is a guide to good and leads to it, with no flaw in its wording or its meaning, so its listener praises it abundantly because he finds it a source of much good, and its speaker is praised without doubt, unlike the polytheists.

In the enumeration of these attributes there is a hint at the folly of those who disbelieved in this Qur'an and the foolishness of their opinions, since they neglected it and so neglected the means of their success in this world and the Hereafter. For this reason the circumstantial clause about the Book was brought right after mentioning their denial of it, when He said: ﴿And indeed it is a mighty Book﴾, and so on.

This is illustrated by "from before it and from behind it," and the intended meaning is to encompass all directions, as an image of the state in which falsehood is absent from it in its outward form and in its interpretation, by analogy with an attacker who drives away a person in order to harm him: he comes to him from the front, and if he is repelled, he deceives him and comes at him from behind. This was mentioned in the Exalted's statement: ﴿Then I will come to them from before them and from behind them﴾ [al-A'raf: 17].

So the meaning of "falsehood cannot approach it" is that it is not found in it and does not enter into it, and the intention is not that falsehood is not claimed against it.

The fifth attribute: it contains wisdom, which is true knowledge, because it is a revelation from the All-Wise, and nothing but wisdom issues from the All-Wise: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269]. The speech of a wise person comes firm, perfected, and sound, and falsehood does not mix into it.

The sixth attribute: it is a revelation from the Praiseworthy. "Hamid" is one who is praised abundantly, meaning worthy of abundant praise. So the speech sent down from Him deserves praise. Speech is praised only when it is a guide to good and leads to it, with no flaw in its wording or its meaning, so its listener praises it abundantly because he finds it a source of much good, and its speaker is praised without doubt, unlike the polytheists.

In the enumeration of these attributes there is a hint at the folly of those who disbelieved in this Qur'an and the foolishness of their opinions, since they neglected it and so neglected the means of their success in this world and the Hereafter. For this reason the circumstantial clause about the Book was brought right after mentioning their denial of it, when He said: ﴿And indeed it is a mighty Book﴾, and so on.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 41, verse 43:

﴿Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you.﴾

This is an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), an answer to a question raised by His words ﴿Indeed, those who distort Our verses are not hidden from Us﴾ [Fussilat: 40] and His words ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it comes to them﴾ [Fussilat: 41], along with the descriptions that intervene between them. So a questioner asks: "Why is it that these people have slandered it?" It is answered that this is the custom of the prophets with their nations: they never lack stubborn deniers who reject what they brought.

If the sentence ﴿ma yuqal﴾ ("nothing is said") is built upon what I permitted earlier, namely that it be the predicate of ﴿inna﴾ (indeed), then it is a predicate and not a resumption.

This is a consolation to the Prophet (ﷺ) by way of allusion (kinaya), and a command to him to be patient over it, just as the messengers before him were patient, by way of indirect reference (ta'ridh).

There are two explanations of this statement:

The first: what the polytheists say about the Qur'an and the Prophet (ﷺ) is the same pattern of their stubborn counterparts before them. So ﴿ma qad qil li-l-rusul﴾ ("what was said to the messengers") is the sayings of those who denied them, meaning that the hearts of the deniers resembled one another, so their sayings were alike. God the Exalted said ﴿Did they charge one another with it?﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 53].

The second explanation: "We have said to you nothing except what We said to the messengers before you." You were not a novelty among the messengers, so your people would have some excuse for denial; but they denied just as those before them denied. So ﴿ma qad qil li-l-rusul﴾ is the religion and the revelation, and this is in the manner of His words ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scriptures﴾ [al-A'la: 18]. Both meanings occur in the Qur'an, so the statement is to be understood as bearing both.

In the expression with the relative ﴿ma﴾ and in the omission of the agent of the two verbs, ﴿ma yuqal﴾ and ﴿ma qad qil﴾, there is a firm composition that carries these two great meanings. And in His words ﴿illa ma qad qil li-l-rusul﴾ there is an eloquent simile. The meaning is: "except the like of what was said to the messengers."

The use of the present tense in ﴿ma yuqal﴾ serves to indicate the renewal of this saying from them and their failure to desist from it, despite the clarity of what should deter them from it.

The conjunction of the verb with ﴿qad﴾ is to confirm that it has indeed been said to the messengers the like of what the polytheists said to the Messenger (ﷺ). It is thus an emphasis on the necessary implication of the report, namely the necessity of patience over their words. This is viewed with regard to the state of those being refuted, who reckoned that they had confronted the Messenger with something that had not occurred to anyone else. This is in the manner of His words ﴿Thus, no messenger came to those before them except that they said: "A magician or a madman."﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 52] ﴿Did they charge one another with it? Rather, they are a transgressing people.﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 53]

* * *

﴿Indeed, your Lord is Possessor of forgiveness and Possessor of painful punishment.﴾

This is a consolation to the Messenger (ﷺ) and a promise that God will forgive him. The occurrence of this report directly after His words ﴿Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you﴾ indicates that this promise is a reward for the harm he suffered for the sake of God, and that the threat is for those who harmed him. So the report is used in its implication.

The meaning of forgiveness for him is the overlooking of the grief that afflicts him from what he hears from the polytheists of much harm. The particle ﴿inna﴾ in it serves to indicate causation and cause-and-effect, not emphasis.

The word ﴿dhu﴾ indicates that both forgiveness and punishment are of His attributes, and He places each by His wisdom in the places deserving of it.

The description of the punishment as ﴿painful﴾, rather than another description, indicates that it is suitable for what they were punished for, since they caused the Prophet's own self (ﷺ) pain through their disobedience and harm.

In the sentence ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Possessor of forgiveness and Possessor of painful punishment﴾ there is the rhetorical device of combination followed by division (muhassin al-jam' thumma al-taqsim). The phrase ﴿ma yuqal laka﴾ combines a speaker and one addressed. So the allusion of the description "Possessor of forgiveness" is to the one addressed, and the description "Possessor of painful punishment" is to the speakers. This follows the method of laff and nashr reversed (al-laff wa al-nashr al-ma'kus), and the context of the situation returns each to its appropriate counterpart.

[Page 312]

**Qur'an 41:44:** ﴿And if We had made it a non-Arabic Qur'an, they would have said, "Why are its verses not explained clearly? Is it a non-Arabic recitation for an Arab audience?"﴾

The coherence of the discourse from the beginning of the surah to this point, and the appropriateness of its shifts through elaboration, explanation, interjection and digression, indicate that His saying ﴿And if We had made it a non-Arabic Qur'an, they would have said﴾ through to the end of the verse is a further step in establishing that their aim is obstinacy. They use the pretexts they invent to turn away from the Qur'an and from benefiting by its guidance, through the false accusations and denials they fabricate against it, and through the baseless excuses they contrive so that by these means they can conceal their appearance as a defeated party brought to submission. So He began to refute their claims point by point, since the surah opened with their challenge by the miracle of the Qur'an, in His saying:

[Page 312 continues]
﴿Ḥā Mīm﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 1] ﴿A revelation from the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 2] ﴿A Book whose verses are explained in detail, an Arabic Qur'an for a people who know﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 3], up to His saying ﴿but most of them turn away, so they do not hear﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 4]. This is a challenge to them and a description of the Qur'an with the attribute of inimitability.

Then He proceeded to nullify their excuses and their accusations, in His saying ﴿And they say, "Our hearts are in coverings from what you invite us to, and in our ears is deafness"﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 5]. Their saying this was intended to show that the proof of the Qur'an does not convince them, out of spite toward the Prophet ﷺ. Then came their collusion in turning away, in His saying ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it that you may overcome"﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 26]. This is an evident incapacity, as shown by His saying ﴿Indeed, those who distort Our verses are not hidden from Us﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 40], and by His saying ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it came to them﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 41] and the verses that follow. Then He followed these with the attributes of the Qur'an's perfection, against which they find no ground for accusation, in His saying ﴿And indeed, it is a mighty Book﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 41], and the verse.

Since these disputations from the beginning of the surah to this point have been a refutation of their pretexts, and since their main support was that the Qur'an is Arabic, its meaning clearly intelligible in their language, as the discourse began with His saying ﴿A Book whose verses are explained in detail, an Arabic Qur'an for a people who know﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 3], and ended here with His saying ﴿And indeed, it is a mighty Book; falsehood cannot approach it from before it or from behind it﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 41], then the proof had already been established against them by its indication of the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ from this aspect. So the discourse moved to another proof, whose basis is the supposition and assumption that the Messenger ﷺ had brought them a Qur'an in a language other than the language of the Arabs.

For this reason, the clause ﴿And if We had made it a non-Arabic Qur'an﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿And indeed, it is a mighty Book﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 41], according to the two considerations mentioned above regarding the position of that clause.

The meaning of the verse is a branch of what His saying ﴿A Book whose verses are explained in detail, an Arabic Qur'an for a people who know﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 3] contains, and of His saying ﴿Say, "I am only a man like you; it is revealed to me"﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 6], from the challenge by the attribute of being unlettered, as you have already learned. That is: if We had brought them another form of the miracle of unlettered-ness, by sending down to the Messenger a non-Arabic Qur'an, while the Messenger ﷺ had no prior knowledge of that language, they would have turned their excuses around and said: "Why were its verses not made clear in a language we understand? How does he address us in a non-Arabic speech?" The discourse here proceeds on the manner of supposition, as is required by the particle *law* (lo), which is the conditional particle of impossibility (*law al-imtina'iyya*), meaning that the second clause is impossible because the first is impossible. This is a demonstration that these people are not benefited by proof and do not stop making excuses, because their disputation is not intended to seek the truth; it is only obstinacy to promote their desires.

[Page 313]

Of this kind of argumentation is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And if We had sent it down upon some of the non-Arabs, and he had recited it to them, they would not have believed in it﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 198]. That is: if We had sent it down in the language of the Arabs upon some of the non-Arabs, and he had recited it to them in Arabic, they would not have believed, since the two proofs share the attribute of unlettered-ness in the language in which the Book is supposed to be sent down. However, that verse is built on the supposition that this Qur'an would descend upon a Messenger who does not know Arabic, whereas this verse is built on the supposition that the Qur'an would descend upon the Arab Prophet ﷺ in a language other than Arabic.

In this verse there is an indication of the universality of the mission of Muhammad ﷺ to both Arabs and non-Arabs. Therefore it is not strange that the Book revealed to him should be in a language other than Arabic, were it not that there is wisdom in its being sent down in Arabic, which God knows. For when God chose the Messenger ﷺ to be an Arab and sent him among an Arab nation, the most deserving of languages for His Book to be sent down to him in was Arabic. For if His Book had come down in a non-Arabic language, all the languages of the nations would have been equal in their entitlement to the descent of the Book in them, and this would have produced jealousy among them. The Arabs, by contrast, were isolated from the nations, so Arabic was rightly preferred, since it is the language of the Messenger ﷺ and the language of the people to whom he was sent. It is not proper that the people he calls should remain unable to understand the Book sent down to them.

Moreover, if the Books had been multiplied according to the number of languages, the miracle of eloquence peculiar to Arabic would have been lost, because Arabic is the noblest of languages and the highest in its characteristics, in its eloquence, and in its excellent rendering of many meanings with concise words. Furthermore, the Arabs are the ones who take on the task of spreading this religion among the nations and clarifying the meanings of the Qur'an for them.

It is reported in the *Tafsir* of al-Tabari, on the authority of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that he said: "The Quraysh said: 'Why was this Qur'an not sent down as non-Arabic and Arabic?' So God revealed: ﴿Why are its verses not explained clearly? Is it non-Arabic and Arabic?﴾" with a single hamza, not in the manner of an interrogative. End of quotation. I do not think this is an interpretation by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, because he did not attribute it to a narrator, nor did he transmit it from anyone else. He regarded the verse as reporting a response to a statement made by the polytheists, who are referred to by the pronoun in *laqalu* ("they would have said").

The context and wording of the verse reject this meaning, and how could it be otherwise, when *law* of impossibility precludes accepting this interpretation and repels it?

[Page 314]

As for what al-Zamakhshari mentions in the *Kashshaf*: "They used to say, out of their obstinacy: 'Why was the Qur'an not sent down in the language of non-Arabs?' So it was said: 'Even if it were as they propose, they would not leave off objection and obstinacy, and they would say: ﴿Why are its verses not explained clearly?﴾,' and so on." We have not found anyone among the exegetes, or among the authors of works on the occasions of revelation, who mentions something like this, and it is nothing but of the same kind as what was reported from Sa'id. Had it been so, the structure of the verse would have been: "And they say: 'Why are its verses not explained clearly?'" and it would not have followed the pattern of *law* and its answer. Nor is it to be thought that the Quraysh would say that except as mockery and derision.

The pronoun in *ja'alnahu* refers to the Reminder mentioned in His saying ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 41].

His saying ﴿Is it non-Arabic and Arabic?﴾ is the remainder of what they would say on the supposition that the Qur'an were made non-Arabic. That is, they cannot escape casting doubt upon the Qur'an under any supposition.

*Law* ("why") here is a particle of urging (*tahḍīḍ*).

The meaning of *fuṣṣilat* here is: made clear and explained, that is, "why were its verses not made Arabic, so that we might understand them?"

The *waw* in His saying (*wa-'Arabiyy*) is for conjunction, in the sense of accompaniment. The meaning is: how can a non-Arabic and an Arabic meet? That is, how can the utterance be non-Arabic while the one addressed by it is Arab? As if they were saying: "Is a non-Arabic utterance addressed to an Arab listener?"

The meaning of *Qur'an* here is a Book to be read. It is reported in a hadith that the Book of Dawud, peace be upon him, was called a Qur'an. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, the Qur'an was made easy for Dawud, so he would recite the whole Qur'an while his horse was being saddled," or as he said.

*A'jamiyy* is the adjective derived from *a'jam*, and *a'jam* is derived from *'ujma*, which is clarity of speech (*al-ifṣāḥ*). So *a'jam* is one who does not speak clearly in the Arabic language, and the addition of the *ya* to it indicates the adjectival form, as in *aḥmariyy* and *dawwāriyy*. Thus *a'jamiyy* is one of the attributes of speech.

He used the singular *'Arabiyy* according to its interpretation as the genus of the listener, and the meaning is: "Is it a Book in Arabic for Arab listeners?" The expected form would be the plural *'Arab*, but it is given in the singular because the basis of the denial is the incompatibility of the state of the Book and of those to whom it is addressed. So the genus is considered here, without regard to singular or plural.

[Page 315]

The summary of the meaning of the verse is that it indicates an unstated statement included among the attributes of the Reminder, namely: that it is in an Arabic tongue, your own language, as a completion of your guidance. But you did not believe in it, you disbelieved, and you made excuses with false pretexts. Had We made it non-Arabic, you would have said: "Why was it not made clear to us so that we could understand it?"
