**Qur'an 41:44 (continued in the commentary):** ﴿Say, "It is, for those who believe, guidance and healing; and those who do not believe, in their ears is deafness, and it is blindness for them. Those are being called from a distant place."﴾

This is an answer implied by His saying ﴿Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 43], that is: nothing is said against you except the accusations of the Qur'an that were leveled at the messengers before you. So its answer is that this Reminder, or Book, is guidance and healing for those who believe. That is, those great qualities of the Qur'an were denied benefit to them by their disbelief, while the believers benefited from them, so it was for them guidance and healing. This refers to what He related of their statement ﴿Our hearts are in coverings from what you invite us to, and in our ears is deafness﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 5], so it is a binding upon them by a judgment on themselves.

The true meaning of healing is the removal of sickness, and it is used here metaphorically for insight into realities and the clearing away of confusion from the self, just as sickness disappears when healing is achieved. It is said: "His self was healed," when its distress departs. Qays ibn Zuhayr said:

*I have healed my soul from Hamal ibn Badr, and my sword from Hudhayfa has healed me.*

Similar to this is the saying: "His thirst was healed," or "His thirst was cooled," for disbelief is like a disease in the self, since it brings about punishment and drives toward evil deeds.

The clause ﴿And those who do not believe﴾ and so on is conjoined to the clause ﴿It is, for those who believe, guidance﴾, so it is a fresh beginning of speech, that is: as for those who do not believe, his verses do not penetrate their souls, because they are like one who has deafness in his ears so that he does not hear it. This is what preceded in the report of their saying ﴿And in our ears is deafness﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 5]. For this reason the meaning of the clause is connected to the states of the Qur'an in relation to the non-believing group, without the strain of supposing that the clause is a predicate about the Qur'an.

[Page 316]

It is also possible that the clause is a second predicate regarding the pronoun of the Reminder, that is, the Qur'an, so that it belongs to the content of the speech. The same applies to the clause ﴿and it is blindness for them﴾. The predication of the two terms *deafness* and *blindness* about it is an eloquent metaphor (*tashbīh balīgh*), and the point of comparison is the absence of benefit from it while its words are being heard. *Waqr* (deafness) is a disease, so its contrast with healing is an embellishment of antithesis (*ṭibāq*).

The pronoun in ﴿and it is blindness for them﴾ appears to refer to the Reminder or the Book, just as the pronoun in ﴿It is, for those who believe, guidance﴾ does. *'Ama* (blindness) is the absence of sight, and it is used here metaphorically for the opposite of being guided, so its contrast with guidance (*huda*) in these terms contains the embellishment of antithesis.

The attribution to the Qur'an, on this reading where the pronoun refers to it and it is blindness for them, is a metaphorical attribution (*isnād majāzī*), because their obstinacy in accepting it was the cause of their misguidance. So the Qur'an was the cause of a cause, like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿As for those in whose hearts is a disease, it adds to them uncleanness upon their uncleanness﴾ [al-Tawba: 125].

It is also possible that the pronoun in *wa-huwa* is the pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr al-sha'n*), to alert to the enormity of their misguidance.

The clause ﴿it is blindness upon them﴾ is the predicate of the pronoun of the matter, that is: and greater than deafness is that there is blindness upon them, that is, blindness upon their sight, like His saying ﴿and upon their sight is a covering﴾ [al-Baqara: 7].

The blindness was attached to their being "upon" themselves only because, since it is a metaphorical blindness, it is determined that its calamity falls upon their very selves entirely, not upon their sight alone. For the blindness of insight is more harmful than the blindness of sight, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿For indeed, it is not the eyes that are blind, but it is the hearts within the breasts that are blind﴾ [al-Hajj: 46].

And the clause ﴿Those are called from a distant place﴾ is a third predicate about those who do not believe. The speech is a figurative representation (*tamthil*, an illustrative comparison) of their turning away from the call when they hear it, by the state of one who is called from a distant place, where the caller's voice does not reach in such a case. This is like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And the likeness of those who disbelieve is that of one who shouts to what hears nothing but a call and a cry﴾ [al-Baqarah: 171], as has preceded in Surat al-Baqarah. The Arabs say to one who does not understand: "You are being called from a distant place."

The demonstrative (*ulā'ika*, "those") refers to those who do not believe, for the purpose of drawing attention to the fact that those indicated, after these attributes, are deserving of the wisdoms that will be mentioned after them on account of them. Compare ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5].

"From a distant place" is connected to (*yunādawna*, "are called"). If the calling is from a distant place, then the one called is necessarily in a distant place as well, as has preceded in the connection of "from the earth" to His saying ﴿Then when He calls you with a call from the earth﴾ [al-Rūm: 25], meaning He calls you from your place on the earth. Accordingly, "from a distant place" may be a stationary adverbial complement (*zarf mustaqarr*) in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun in (*yunādawna*). That is not feasible in His saying ﴿When He calls you with a call from the earth﴾ [al-Rūm: 25].

﴿And We had certainly given Moses the Book, but it was disputed over.﴾

This is an interjected clause (i'tiraḍ, a parenthetical sentence placed within the discourse) that consoles the Prophet (ﷺ) over the denial and disbelief of the polytheists regarding the Qur'an. He is not alone in this, for Moses was given the Torah (al-Tawrāh), and those he called disputed about it: some of them believed in it and some of them disbelieved.

The purpose is to draw a lesson from the disputes over the Torah, for they are more severe than the disputes over the Qur'an. The disputes over the Torah took two forms. The first was a dispute between those who believed in it and those who disbelieved. Pharaoh and his people disbelieved in the call of Moses, as did some of the Children of Israel, such as Qarun (Korah), and those who worshipped the calf during Moses' absence for private communion with God. The second was a dispute among those who believed in it, which led them to suspend some of its rulings, as God said: ﴿But they differed, so some of them believed and some of them disbelieved﴾ [al-Baqarah: 253]. Both kinds of dispute are a source of admonition and an example for the disputes of the polytheists over the Qur'an. This is why God protected the Qur'an from the like of it, when He said: ﴿And indeed, We are its guardians﴾. Thus the consolation to the Messenger (ﷺ) through this is more effective. This relates to His earlier words: ﴿Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you﴾, in the second of its two meanings, by mentioning one particular instance of that general statement, namely the greatest and most important one.

* * *

﴿Had it not been for a word that had already gone forth from your Lord, it would have been decided between them. And indeed they are in disquieting doubt about it.﴾

This relates to those among the Arabs who denied the Qur'an, because His saying ﴿it would have been decided between them﴾ implies that God deferred the judgment between them and the believers until a term determined by His wisdom. As for the people of Moses, judgment was passed between them by the annihilation of the people of Pharaoh, by the Assyrians' mutilation of the Jews after Moses, by the ruin of Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis), and by the eventual end of the kingdom of Israel. This statement belongs to completing the consolation to the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers regarding their impatience for victory.

The "word" is the word of respite until the Day of Resurrection with regard to some of the deniers, and respite until the Day of Badr with regard to those who were struck down at Badr.

Referring to God by the term "your Lord" (rabbika) reflects the tenderness and support that the meaning of "Lord" carries, and the honour conferred by attributing Him to the pronoun of the Messenger (ﷺ). Both of these strengthen the consolation.

You may also take the word "between" (bayn) as indicating another term that is implied, as an abbreviation by omission. The implied meaning would be: "between them and the believers," that is, by what would manifest the victory of the believers. It is common to say "between such-and-such and such-and-such," as God said: ﴿And a barrier was placed between them and what they desire﴾ [Saba': 54].

The meaning of "had already gone forth" (sabaqat) is that it had preceded in His knowledge, in accordance with the requirement of His wisdom and His will.

The "appointed term" (al-ajal al-musamma) is a general category that covers every term by which their punishment was deferred in God's knowledge. As for the pronoun in ﴿And indeed they are in disquieting doubt about it﴾, it refers specifically to the polytheists who doubted the resurrection and doubted that God would support His Messenger and the believers.

Al-rayb means doubt. The description of "doubt" (shakk) as "disquieting" (murīb) is a metaphorical attribution (isnād majāzī) for the sake of emphasis, by deriving for it an attribute from its own name, as in their saying: "laylun alyal" (a very dark night) and "shi'run sha'ir" (a poem that is truly poetic).

This is among the complements of consolation (al-tasliyah) and among the contexts in which the appointed term (al-ajal al-musamma) is mentioned. It carries the sense of a concluding statement (al-tadhyil), because *man* in both places indicates generality, whether it is regarded as conditional or as relative (mawsulah). The presence of the *fa'* in both places is either because they are two responses to the condition, or because the relative pronoun is treated like the conditional, which is a very common usage. The meaning is that the granting of respite is a warning (i'dhar) to them so that they may make up for their affairs.

A passage close to this verse has preceded in Surat al-Zumar, and a counterpart of ﴿وما رَبُّكَ بِظَلّامٍ لِلْعَبِيدِ﴾ in wording has preceded in Surat Ghafir.

The particle *'ala* indicates accountability and the bearing of burdens, just as the *lam* in His words *fa-li-nafsihi* indicates bestowal.

The address in *rabbika* is to the Messenger (ﷺ). In it is what has preceded of reinforcing his consolation, at His words just before, ﴿ولَوْلا كَلِمَةٌ سَبَقَتْ مِن رَبِّكَ﴾ [Fussilat: 45, "Had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord"], by the shift to the word "Lord" (al-Rabb) attached to the pronoun of the addressee.

The intended meaning of negating injustice (al-zulm) from God Exalted toward His servants is that He does not punish one who is not a criminal. For when God set down laws for people, and made clear the good deeds and the bad deeds, and promised and threatened, He made that a statute (qanun). Thus, departing from it to punish one who is not a criminal would be injustice, since injustice is the transgression upon the right of another within the laws received from the divine legislations or within the positive laws derived from wise minds.

As for the form *zallam*, which implies intensification in injustice, it is taken into account before the negation enters the sentence in which it occurs. As if it were said: "If God were to punish the evildoer, He would be a great wronger toward him, and He is not a wronger." This is the meaning of the statement of the scholars of rhetoric (ulama' al-ma'ani) that when negation is directed at a restricted statement, the negation may be a negation of the restriction, or the restriction may be a restriction within the negation; and they illustrated this with this verse. This is a subtle usage in eloquent speech, in negating an attribute formed in the intensive pattern, as part of the completion of God Exalted's justice, in that He made all degrees of injustice fall within the rank of severe injustice.

[p. 319]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 41, verse 47–48:

[Page 5]
﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour. No fruit comes out of its sheaths, nor does any female conceive or give birth except with His knowledge.﴾
When they were warned of resurrection and its Hour, they mocked and asked about its time, and this was something they repeatedly did. The Exalted said: ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when will it come to pass?﴾ [al-A'raf: 187]. When the mention of the proof of the revival of the dead came, and the mention of the atheism of the polytheists in its indication through their asking about it mockingly, the discourse moved to relating their question as a preparation for the answer concerning its outward form. The fronting of the prepositional phrase before its governing element (ilayhi, "to Him") serves to express restriction (al-hasr), meaning: the knowledge of the Hour is entrusted to God, not to me; it is thus a restriction of reversal (qasr qalb). He answered them by way of the wise method (al-uslub al-hakim), i.e., it is more fitting that you know that no one knows when the Hour will come, and that you believe in it and prepare for it. Similar to this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ when a man from among the Muslims asked him: "When is the Hour?" He said to him: "What have you prepared for it?", meaning that your preparation for it is more deserving of attention than asking about its time.

Al-radd (the return) is the sending back, and it is used here for entrusting the knowledge of that to God and disclaiming that the one asked has any knowledge of it; it is as if the question was brought to the Prophet ﷺ and he referred it back to God. In the authentic hadith of Musa with al-Khadir: "God rebuked Musa for not referring the knowledge to Him," and the Exalted said: ﴿And if they had referred it to the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa': 83], the verse.

The coordination of the clause ﴿and no fruit comes out of its sheaths﴾ and what follows it is a directive to turn the knowledge of the time of the Hour over to God by mentioning analogues that people do not know, and the knowledge of the Hour is not nearer to them than these, for these are observable matters, and no one knows the details of their state except God. That is, the lack of knowledge of the time of the Hour is no proof against the one who warned of it, because they said ﴿When is this promise, if you are truthful?﴾ [Yunus: 48], meaning: if you do not explain to us its time, then you are not truthful. This is the purpose of mentioning those analogues, and they are three things:

First: the knowledge of what the sheaths of palm trees bring forth of dates, regarding its measure, its quality, and whether it remains or falls. The pronoun in (akmamiha) refers to the fruits. Al-akmam is the plural of kimm (with a kasra on the kaf and a shadda on the mim), and it is the container of the fruit, which is the spathe that emerges from the palm tree containing the spadix of the fruit.

Second: the conception of the female, among humans and animals, and no one knows which one is fertilized and which is not except God.

Third: the time of the delivery of the fetuses; females are pregnant and heavy, and no one knows the time of their delivery by day and hour except God.

He turned away from repeating the particle (ma) a second time, to avoid mentioning one particle three times; because the equality of these three negated matters in the knowledge of God the Exalted, and in that the times of their occurrence are the same with respect to the present and the future, closes off for us the door of the claim of the majority that there is a difference between (ma) and (la) in restricting the present tense to present time with (ma) and restricting it to the future with (la). It supports the rebuttal of Ibn Malik against them, for the truth lies with the view of Ibn Malik:

And the particle (min) after the two words (ma) in both positions serves to express the generality of the negation, and it is called a superfluous particle.

The ba' in (bi-'ilmihi) is for accompaniment (mulabasa). Its parallel was mentioned in Surat Fatir.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Hafs from 'Asim read (thamarat) in the plural. The rest read (thamarat) in the singular, the singular of thamarat.

* * *

[Page 7]
﴿On the day He calls out to them, "Where are My partners?" they will say, "We declare to You that none of us bears witness." And what they used to invoke before has strayed from them, and they will realize they have no way of escape.﴾
This is a coordination with the sentence before it, for when His saying ﴿To Him is referred the knowledge of the Hour﴾ included the refutation of their doubt that the absence of a statement of its time indicates the negation of its occurrence, and this was followed by analogues to the time of the Hour from what is continually happening in the world, the discourse returned to the matter of the Hour in the manner of warning, requiring the affirmation of the occurrence of the Hour by mentioning some of what they will encounter on its day.

(Yawma) is connected to an omitted element that is commonly omitted in the Qur'an; its estimate is: "Remember the day He calls out to them."

The pronoun in (yunadi) refers to your Lord in His saying ﴿Your Lord does not wrong the servants﴾ [Fussilat: 46], and the calling is a metonymy for open address, as in His saying ﴿They will call out to them, "Were we not with you?"﴾ [al-Hadid: 14]. The discussion of calling was already presented at His saying ﴿Our Lord, we heard a caller calling to faith﴾ [Al 'Imran: 193] in Al 'Imran, and at His saying ﴿And they will be called out: "This is the Paradise you have been made to inherit"﴾ [al-A'raf: 43] in Surat al-A'raf.

The clause (Where are My partners?) may be a quotation of an omitted saying, as was made explicit in another verse: ﴿On the day He calls out to them and says, "Where are My partners whom you used to claim?"﴾ [al-Qasas: 62] and ﴿On the day He calls out to them and says, "What answer did you give the messengers?"﴾ [al-Qasas: 65]. The omission of the saying is not rare.

It may also be that it explains what is implied by (yunadihim) of the meaning of an open speech. The clause (﴿They said, "We declare to You"﴾) comes unconnected by a conjunction because it follows the manner of relating dialogues, as was already mentioned at His saying: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels...﴾ up to His saying: ﴿what you do not know﴾.

(﴿Adhannaka﴾): we informed you and made you know. The root of this verb derives from the solid noun udhun (with a damma on the hamza and a sukun on the dhal). The Exalted said: ﴿So I have announced to you on equal terms﴾ [al-Anbiya': 109], and al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:

*Asma' has announced to us her separation*

The past form in (﴿adhannaka﴾) is performative (insha'), so it carries the meaning of the present, like: "I sell" and "I divorce," meaning: we declare to you and acknowledge that none of us bears witness.

The shahid may mean "the one who observes," i.e., the one who sees, meaning: none of us sees those whom we used to invoke as Your partners now, that is, we do not see any one of the idols we used to worship. Then the clause (﴿And what they used to invoke before has strayed from them﴾) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and the waw is the waw of circumstance. It may also be that the shahid means "the witness," meaning: none of us testifies that they are Your partners, and then this is an acknowledgment of their lying in what has passed, and the clause (﴿And [it] has strayed from them﴾) is coordinated with the clause (﴿They said, "We declare to You"﴾), meaning: they said that and did not find any one of their idols.

The verb (﴿adhannaka﴾) is suspended from operating because a negation follows it.

(Dalla): its literal meaning is "it was absent from them," meaning they did not find what they used to invoke before in the world. The Exalted said: ﴿Rather, they have gone astray from them﴾. So what is meant here is the absence of their idols from them and their non-existence in that presence, regardless of whether they are cast into Hell or remained in the worldly realm at its annihilation.

Since they did not find what they used to claim, they knew that they have no escape, meaning no refuge for them from the punishment whose preparation they witnessed. Thus the verb "thought" (zannu) here means certainty.

Al-mahis is either a noun of place or a masdar mimi from: haṣa yahis, when he fled, meaning: they have no escape from the Fire.

[p. 9]

﴿Man never tires of asking for good, but if evil touches him, he is despairing and hopeless.﴾ ﴿And if We let him taste mercy from Us after some hardship has touched him, he will surely say, "This is mine, and I do not think the Hour will ever come. And if I am returned to my Lord, I will have the best with Him."﴾ [Fussilat: 50].

This is an interjection (i'tiraḍ) between the parts of the warning. The meaning is: "and they know that they have no escape." They used to deny the Hour whenever blessings reached them. So the sentence "Man never tires of asking for good" up to His words "despairing and hopeless" is a preparation for the sentence "And if We let him taste mercy from Us," and so on.

The placement of these verses after His words "And on the Day He calls to them, 'Where are My partners?' They will say, 'We have declared to You that none of us bears witness'" [Fussilat: 47] requires a connection in the arrangement of the discourse that calls for this interjection. That connection indicates that the man described as one who never tires of asking for good, and what is coordinated with him, belongs to the category of people whose stories were mentioned before this verse, namely the polytheists. Then either the intended meaning is a group of the human species, so that the definite article in "al-insān" is the generic definite (ta'rif al-jins), but its generality is customary by context, and this is what is exemplified in the science of meanings (ʿilm al-maʿānī, the science of rhetorical meanings) by your saying, "The prince gathered the goldsmiths." Or the intended meaning is a specific individual of this category, and then the definite article is the definite of reference (ta'rif al-ʿahd). Just as the report about "man" that he says, "And I do not think the Hour will ever come" [Fussilat: 50] is clear that the one spoken of is a polytheist, whether specific or general in customary generality. It has been said that the intended meaning of "man" is all the polytheists. It has been said that a specific polytheist is intended. It has been said he is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, and it has been said he is 'Utba ibn Rabi'a. Whichever it is, the report is about a disbelieving human being.

The eloquent expression implies that attaching these reports to a category of polytheists, or to a specific polytheist, under the title "man," indicates that the human nature has a strong effect on the character from which this belief arises, except for those whom God protects with the restraint of faith. The root of this character is a disposition fixed in the human soul: turning toward seeking what is agreeable and beneficial, and forgetting what may befall him of what is painful and harmful. Thereby he becomes at ease with good when it comes to him, so he increases his striving to obtain it, and regards it as if it were inherently his own. So he does not reflect on the Giver until he thanks Him and asks Him for more, in humility,

[p. 10]

and he forgets what may befall him of harm, so he does not prepare to avert it from himself by asking the free, chooser Agent to repel it from him and protect him from it.

As for the statement "Man never tires of asking for good," its meaning is that he is never content. So "tiredness" (sa'āma), which is weariness, is applied metaphorically to contentment and satisfaction, by likening the continuous pursuit of good by man to a perpetual labor which its worker usually grows tired of. So the negation of tiredness from him is a symbolic indication of the metaphor (isti'āra, metaphor).

In a hadith: "If the son of Adam had two valleys of gold, he would love to have a third. And if he had three, he would love to have a fourth. And nothing fills the eye of the son of Adam except dust." And God the Exalted said: "And indeed he is intensely fond of wealth" [al-'Adiyat: 8].

As for "du'ā'" (asking, supplication): its origin is request by speech, and here it is a figurative use for request in general. So its annexation to "good" is an annexation of the verbal noun to what has the sense of its object, i.e., "asking for good" or "seeking good."

It is also possible that "du'ā'" is a implicit metaphor (isti'āra makniyya), in which good is likened to a rational being whom the person asks to turn toward him. Then the annexation of "du'ā'" is an annexation of the verbal noun to its object.

As for "man is despairing and hopeless if evil touches him," that is from the character of little patience of man with what wearies him and burdens him, so he becomes distressed if evil reaches him, and he does not balance it against the good he had. He says: "If evil touches me for a while, good has come to me for a long time. So it is right that I bear what has befallen me, just as I enjoyed what good I had." Then he does not wait for the time when the evil lifts from him, and he forgets turning to ask God to remove the harm from him. Rather, he despairs and becomes hopeless out of anger and arrogance, and he does not await the return of good upon him, with the visible trace of despair in him as humble sorrow.

Despair (al-yaʾs) is an inner act: believing that what is despaired of will not occur.

Hopelessness (al-qunūṭ) is an emotional state that brings one near to the effect of despair, and it is breaking down and shrinking. Here it is not stated that he is one who supplicates to God, as in His later words: "And when evil touches him, he is one of lengthy supplication" [Fussilat: 51], because the intended ones are the people of association (shirk), and they only turn to their idols.

[p. 11]

The Sharia's upbringing of the community has come upon condemning hopelessness. God the Exalted said, relating about Abraham: "He said, 'And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except the astray?'" [al-Hijr: 56]. And in a hadith: "Waiting for relief after hardship is worship."

So the verse describes two blameworthy characters: one is the character of arrogance (baṭar) toward blessing and heedlessness of thanking God for it; the second is despair of the return of blessing when it is lost.

In the arrangement of the verse there are subtle points of eloquence:

The first: the expression of the continuance of seeking blessing by the absence of tiredness, as you have known.

The second: the expression of love of good by "asking for good."

The third: the expression of the attribution of harm by "touch" (mass), which is the weakest perception of affliction. God the Exalted said: "No evil shall touch them" [Al 'Imran: 174 / cf. al-Zumar].

The fourth: the conjoining of the condition "touching evil" with "in" (in), which by its nature enters upon what is rare in occurrence, because the striking of evil upon man is rare compared with what he is overwhelmed by of blessings.

The fifth: the form of intensification in "yaʾūs" (very despairing).

The sixth: the following of "yaʾūs" with "qanūṭ," which is passing from the perception of despair to the outward appearance of the body by shrinking, and this is from the intensity of his despair. So two intensifications were achieved in expressing his despair: that it is a belief in his heart, and an emotion visible in his bodily aspect.

So the polytheist has this character rooted in him, and it grows with the passage of time. The believer, the upbringing of faith continually restrains him from this character until it departs from him or nearly so.

Then the verse explains another character in man: that when his distress departs and blessing returns to him, he forgets the hardship he had been in, and he does not reflect on God's gentleness toward him, so he becomes arrogant about the blessing and says: "I have regained my goods by my cunning and planning, and this good is my right, which I have obtained." Then if he is of the people of association (shirk), who are the ones spoken of, you see him, when he hears the Prophet ﷺ warning of the Hour, or when the thought of the end of this life crosses his mind, he says to the one who calls him to work for the Day of

[p. 12]

Reckoning, or says to himself: "And I do not think the Hour will ever come" [Fussilat: 50]. "And if I suppose the Hour comes on a weak probability, I will surely find with God the treatment of the best, because I am one of the people of wealth and ease in this world, so likewise I shall be on the Day of Resurrection." This is from their evil belief, that they think the conditions of this world will accompany them in the Hereafter, as God the Exalted related about al-'As ibn Wa'il when Khabbab ibn al-Aratt demanded from him money he owed for the work of making a sword. He said to him: "Not until you disbelieve in Muhammad?" Khabbab said: "I will not disbelieve in Muhammad until God causes you to die and resurrects you." He said: "Am I, when dead, to be resurrected?" He said: "Yes." He said: "If God resurrects me, I will surely have wealth and children, and I will pay you then." So God sent down: "Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our verses and said, 'I will surely be given wealth and children'?" [Maryam: 77] and the verses in Surah Maryam.

Perhaps His words "And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely have the best with Him" [Fussilat: 50] are said by way of mockery, as in the statement of al-'As ibn Wa'il.

The mention of the denial of resurrection here is an embedding (idmāj) within the mention of the conditions of the polytheist human being within the general conditions of humanity.

In relating His words "And if I am returned" [Fussilat: 50], the conditional particle "in" was used, which usually occurs with a condition whose occurrence is doubtful, because he made his return to God a supposed matter of weak probability.

As for the entry of the lam of preparation for the oath (al-lām al-muwaṭṭi'a lil-qasam) upon it, the place of confirmation by oath is the occurrence of the answer if the condition occurs.

Likewise, the emphasis with "inna" and the lam of initiation (lām al-ibtidā') has as its place the answer of the condition. Likewise, the fronting of "lī" (for me) and "ʿindahu" (with Him) before the subject of "inna" is to strengthen the consequence of the answer upon the condition.

"Al-ḥusnā" is an attribute of an omitted noun, i.e., "the good state" or "the good treatment." The more apparent view is that "al-ḥusnā" became a noun for abundant goodness, taken from the superlative form.

Know that the human being varies individually in this character attributed to him here, according to the variation of individuals in delusion. Since most people at that time were polytheists, this character was widespread among them, as the religion of association required it.

[p. 13]

There is no reference in the verse to those among the Muslims at that time, because they were rare. Moreover, a Muslim may have some trace of this character, and some signs of it may appear in him, but his faith turns him away from it to the degree of his faith's strength. It is known that it does not reach the point where he says, "And I do not think the Hour will ever come" [Fussilat: 50]. But the deeds of some Muslims may take the form of the deeds of one who does not think the Hour will come, like those who commit evil deeds and then say, "God is Forgiving and Merciful," and "God is free of need from our punishment." And when the Day of Recompense is mentioned to them, they say, "There is nothing but good," and similar things. So God in this verse made a reproach for the polytheists and an admonition for the believers, as a rebuke to the first and a rescue for the latter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 41, verse 50:

﴿So We will surely inform those who disbelieved of what they did, and We will surely make them taste a severe torment.﴾

This is a consequence (*tafri'*) of the statement ﴿And on the day He calls to them, "Where are My partners?"﴾ [Fussilat: 47] and what is connected to it. That is: "We will surely make them know publicly what they did, so that they know by it that nothing of what they did is hidden from Us, and as a rebuke to them."

The phrase "those who disbelieved" is an explicit noun in a place where a pronoun would be expected (*iẓhar fi maqam al-iḍmar*). The apparent construction would be "and We will surely inform them of what they did," but he shifted to the relative pronoun and its clause (*al-mawsul wa silatuhu*), because the clause indicates the reason that makes them deserve the tasting and the torment for what they did. His saying ﴿and We will surely make them taste a severe torment﴾ is the real purpose of the consequence.

*Al-ghalīẓ* (the severe) literally means the hard, the firm. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So it became firm and stood upon its stalk﴾ [al-Fath: 29]. Here it is used metaphorically for what is strong within its kind, that is, a torment of intense pain and punishment. Similarly it is used metaphorically for harshness in dealing, as in His saying: "and be harsh with them" and His saying: ﴿and let them find in you harshness﴾ [al-Tawbah: 123].

*Al-idhāqa* (causing to taste) is a metaphor for mere reaching of the senses, so as to make them hope that it is a light touch, like the touch of taste by the tongue. This is a first abstraction (*tajrīd*) of the metaphor, just as describing it as "severe" is a second abstraction. From this results a beginning that raises hope and an end that brings despair.

[Page 14]

﴿And when We bestow favour upon man, he turns away and withdraws with his side; and when evil touches him, he is one of lengthy supplication.﴾

This is a description and a reminder of another kind of the transgression of the human soul. It is not specific to the people of polytheism but is spread among all people to varying degrees, except those whom God protects. It describes the impulsiveness of the human soul and its lack of steadfastness. When prosperity (al-sarra'*) reaches it, it becomes arrogant and haughty, forgets the thanks of its Lord, forgetting either slightly or greatly, and becomes preoccupied with its pleasures. When adversity (al-darra'*) reaches it, it does not endure patiently, becomes distressed, and turns to its Lord, persistently asking for the removal of the adversity quickly. In mentioning this kind there is an allusion to God's action and decree concerning the two states, prosperity and adversity.

It is a criticism of human conduct in both states and an expression of wonder at his condition. The point of criticism and wonder in his turning away and withdrawing his side is clear. As for the point of censure and wonder in his being "one of lengthy supplication" when evil touches him, it lies in the fact that he remembers turning to the supplication of his Lord only when evil touches him, whereas the proper course would be not to be heedless of this in a state of blessing, so that he would ask for its continuation, give thanks to his Lord for it, and hope that his thanks are accepted, because that state deserves more attention than the state of being touched by harm.

As for what preceded in His words ﴿Man does not tire of asking for good﴾ [Fussilat: 49] up to His words ﴿surely the best (reward)﴾ [Fussilat: 50], it is a description of another, more severe kind, specific to the people of polytheism, because of what occurred in his words: "And I do not think the Hour will be established." Therefore His words "And when We bestow favour upon man, he turns away and withdraws his side, etc." are not a repetition of His words "Man does not tire of asking" [Fussilat: 49] and what follows.

This variety in describing the states of man with his Lord is what led to the partial repetition contained in the words "And when We bestow favour" in relation to what was mentioned in the preceding kind, to add emphasis to it, and to indicate the difference between the two states in terms of polytheism and its absence, while both share the same source in the human natural disposition, and in terms of what God has decreed for man.

Al-i'rad (turning away) is turning away from something. It is used here metaphorically for heedlessness of the thanks due to the Benefactor, or for deliberately abandoning thanks.

[Page 15]

The object of the verb a'rada (he turned away) is omitted, its meaning being indicated by the context. The implied meaning is: he turned away from Our call.

Al-nay' (distancing) is remoteness. It is used here metaphorically for not reflecting on the Benefactor, so his not being occupied with that is likened to distance.

Al-janib (side) of a person is the extremity of his body from one of the two directions that are not opposite his face or his back. It is also called al-shiqq and al-'itf (with a kasra on the ʿayn). The bā' is for transitivity. The meaning is: he made his side distant, a metonymy for distancing himself, i.e., he turned away, not turning his face toward the thing from which he himself has moved away.

The meaning of "evil touched him" is: an evil afflicted him through an ordinary cause. He shifted from attributing the affliction of evil to God, teaching courtesy toward God, as Abraham said: "[He] who created me, and it is He who guides me," etc. Then he said: "And when I am ill, it is He who heals me," and he did not say "and when He makes me ill." In this there is a secret: blessings and good are subjected to man in the original constitution of his creation, so they are the predominant ones over him, because they are manifestations of the law (namus) of the survival of the species. As for evils and harms, most of them come to man through his own bad conduct and his exposure to what the revealed laws and inspired sages have warned him against, so man rarely falls into them except through his own action and boldness.

Al-du'a' (supplication) is the supplication to God for the removal of evil from him. Describing it as "broad" ('arid) is a metaphor, because al-'ard (with a fatha on the ʿayn) is the opposite of length, and a broad thing is one whose extent in width is great. So he likened the repeated, insistent supplication to a broad garment or a broad place.

He turned away from saying "fa-dāʿin" (one who supplicates) to "dhū duʿāʾ" (one possessed of supplication), because of what the word dhū indicates of the constant attachment of supplication to him and his being possessed by it.

Supplication to God is one of the habits of the believers, who differ in frequency and infrequency of it according to the differing degrees of their awareness of the divine realities.

The turning of the polytheists to God in supplication consists of utterances that flow on their tongues, which they inherited from ancient customs from the times when they followed the ḥanīfiyya (the primordial monotheism) before the worship of idols entered them and took root among them. So when they call upon God they are heedless of the contradiction between their utterances and the beliefs of their polytheism.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 41, verse 52:

Page 16
﴿Say: "Have you considered? If it is from Allah, and you disbelieve in it, who is more astray than those who are in extreme opposition?"﴾ This is a fresh resumption (istinaf ibtida'i) connected to His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the Reminder when it comes to them [are in error]﴾ [Fussilat: 41], up to His saying: ﴿...indeed, they are in disquieting doubt concerning it﴾. This is a transition to disputation concerning the matter of the Qur'an, by which He returns to the original purpose of this surah, which is clarifying the truth of the Qur'an, its veracity, and the veracity of the one who brought it.

This is an invitation to employ reflection on the proofs of the Qur'an's truthfulness, such as its inimitability (i'jaz), its coherence, its parts confirming one another, and its being a confirmation of the Books before it, and those Books being a confirmation of it.

The meaning: what you hold of denying the truthfulness of the Qur'an does not proceed from reflection and scrutiny that produces certainty. Rather, you have gambled on it before reflecting. Had you considered, reflection could have yielded that it is from Allah, or that it is not from Him. If the first possibility is assumed, then you have thrown yourselves into a severe opposition. This is speech that is fair (min al-kalam al-munsif), and He restricted himself to mentioning the state that fits their attributes, by allusion (ta'ridan) that this is the prevailing side in this matter. It is as if He says: just as you have judged that it is not from Allah, and that this is not known by necessity, so too is its being from Allah; so come, let us reflect upon the proofs. When they denied that it could be from Allah and barred themselves and their common people from listening to it and pondering it, they gave free rein to the desires of their souls and neglected taking precaution for themselves by pondering it, so that they would be certain of their position regarding it. Yet if they pondered it, they would not delay in knowing its truthfulness. So Allah summoned them to reflection by way of supposing that it may be from Allah, for if that is permitted, and they have disbelieved in it without reflection, they have passed sentence against themselves with severe error; and if they are so, then the words of threat have become due against them.

The conditional (in) ordinarily enters upon a condition whose fulfilment is doubtful, so its use here is loosening the reins with them in order to draw down the bird of their denial, until they turn to reflection upon the proofs of the Qur'an's truthfulness.

It seems that the intended addressees of this address and raising of doubt first are the common masses of the polytheists who did not reflect on the indication of the Qur'an, or did not prolong their reflection and did not reach the limit of inference.

As for their leaders and elders and those of them with intellect, they know that it is from Allah, but love of leadership overcame them, while they differ in this knowledge, to the extent that some of them reach a state close to that of the common masses. But the Qur'an cast this doubt among them by way of prevailing and taking into account the differing ranks of the obstinate, and by accommodating their claim that they were not guided through reflection, according to their saying: ﴿Our hearts are in coverings against what you call us to, and in our ears is deafness﴾ [Fussilat: 5].

The "then" (thumma) in His saying (﴿thumma kafartum﴾) denotes graded sequence (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), because disbelief in what is from Allah is a matter more grave than the Qur'an being from Allah.

The first "who" (man) is interrogative, used in the sense of negation: meaning, no one is more astray than those who are in extreme opposition, once the condition is realised.

The second "who" (man) is relative (mawsula), and its referent is the addressees in His saying (﴿kafartum bihi﴾). He turned away from the pronoun to the form of the relative because the relative clause allows the reason that they are the most astray of the astray by being intensely opposed, and that is a metonymy for their being the people most deserving of punishment, since it is known that error is a cause of loss.

Al-shiqaq (opposition) means disobedience, and what is meant is disobedience to the command of Allah, since it is evident that the Qur'an is from Him on this supposition among us.

Al-ba'id (far) means the one of wide distance, and it is used here metaphorically for intensifying its kind. The suitability of this metaphor for error is that error is originally the failure to reach the path, and distance suits opposition, because the one who splits off has departed from that from which he split, so his separation is far, with no hope of return to closeness. This was mentioned before in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who differ concerning the Book are in far opposition﴾ [al-Baqarah: 176] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The verb (ara'aytum) is suspended from operating (mu'allaq 'an al-'amal) because of the interrogative occurring after it, and the seeing (ru'ya) is cognitive ('ilmiyya).

[p. 18]

﴿We shall show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves, until it becomes clear to them that it is the Truth﴾ [41:53].

After Allah commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to say to the polytheists what would frighten them about the consequences of their opposition, on the supposition that the Qur'an is from Allah while they have disbelieved in it, and so on through what was established just before, He promised His Messenger (ﷺ), as consolation and good tidings, that Allah would overwhelm the polytheists with a portion of His signs by which they would realize that the Qur'an is truly from Allah, so that they would have no choice but to believe in it. That is, the Qur'an is a clear truth that does not depend on their acknowledgment of its truth. The evidences of its truth will appear in the distant horizons far from them and in their own tribe and selves, so the evidences will converge to show that it is the Truth, and they will find no way to deny them. What is meant is that they will believe in it on that day together with all who believe in it.

In this promise to the Messenger (ﷺ) there is an indirect address to them, as they hear it, in the manner of: "Hear, O neighbour" (fa-asmaʿi ya jarah).

The position of this sentence, both explicitly and implicitly, relative to the sentence before it is that of a reason (ta'līl) for the command to the Messenger (ﷺ) to say to them what he was commanded to say. The reasoning returns to placing them before their own doubt about their position, in order to discredit the Qur'an.

It has passed over what follows from the appearance of the signs in the horizons and in themselves, which make clear that the Qur'an is true, because what precedes it, namely His saying: ﴿Tell me, if it is from Allah and you disbelieve in it, who is more astray than one who is in extreme opposition?﴾ [41:52], points to its implied supposition. That is: they have no choice but to believe that it is true. Whoever among them was doubting before, out of lack of insight, will gain knowledge afterward. Whoever disbelieves only out of obstinacy and a desire to preserve leadership will have his slander exposed and his foolishness laid bare by his neighbours. Both have lost, by delaying faith, a great good of the Hereafter, through what they wasted of provision of reward during their period of disbelief, and a good of this world, through what they missed of the honour of precedence in faith and emigration, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest; those are greater in rank than those who spent and fought afterward. But to each Allah has promised the best﴾ [57:10].

In this verse there is a facet of inimitability (iʿjāz) through reporting the unseen, since it informed of the promise of victory for him and his religion. That was accomplished through what Allah facilitated for His Messenger (ﷺ) and his successors after him, in the horizons of the world, east and west in general, and in the heartland of the Arabs in particular, of conquests and their endurance and the impression left by them on the nations, the like of which was not facilitated for any kings of the earth, the Caesars and the Chosroes, despite the paucity of the Muslims if their number is compared with the number of the nations whose horizons they opened by spreading the call of Islam across the lands. History bears witness that what was made possible for the Muslims of wondrous expansion and dominion over the nations is an extraordinary matter beyond custom. Thus it becomes clear that the religion of Islam is the Truth, and that whenever the Muslims held fast to the bonds of Islam they encountered from Allah's help a wondrous matter, as attested by both the earlier and the later. Allah challenged them with this in His saying: ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its edges? And Allah judges; there is no repeller of His judgment, and He is swift in reckoning﴾ [13:41]. Then He said: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "You are not a messenger." Say, "Sufficient is Allah as witness between me and you"﴾ [13:43].

The manifestation of Islam did not stop at the conquest of kingdoms and dominance over kings and tyrants, but went beyond that to penetrate the souls of diverse nations. They adopted it as a religion, its manners and ethics spread among them, and it reformed their customs and their diverse civil systems that they had been following. They came to a uniform and harmonious civilization, and they produced a new civilization free from crudeness. The language of the Qur'an spread, and nations of different tongues addressed one another with it and came to know one another through it. Among them arose outstanding scholars of religion, scholars of the Arabic language, leaders of Arabic literature, mighty poets, and famous kings who spread Islam across the realms through their conquests.

Therefore, by "the signs" in His saying ﴿We shall show them Our signs﴾ is meant what includes evidences outside the Qur'an and what includes the verses of the Qur'an, for among the meanings of seeing them is seeing what confirms their reports and makes clear their advice to them, by calling them to the good of this world and the Hereafter.

"Al-āfāq" (the horizons) is the plural of ufq, which is also read with its first letter sukūn: it is the region of the earth distinguished from others, and the region of the dome of the sky.

The conjunction ﴿and within themselves﴾ may be a conjunction of the specific upon the general (ʿaṭf al-khāṣṣ ʿalā al-ʿāmm), meaning "and in the horizon of themselves", that is, Mecca and what is around it, with an elided modifier.

[p. 20]

The better view is that ﴿in the horizons﴾ is on its general sense, which includes their own horizon, and the meaning of ﴿and within themselves﴾ is that they see the signs of his truthfulness in conditions that afflict their selves, that is, their persons, such as the famine for which the Prophet (ﷺ) invoked against them, and concerning which the Exalted's saying was revealed: ﴿So watch for the day when the sky will bring a visible smoke﴾ [44:10]; and like what they witnessed of the downfall of their chiefs on the day of Badr, which the Qur'an had threatened them with in His saying: ﴿On the day We strike the greatest blow; indeed, We will take retribution﴾ [44:16]. And what lesson is greater than the killing of Abu Jahl on the day of Badr, when two youths of the Ansar struck him and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd took charge of slaughtering him, and all three of them were among the weak Muslims, while he was that tyrant and stubborn one. He said at his death: "If only a farmer had killed me." And from the killing of Ubayy ibn Khalaf that day at the hand of the Prophet (ﷺ), who had said to him in Mecca: "I will kill you," and he was certain of it. He said to his wife on the night he set out for Badr: "By Allah, if he but spat on me, he would kill me."

* * *

﴿Is it not sufficient concerning your Lord that He is witness over all things?﴾ [41:53]

This is a conjunction upon the informing of the Messenger (ﷺ) about what will appear of the proofs of the truth of the Qur'an and the truth of the Messenger (ﷺ), as an increase in firming up the Messenger and expanding his breast, by the fact that Allah undertook for him the manifestation of His religion and the clarity of his truthfulness throughout all regions of the earth and in the land of his people. It is in the manner of an interrogative of affirmation (istifhām taqrīrī), to confirm the Prophet's (ﷺ) certainty of his Lord's guarantee, so that it was among matters to be affirmed upon him, as a metonymy for certainty about it. The interrogative is therefore affirmative.

The meaning: the testimony of your Lord to your truthfulness suffices you, so do not turn toward their denial. This is in the manner of His saying: ﴿But Allah bears witness to what He has sent down to you; He sent it down with His knowledge, and the angels bear witness, and sufficient is Allah as witness﴾ [4:166], and His saying: ﴿And We sent you to mankind as a messenger, and sufficient is Allah as witness﴾ [4:79]. This is one view on the placement of this verse.

There is another view: that its context is that of instructing the Prophet (ﷺ) to call upon Allah as witness that the Qur'an is from Allah, so its position is that of an oath by calling Allah to witness. This is a severe oath, in which there is the sense of attributing what is sworn to as something Allah bears witness to. The interrogative is then denunciatory, a denunciation of not being content with an oath by Allah, a metonymy for the oath, and for their not affirming the oath, so the meaning of the verse is close to the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Sufficient is Allah as witness between me and you"﴾ [29:52] and His saying: ﴿Say, "Sufficient is Allah between me and you as witness"﴾ [29:52].

The meaning of the verse is not a denunciation of the polytheists for not being content with Allah's witness to the truth of the Qur'an or to the truth of the Messenger (ﷺ), because they do not acknowledge that Allah bore witness to that, so the denunciation does not clearly apply to them.

The statements of the exegetes on the interpretation of this verse indicate hesitation in drawing out its meaning from its wording.

His saying ﴿that He is witness over all things﴾ is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimāl, i.e., a second noun that includes the first) from "your Lord". The estimated sense is: "Does your Lord not suffice them by His knowledge of everything?" That is, He will fulfil what He promised you of overpowering them with the proof that indicates your truthfulness. Or: whoever calls Him as witness has spoken truly, because Allah does not confirm someone who lies about Him, so he will not persist before He seizes him.

In the verse, on the second of the two aspects of His saying ﴿Is it not sufficient concerning your Lord that He is witness over all things?﴾, there is an allusion that Allah does not confirm one who lies against Him, so his affair is not completed. This is the meaning of the saying of the imams of the principles of religion (uṣūl al-dīn, i.e., theology): the indication of a miracle (muʿjiza) as proof of truthfulness is that Allah's altering of custom in response to the challenge of the Messenger (ﷺ) stands in place of His saying: "My servant has spoken truly concerning what he reported from Me."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 41, verse 54:

﴿Surely they are in doubt about the meeting with their Lord. Surely He encompasses all things.﴾

These two closing statements (tadhyilan) of the surah are summations (fadhlakatan), and both are introduced with the particle of alerting (harf al-tanbih), out of concern for what they contain.

As for the first closing statement, it gathers what the surah contained of the states of the obstinate polytheists, since their states mentioned therein arise from their denial of resurrection (al-ba'th). Thus they were secure from reflecting on what comes after this life, so their efforts were confined to managing the worldly life, and they devoted themselves to whatever would bring them benefit in it.

The pronoun in (innahum) refers back to them, just as the plural pronoun in (sanurihim) referred to them.

As for the second closing statement, it comprehends everything the surah contained of refutation of their statements and correction of their deviance, because all of that is among the effects of God's knowledge of the unseen and the witnessed.

The emphasis of the two sentences with the particle of emphasis (harf al-ta'kid), although the addressee does not doubt it, is for the purpose of giving them concern and calling for reflection in order to extract the meanings and details they contain.

Al-miryah, with a kasra on the mim, is the more well-known form and the one on which the mutawatir recitations agree; it is also said with a damma on the mim (al-muriyah)? No: the form with a kasra on the mim is the one agreed upon by the mutawatir recitations, and it is a dialect form like khifyah and khufyah. Al-miryah means doubt (al-shakk). The particle of place (harf al-zarfiyyah) is used metaphorically for the firm settling of doubt in them, as if they were enclosed within it. The (min) is for origin (ibtida'iyyah), and doubt-verbs are construed with it to the matter doubted, by treating the object of the verb as the source of the action, likening the object to the origin, as if doubt came from a place which is the very thing doubted.

In attaching it to the thing itself, although doubt properly relates to judgments, there is an intensification in the manner of ascribing affairs to entities while meaning their attributes. So the estimate of "in doubt about the meeting with their Lord" is: in doubt about the occurrence of the meeting with their Lord and its non-occurrence, like His saying: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23], meaning, in doubt about whether it is sent down.

Doubt was applied to their firm judgment of the non-occurrence of resurrection, because their firm judgment lacks the proof that would require it. So applying the term doubt to it was a veiled reproach, that it would have been better for them to be in doubt at least.

Describing God as "the Encompassing" (al-Muhit) is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), because what encompasses everything is His knowledge; so encompassing was ascribed to the name of God, since "the Encompassing" is one of His attributes, namely knowledge.

With these two closing statements he signalled the conclusion of the speech, and so this was of the excellence of the conclusion.
